Makkah Defence Alliance military chiefs vow to 'immediately' translate commitments into effective military cooperation: ISPR
items.description: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have expressed a shared determination to “immediately translate” their commitments under the Makkah Defence Alliance into effective military cooperation, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Saturday. The meeting took place against the backdrop of the kingdom being dragged into fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government, with the former declaring a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. In recent weeks, Houthis have also carried out attacks in Saudi Arabia. Earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) had shared that the three countries were mulling a military chiefs’ meeting to consider ways to assist Riyadh under the Makkah pact. The commitment was made at a meeting of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir and the chiefs of general staff of Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, held in Riyadh on Friday. According to the ISPR, the participants discussed ways to advance cooperation among their armed forces, including enhanced intelligence sharing, military coordination and integration of capabilities. The measures, it said, would help strengthen deterrence and collective defence. The military chiefs also reviewed the security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia, and strongly “resented” attacks targeting the holy city of Makkah as well as civilian and economic infrastructure. They appreciated the vigilance and professionalism of the Saudi armed forces in ensuring the safety of the people and security of the Kingdom, according to the ISPR. The participants also commended the longstanding relations and mutual trust between the three countries and their armed forces. The ISPR said the Riyadh meeting reflected the strength of the defence partnership among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye and their shared determination to implement the commitments made under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The participants further affirmed their commitment to collective defence, demonstrating, according to the ISPR, the resolve of the three countries to defend the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Saudi Arabia. items.title: Bab el-Mandeb : le contrôle houthiste fait peser un risque sur les approvisionnements européens en diesel et kérosène
items.description: Les 10 et 11 septembre, les Houthis se sont emparés du port de Mocha et ont progressé vers l’île de Perim, prenant de facto le contrôle du détroit de Bab el-Mandeb. Alors que le détroit d’Ormuz fait toujours l’objet d’un blocus imposé par l’Iran, ce passage constitue l’une des rares voies permettant encore de contourner partiellement les perturbations dans le Golfe. Le pétrole brut du Golfe ne représentait qu’environ 7 % des importations européennes en 2025. Selon une note du Global Trade Policy Observatory, le continent est toutefois particulièrement vulnérable pour ses approvisionnements en produits raffinés, notamment le diesel et le kérosène Europe's other oil problem : Diesel, Jet Fuel, and the chokepoints that matter , GTPO, 24 septembre 2026.'> 1 . Avant les attaques houthistes de fin 2023, 66 % des importations européennes de kérosène et 58 % de celles de diesel empruntaient des routes maritimes passant par Bab el-Mandeb. Pour le pétrole brut, cette proportion était de 17 %. L’Union exporte davantage de produits raffinés qu’elle n’en importe, mais elle reste importatrice nette des deux carburants dont dépend une large part de son économie. Le gazole est consommé aux trois quarts par le transport routier, tandis que le kérosène est presque entièrement absorbé par l’aviation. Début septembre, le diesel a dépassé les 200 dollars le baril aux États-Unis – soit près de deux fois le niveau d’avant-guerre –, et les prix européens ont connu une évolution comparable. Dans le même temps, les exportations de diesel du Golfe et de Russie sont désormais inférieures de 1,6 million de barils par jour par rapport à leur niveau de février. En 2013, la Russie fournissait 35 % du brut importé par l’Union. Depuis 2022, elle a été remplacée par la Norvège, les États-Unis et le Kazakhstan. Pour le diesel, ce sont principalement les pays du Golfe qui ont remplacé la Russie : leur part dans les importations européennes est passée de 2,4 % en 2013 à 31,6 % l'an dernier. Ce basculement repose sur une vague d’investissements : les raffineurs du Golfe ont ajouté environ 1,6 million de barils par jour de capacité entre 2020 et 2024. Ce sont ces installations qui ont été visées par les frappes iraniennes, notamment Ruwais aux Émirats arabes unis et Mina Abdulla au Koweït. L’Europe a ainsi réduit sa dépendance vis-à-vis de la Russie depuis 2022, mais a accru son exposition aux pays du Golfe. Depuis 2009, l’Europe consomme chaque année davantage de kérosène qu’elle n’en raffine. En 2024, cet écart est revenu à un niveau comparable à son pic d’avant la pandémie. Entre 2013 et 2025, la consommation a augmenté de 23 %, tandis que la production n’a progressé que de 12 %. Près de la moitié des importations proviennent du Golfe, avec une dépendance accrue vis-à-vis du Koweït. L’évolution des stocks confirme cette exposition : entre janvier et juin, les réserves européennes d’urgence de kérosène ont diminué de 35 %, contre 29 % pour l’essence et 20 % pour le gazole. Les installations européennes ne sont pas en mesure de raffiner davantage de pétrole brut pour reconstituer ces réserves, car la plupart ont été conçues pour traiter des bruts moyens et soufrés, comme l’Oural russe, qui fournissent une proportion plus importante de diesel et de kérosène que des bruts plus légers. Or, ces bruts « medium sour » ne représentent plus que 6 % des importations européennes, contre 31 % en 2013. Ils ont ainsi été remplacés en grande partie par des bruts plus légers et moins soufrés, qui produisent mais moins de distillats moyens par baril. Les bruts de remplacement adaptés sont également devenus plus chers, car ils sont transportés de plus loin et sont disputés par les autres grands importateurs. À cela s’ajoute le recul de l’industrie européenne elle-même. La capacité de raffinage de l’Union a diminué d’environ 13 % depuis 2000, et sept États membres n’ont plus de capacité significative de raffinage. Depuis 2009, près d'un tiers des raffineries européennes ont d’ailleurs été fermées ou transformées. Entre février et juin, les importations européennes de diesel américain ont presque doublé par rapport à 2025. Dans le même temps, les États-Unis ont puisé dans leurs réserves beaucoup plus vite que les Européens. Leurs stocks commerciaux de distillats ont ainsi reculé de 10 %, contre 5 % pour les stocks commerciaux européens de diesel. La réserve stratégique américaine avait quant à elle diminué de 21 % entre février et juin, et de 31 % à la mi-septembre. Sous la pression des prix intérieurs, l’administration américaine envisage désormais de restreindre voire de suspendre les exportations de diesel. Une telle décision priverait l’Europe de l’une de ses principales sources d’approvisionnement hors du Golfe, avec un impact significatif à la fois sur les prix et sur la relation transatlantique. L’article Bab el-Mandeb : le contrôle houthiste fait peser un risque sur les approvisionnements européens en diesel et kérosène est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Manchester City accusé de violations des règles financières de la Premier League
items.description: Le club anglais de Manchester City a été reconnu coupable, vendredi, de la quasi-totalité des 115 accusations de violations présumées du règlement financier de la Premier League, selon des informations rapportées par plusieurs médias britanniques. Aucune sanction n’a toutefois été officiellement annoncée à ce stade et le club devrait faire appel de la décision. Les sanctions envisagées pourraient notamment inclure une déduction de points, une amende financière, voire une relégation, tandis que la question d’un éventuel retrait de titres remportés par Manchester City depuis le rachat du club en 2008 pourrait également se poser, selon les médias. « Le processus est toujours en cours, avec des éléments importants restant à finaliser, et il est soumis à des règles strictes de confidentialité », a déclaré un porte-parole de Manchester City. « La position de Manchester City reste donc conforme à la déclaration du club de février 2023. » Le club a ajouté avoir « diligemment respecté les procédures » pendant les huit années de la procédure, en estimant que la direction de la Premier League devait agir comme un régulateur « indépendant, impartial et équitable, libre de toute influence partisane ». Manchester City a toujours nié les accusations et affirmé disposer d’éléments « irréfutables » pour défendre sa position. Le club avait constitué une importante équipe juridique pour contester les accusations devant la commission indépendante chargée du dossier. Selon les informations rapportées par la presse, la commission aurait notamment retenu des griefs portant sur la fourniture d’informations financières exactes, la valorisation de certains contrats de sponsoring et la divulgation de paiements effectués à des joueurs ainsi qu’à l’ancien entraîneur Roberto Mancini. Les accusations couvrent une période allant de la saison 2009-2010 à la saison 2022-2023, année au cours de laquelle l’enquête de la Premier League a pris fin. Elles portent ainsi sur une période durant laquelle Manchester City a remporté 20 trophées majeurs. Sous la direction de Pep Guardiola, parti à l’issue de la saison dernière, Manchester City a notamment remporté un triplé historique en 2023 et un quatrième titre consécutif de champion d’Angleterre en 2024. La décision de la commission indépendante de la Premier League, si elle est confirmée officiellement, pourrait constituer l’un des dossiers disciplinaires les plus importants de l’histoire du football anglais. La procédure reste toutefois susceptible d’appel et aucune sanction définitive n’a encore été annoncée. items.title: India’s killer tourists
items.description: THE date was January 2024, and Israel’s destruction of Gaza was underway for all to see. Among the Israeli soldiers demolishing Palestinian homes was a man named Eitan Gilboa. In videos obtained by the Hind Rajab Foundation , which analyses publicly available data to identify Israeli soldiers it alleges are implicated in war crimes, Gilboa and his unit can be seen detonating residential buildings and celebrating their destruction. The foundation alleges that in June of the same year, Gilboa was in Rafah ordering the demolition of multiple buildings and in July was involved in another demolition. It argues that Gilboa’s actions — and the actions of thousands of Israeli soldiers who took part in similar mayhem — are in violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention. Where do these Israeli war criminals go to ‘rest’ after destroying the lives of innocent Palestinians? Many go to India, following a backpacking route so well known for hosting Israeli soldiers that it is called the ‘Hummus Trail’. It stretches through destinations like Kasol and the Parvati Valley, Dharamkot and Tosh in Himachal Pradesh and on to places like Pushkar in Rajasthan, and Goa. Around 80,000 Israeli soldiers are said to travel there annually. This is also where Gilboa went. The path of guest houses frequented by Israeli travellers is well established and Indians have gone through a lot of trouble to accommodate them. Attractions include raves where visitors can lose themselves in trance music and drugs. So established is this trade in providing peace and ‘healing’ that one writer called towns on the Hummus Trail the “ashrams for war criminals”. Dharamsala even boasts of a ‘mini-Israel’, where shopkeepers speak Hebrew and serve Israeli food. In 2015, a cafe in Kasol was accused of refusing to serve Indian customers while admitting white tourists. Israeli soldiers reviled in other parts are welcome in India. The most important thing that India provides is absolution. Here, Israeli soldiers condemned and excoriated in most other parts of the world, are welcome. They can partake of a commercialised, tourist-friendly mix of ‘healing’ from the trauma of war, without having to take accountability for their actions in Gaza. Gilboa was no different. The Hind Rajab Foundation analysed photographs and other material from his Indian journey and filed complaints with the Himachal police, the home ministry and the Bureau of Immigration seeking his arrest. No arrest followed and Gilboa eventually left India. India’s ties with Israel run deep and increasingly point to an ideological, economic and military alignment. Hindutva’s founder Vinayak Damodar Savarkar praised the idea of a Jewish state in Palestine, describing Palestine as the Jews’ “Fatherland and Holyland”. Zionism’s blend of attachment to a motherland and religious attachment to a holy land was precisely what Savarkar wanted for Hindus. Modi’s India in this sense is like Zionist Israel. India’s Citizenship Amendment Act created an expedited route to citizenship for specified non-Muslim migrants from neighbouring countries while excluding Muslims from its provisions. Israel’s 2018 nation-state law similarly privileged Jewish national identity by declaring that the right to national self-determination in Israel is unique to the Jewish people. In contemporary India, the state supports these Israeli enclaves on the Hummus Trail even as it punishes people for expressing their support for Palestinians. An editorial published in The Edict , a newspaper at Ashoka University, noted how eager Hin­­dutva supporters want to fraternise with Israeli tourists, imagining their sha­red hostility tow­ards Muslims as a natural alignment, while some Israeli travellers treat br­­own Indians as les­ser locals there to serve them. In Pu­­shkar, The Edict re­­ported that the Chabad House has Hebrew signage and a perimeter fence, with Indians facing restrictions on entry while white tourists were admitted with less scrutiny. So India welcomes Israeli soldiers on their ‘healing journeys’, including those facing allegations of war crimes. The Indian state — as evidenced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s eager embrace of Israeli officials — is keen to emphasise the closeness of the two countries. In his speech at the Knesset, Modi even peddled yoga and ayurveda as sources of holistic wellness that Israelis could partake in when they visited India. This, then, is the tale of two hatreds. Men like Eitan Gilboa, accused of participating in the destruction of civilian homes, can leave Gaza and seek succour in a new environment where they can forget the cruelties of war. Hosting those accused of such acts without demanding accountability raises its own moral questions, but this is a truth that India, drowning in its own hatreds, appears unable to acknowledge. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: Killer police web: Inside the deadly squad linked to Mbobu and Mutiso killings
Discussions on terrorism
items.description: WHILE visiting the British parliament a few years ago, I was struck by the tradition —observed by prime ministers — of paying homage and expressing gratitude at the start of the weekly question time session to British armed forces personnel who had been killed or injured in action. It was the time of the Afghan war and British troops were stationed in Afghanistan. I thought it was a great tradition that reminded everyone of the sacrifices made by the soldiers and sent a powerful message to the troops that their countrymen had the highest regard for them and their sacrifices. Although Pakistan follows the British parliamentary system, almost all Pakistani prime ministers have avoided personally answering questions in parliament. As prime minister, Yousuf Raza Gilani used to answer many supplementary questions himself when he was in the House — but that was not a part of the set parliamentary procedure. Imran Khan had promised to follow this British tradition when he was prime minister and personally answer questions. However, he neither tried to change the parliamentary rules nor did he ever answer any questions in parliament. Both Houses and the provincial assemblies observe question hour but there is no parliamentary tradition of routinely acknowledging the sacrifices of the country’s shuhda and ghazis. The president, prime minister, ministers and senior civil and military officers do issue statements, and legislatures occasionally pass resolutions honouring those fighting a bloody war against terrorism; but the possibility of a weekly tribute did cross my mind. After all, hardly a day passes without hearing of security personnel — in the armed forces, paramilitaries, police and other security bodies — who have lost their lives in the line of duty. We need committees that are more active in debating national security. Almost all sources of information show that the number of violent terrorist incidents, casualties and fatalities in Pakistan have reached their highest level in a decade. In fact, 2025 was the bloodiest year since 2014. According to the South Asian Terrorism Portal, the number of violent terrorist incidents in 2025 was 1,077 with fatalities among the forces and civilians touching 1,229 and 655 respectively during the year. The data gathered for 2026 points to even higher figures when compared to the average monthly figures for 2025. For example, the number of terrorism incidents increased to a monthly average of 118, compared to 90 in 2025. Similarly, average monthly fatalities of civilian and security forces personnel in the first nine months of 2026 (up to Sept 21) have increased to 74 from 55 last year and to 114 from 102, respectively. These figures indicate a steep spike in attacks, particularly carried out by two major terrorist groups that the state aptly refers to as Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan. We do not see the level of concern and debate within democratic institutions that is warranted by the rise in acts of terrorism. We have four key standing committees relating to the issue in parliament — separate Senate and National Assembly standing committees on defence and two other committees of the Senate and National Assembly on the interior. In addition, each of the four provincial assemblies has a standing committee on home affairs. Whatever little record is available on these legislatures’ official websites does not indicate that the committees have been often and actively debating the rising incidence of terrorism in the country — especially in KP and Balochistan —in detail, which should have been done in view of the situation. The plenaries of the six national and provincial legislatures have debated the issue on and off, and passed resolutions too. I am sure that more frequent discussions in the legislative bodies would not only contribute to finding more effective ways in which the menace of terrorism can be combated at the people’s level, but the attention given by the legislators to this issue would further boost security personnel’s morale. In 2019, the Speaker of the National Assembly had constituted a joint (National Assembly and Senate) committee on national security under his own chairmanship and included the senior-most parliamentarians and ministers. But since the last election in 2024, the committee has apparently ceased to exist. It doesn’t necessarily mean that we need a parliamentary committee on national security while the committees on defence and interior already exist. However, what we need are committees that are more active in debating national security. The public should be confident that national security issues are being discussed and timely decisions being made at the appropriate forum. In this context, it is difficult to understand the relatively inactive state of the National Security Committee, which was created in 2013. The Committee, which brings together the top civil and military leadership under the chairmanship of the prime minister, has not met even once during the current calendar year. Given the prevailing circumstances and the mandate of the NSC, it should meet more regularly, preferably on a monthly basis. Just for comparison, Britain’s National Security Council meets every week under the prime minister although the UK has far fewer security issues than Pakistan. It is hoped that the National Counter Terrorism Authority — a very important body especially in the present context — will not only become more active under its new national coordinator Maj-Gen Faisal Naseer but will also attempt to raise its public profile by, for example, sharing at least a sanitised version of the progress on the implementation of the National Action Plan with the people, their representatives and the media. Extending its outreach will bolster public trust. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: Gathering clouds
items.description: THE clock may have been pushed back, but the countdown to another confrontation between the PTI and the state has not stopped yet. In one camp, a millennial politician is taking the big decisions, if only on behalf of a jailed Imran Khan. The chief minister of KP, Sohail Khan Afridi, is all of 37 years old. He was slated to lead the PTI this Sunday into yet another showdown with the state. Late Friday, however, his party’s long march to Islamabad was put off by a week, giving everyone some breathing space. Afridi must live up to some daunting expectations from the hardliners within his ranks. He has to succeed where others more experienced than him have failed, or face relegation and possibly political oblivion. The odds remain stacked against him, and the PTI’s opponents have left no stone unturned to impress upon him and his party what their prospects are if they march on Islamabad. That is why it would be premature to say the pressure has been released. Yet the other side is hardly in a better position. Intoxicated by the impunity granted to it under the current configuration of state, and seemingly oblivious to the optics and potential consequences of an overreaction on its part, the government is making it abundantly clear that it will ‘fix’ the PTI ‘for good’ if it dares march. That, however, will not solve its problems. Whatever calm the country has seen of late has merely been the lull before another storm. Ordinary Pakistanis have endured years of economic hardship. The protracted war in the Gulf has now handed this government another painful economic test — one it does not appear equipped to pass. Its show of strength is, in large part, a mask for that weakness. In short, both sides appear to be in varying states of desperation. And this is why the coming days could prove dangerous for the federation: a province marching on a barricaded capital. De-escalation is required, however remote a possibility it may seem at this point. Those in power must realise that no matter what they accomplish and no matter how comprehensively they are able to thwart the opposition, power is fleeting and the future will bring consequences in one form or another. Pakistan’s history is replete with missteps and unfortunate decisions that continue to hurt its present generations. The PTI, too, must realise that politics and negotiation remain the most viable path forward. There is a real danger that its march, if it goes ahead next weekend, may still end in violence and bloodshed. Fresh bloodshed will not advance its cause. Both sides must meet each other halfway, with the state permitting protest and the PTI keeping it peaceful, to prevent another tragedy from playing out. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.description: Recapitulemos: la crisis de Ceuta no fue de partida una crisis migratoria; fue una crisis geopolítica: Marruecos olfateó la debilidad nacional e internacional del Gobierno español y organizó, alentó o toleró la entrada de casi 80.000 personas en Ceuta para mostrarle al mundo lo que puede hacer con Ceuta . Solo más tarde, cuando la mayoría de los que entraron había salido, la crisis geopolítica se trocó en una crisis migratoria todavía irresuelta, agravada por la torpeza y la gandulería de un Gobierno cuyo presidente siguió de vacaciones durante semanas en vez de hacer lo que debía haber hecho de inmediato: plantarse en Ceuta con su Gobierno en pleno y encerrarse allí a cal y canto hasta haber controlado la situación. Dicho esto, era inevitable que la internacional nacionalpopulista aprovechara la crisis para proseguir su tarea de demonizar la emigración intentando demostrar que constituye la causa de todos nuestros males. Es una mentira flagrante y una perversión sin paliativos. Infinidad de razones justifican este aserto; menciono tres. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Qué es Sociedad Civil Española: así es la red derechista tras la manifestación “ciudadana” para juzgar a Sánchez por “traición”
items.description: Si todo sale como pretenden el PP y Vox , este sábado será un día de explosión multitudinaria de banderas españolas y rechazo a Pedro Sánchez en Madrid. Los partidos que lideran Alberto Núñez Feijóo y Santiago Abascal han apoyado y confirmado oficialmente su asistencia a una manifestación contra el Gobierno que arrancará a las 10.00 de la Plaza de Cibeles. En ambos casos, lo han hecho difundiendo una convocatoria con un cartel cargado de lemas: “No a la invasión de Ceuta y Melilla”, “En defensa de España”, “Todos juntos. Por España”, “No nos hemos ido de vacaciones en defensa de España”, “Por la dignidad. Por la libertad. Por nuestro futuro”. No hay logos de partidos. El cartel que han difundido el PP y Vox y que circula por webs, redes sociales y canales de mensajería presenta como convocante a una organización llamada Sociedad Civil Española (SCE), que presume de impulsar una “iniciativa ciudadana” de carácter “independiente” y “plural”, “sin partidos”, que llama a gente “de toda ideología” a exigir al presidente del Gobierno que convoque elecciones como muy tarde el 15 de noviembre. items.title: Alberto Muñagorri: vida y vértigo del niño de la bomba
items.description: Cuando escuchó la explosión, que resonó por todo el casco viejo, lo primero que le vino a la cabeza a Sara Berdasco fue que menos mal que había dejado las ventanas del salón abiertas. “Si no”, pensó, “me destroza los cristales”. Aquella bomba, que se detonó en el interior de una mochila abandonada en la calle el mediodía del 26 de junio de 1982, no destrozó los cristales del piso de Sara. Destrozó el cuerpo de su hijo pequeño, de 10 años, que yacía requemado en la calzada a dos manzanas de allí, sobre un charco de sangre espesa, la pierna izquierda hecha trizas, los tímpanos reventados, el ojo derecho sin visión y el izquierdo dañado, el pequeño cuerpo lleno de metralla. El estruendo de la explosión, el aullido de la ambulancia. Después, el silencio. La banda sonora intermitente de Rentería, Gipuzkoa, y de tantos otros pueblos vascos, en los años de plomo de ETA. Esta es la historia de Alberto Muñagorri. Seguir leyendo La mochila. Vida de Muñagorri Ander Izagirre Libros del K.O., 2026 408 páginas. 23,90 euros

items.title: Un genio del Mal llamado Sánchez
items.description: Era un señor educado, afable y de opiniones aparentemente sensatas. Se adivinaba en él una cierta tendencia conservadora sin grandes estridencias. Aquella mañana disfrutaba de una de esas amenas charlas con el gestor cultural del pueblo de la costa gallega que frecuentaba los veranos y con el que había hecho buenas migas. Lo interrumpió un pitido en el teléfono. El interlocutor de nuestro hombre pudo ver que se trataba de una alerta informativa de uno de esos diarios digitales de la capital entregados con portentosa abnegación a demoler minuciosamente cada pequeño acto del presidente del Gobierno. El señor le echó un vistazo, sacó conclusiones y buscó complicidad: Seguir leyendo

items.title: Todos contra la inmigración, pero divididos frente a Putin: qué une y qué separa a la extrema derecha europea
items.description: Alternativa para Alemania (AfD) ganó el 6 de septiembre las elecciones de Sajonia-Anhalt , donde todo indica que podrá formar gobierno, algo que no ocurre en ese país desde el fin de la II Guerra Mundial. Dos semanas después, repitió victoria en Mecklemburgo-Pomerania Occidental. Sus triunfos aceleran el avance de la extrema derecha en la Unión Europea, donde ya está presente en los Ejecutivo de seis países (Italia, Finlandia, República Checa, Eslovaquia, Croacia y Eslovenia), lidera las intenciones de voto en otros cuatro (Alemania, Francia, Austria y Rumania) y sus tres grupos en la Eurocámara suman más escaños que el Partido Popular Europeo, el que más diputados tiene. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Friedrich Merz, el impopular ‘canciller de las reformas’ que lucha por mantenerse a flote
items.description: Nunca ha despertado pasiones, ni entre sus filas, ni entre el electorado. Pero el democristiano Friedrich Merz (CDU) logró convertirse en canciller de Alemania tras una accidentada investidura en mayo del pasado año . Asumía un país inmerso en una profunda crisis estructural y debilitado tras años de disputas internas en el anterior Gobierno del socialdemócrata Olaf Scholz, que terminó antes de tiempo. Tomó las riendas con una promesa: emprender cuanto antes una serie de reformas para garantizar la prosperidad del país. La CDU le calificó como el “canciller de las reformas”. Un camino que sigue manteniendo y que tras los últimos batacazos en varias elecciones regionales defendió como el “antídoto” contra el auge de los extremismos, a pesar de las críticas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Es China una superpotencia tecnológica? Los gráficos de su fuerza en robots, patentes y notas de PISA
items.description: En treinta años China se ha convertido en una potencia económica. En 1990 su PIB era el 3% del mundo —no mucho mayor que el español—, ahora es la primera potencia en poder de paridad de compra, por delante de EEUU y la Unión Europea. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Yalda Moaiery, fotoperiodista iraní condenada a 15 años de prisión: “La guerra ha dado paso a la peor versión de la República Islámica”
items.description: Sus ojos y la cámara son su medida “de la verdad”, asegura la fotoperiodista iraní Yalda Moaiery (Teherán, 44 años). En sus fotos de las manifestaciones de enero contra la República Islámica “no hay muertos” porque ella no los vio, recalca por videollamada desde Teherán esta fotógrafa, quien, sin embargo, subraya que esas víctimas fueron “miles” . Los poderosos pueden decir que un periodista miente en un texto; las imágenes son más incuestionables. Por esa razón, la República Islámica “las teme”, afirma esta profesional que saltó a la fama en 2019, cuando Donald Trump usó una de sus fotos sin permiso en un tuit : la de una joven alzando el puño al emerger de una nube de gas lacrimógeno en una manifestación en Teherán. El pasado julio, su trabajo le valió una condena a 15 años de prisión, pendiente de recurso, en un juicio al que ni siquiera pudo asistir. Las autoridades iraníes habían tratado de convocarla llamando a un número de teléfono que ellas mismas habían previamente bloqueado. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Gobierno insta al Senado a aprobar el Tratado de Amistad con Francia
items.description: El Gobierno insta al Senado a aprobar “con carácter prioritario”, tras haber obtenido el aval por unanimidad del Tribunal Constitucional , el Tratado de Amistad y Cooperación entre España y Francia en el pleno de la próxima semana que se celebrará el martes y el miércoles. La premura se debe a que Emmanuel Macron tiene prevista una visita de Estado para los días 29 y 30 de septiembre en Madrid en la que los Reyes le invitarán a una cena de gala, se reunirá con Pedro Sánchez y mantendrá citas empresariales al máximo nivel. “Ruego que tenga en cuenta la pertinencia de que el Tratado sea ratificado lo antes posible, dada la visita que el Presidente de la República Francesa llevará a cabo en nuestro país”, solicita Rafael Simancas, secretario de Estado de Relaciones con las Cortes, al presidente de la cámara Alta, Pedro Rollán, en un escrito al que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Aliança Catalana-Vox: los vasos comunicantes de una relación no tan distante
items.description: A Rosa Maria Soberana, la segunda diputada de Aliança Catalana en el Parlament de Cataluña, aún se la veía afectada el miércoles por la mañana. No hacía ni 24 horas que su partido había admitido como un “error” haber apoyado en la Junta de Portavoces de la Cámara catalana que no se sancionara al partido de Santiago Abascal e Ignacio Garriga por llamar en 2025 “asesino” a Lluís Companys. Cuando un diputado de Vox se le acercó, la propia Soberana dio a entender que el partido le había urgido a recular. “Fue un error”, defienden desde el partido para admitir la rectificación. Seguir leyendo

items.title: De “¿eres mantero?" a “¿eres modelo?“: la historia de Cheikh, de una patera a las pasarelas
items.description: Vivimos tiempos en los que conceptos como “Lo mejor” y “Lo peor” acaban por no poder diferenciarse de lo mucho que se han aproximado sus extremos. Podemos ser testigos de un acto de heroicidad que asombre y, seguidamente, de otro de crueldad que nos devuelva a ese mutismo inicial. Podemos quedar anonadados con la colección de una firma en un desfile y sorprendidos por las condiciones laborales detrás de los cortinones. ¿Cómo contar, entonces, aquellas historias que han conocido de primera mano el paso de un aspecto a otro? Sencillamente, dándoles la palabra. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Revelaciones de una lectura pausada del libro de Charles Spencer sobre Diana de Gales: humillaciones, los desplantes de Carlos III y un romance secreto de la reina Isabel
items.description: Hay pérdidas que ni el tiempo consigue convertir en pasado. La historia y el legado de Diana de Gales siguen presentes, a pesar de los 29 años que han pasado del trágico accidente de coche en París que terminó con su vida. Se han escrito decenas de libros y se han producido cientos de documentales y películas sobre ella y su vida, de antes y después de convertirse en uno de los miembros de la familia real británica más queridos en todo el mundo. Con la cuenta atrás para el 30º aniversario de su muerte, el hermano de Lady Di, Charles Spencer , ha decidido que es su momento de relatar sus recuerdos en un homenaje que ha hecho tambalear los cimientos del palacio de Buckingham. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La chirigota feminista de Cádiz que actuará en las calles del Macondo de Shakira: “Nosotras lloramos mientras facturamos”
items.description: Cualquier sitio callejero de Cádiz es proclive a una femisfanía, al golpe de ingenio de la chirigota callejera de las Cadiwoman. Esa esquina donde el biruji de las noches frías de febrero pega menos o ese portal donde un vecino malaje se aguanta las ganas de tirar un cubo de agua con lejía son escenarios perfectos para dejarse imbuir por esa suerte de epifanía feminista por la vía del humor. El término lo acuñó la autora de la agrupación, Susana Ginesta, en la tesis doctoral en la que exploró los poco investigados caminos del humor feminista. Después de 17 carnavales, no se puede decir que a las Cadiwoman no les falten trienios en esa tarea. Hoy sábado, 26 de septiembre, y el domingo, 27, sumarán otro hito: cambiar las calles de Cádiz por las de ese Macondo Park que la artista Shakira ha montado para su residencia artística de 12 conciertos en Madrid. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La lenta agonía del alquiler de vivienda en España: ¿Qué salió mal?
items.description: Alquilar ha dejado de ser una opción para una parte de la población. Además de dramático, el hecho resulta paradójico porque durante años gobiernos y expertos defendieron la necesidad de potenciar el alquiler frente a la compra . “Las ventajas económicas, sociales y laborales que ofrece el alquiler son innumerables. Entre otras, facilita la elección de vivienda de los ciudadanos, adecuándola a las diferentes necesidades del ciclo vital, propicia el aumento de la movilidad geográfica de los trabajadores, permite disminuir el endeudamiento de los hogares y ofrece mayor flexibilidad ante cambios en los ingresos de la unidad familiar”. Con este texto arrancaba el preámbulo de la Ley de medidas de fomento y agilización procesal del alquiler y de la eficiencia energética de los edificios, publicada en 2009. Durante el segundo Gobierno de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero (PSOE), se aprobó esta norma destinada expresamente a fomentar el arrendamiento, que entonces apenas rascaba el 11% del mercado residencial, frente a una media europea que la propia ley situaba en el entorno del 40%. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘Maxximiza’, exprímete a ti mismo: la insana obsesión por optimizarlo todo
items.description: Hubo un tiempo en que la moderación era virtud y el término medio, sabiduría. La hipérbole no pasaba de ser un recurso literario o retórico. Pero ya no. Estamos instalados en los máximos. Llevarlo todo a su potencial más elevado es el Zeigeist que nos ha tocado en suerte, y viene acompañado por un sufijo que coloniza internet: maxxing . Sufijo versátil donde los haya, pues puesto tras la palabra adecuada significa que, haga lo que haga, usted lo está dando todo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Beth, 24 años después de ‘OT’: “Me da pena que parezca que, como no sales en la tele, estás muerta”
items.description: “¿Qué fue de Beth?”. La pregunta aparece una y otra vez cuando se escribe su nombre en internet. Ella sonríe, pero niega la premisa: “Mucha gente cree que desaparecí, pero no he dejado de trabajar nunca”. Mientras el gran público seguía recordándola por su participación en la segunda edición de Operación Triunfo (la de 2002), por su himno Dime (que la llevó a Eurovisión en 2003) y por una estética —las rastas, el piercing — que marcó a una generación, la catalana actuaba en su tierra, hacía teatro, creaba una marca de ropa y formaba una familia. Ahora, después de reconciliarse con la canción que durante dos décadas no quiso cantar y con nuevo disco en camino, Beth mira hacia atrás sin nostalgia. Porque el éxito no se mide solo en conciertos de estadio. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Cómo lidiar con un jefe tóxico (y no morir en el intento)
items.description: Un profesor que brilla demasiado al que el responsable del departamento le aparta de los actos públicos para acudir él. Una periodista cuyas ideas son rechazadas por su superior, que las plantea como propias ante la dirección. Un ingeniero informático que ha abandonado la empresa en la que trabajaba para no aguantar los abusos de su mando directo. Los jefes tóxicos son una constante en la empresa, española y extranjera, actual o pretérita, aprecia Santiago Álvarez de Mon, experto en liderazgo de IESE Business School. “A lo largo de mi carrera, me he encontrado a muchos jefes autoritarios y abusivos. Están en toda la pirámide organizativa y en todo tipo de industrias y culturas empresariales . Aunque es cierto que el management ha mejorado mucho en los últimos años, este tipo de liderazgo es más fácil que progrese en las compañías en las donde prima mucho la jerarquía”, explica. Seguir leyendo La triada oscura La creciente ola de populismo que vive el mundo está provocando el auge del jefe autoritario. “Es más probable que los líderes a los que recurrimos en busca de orientación en tiempos convulsos manifiesten altos niveles de narcisismo, psicopatía y maquiavelismo (lo que se conoce como la ‘triada oscura’ de la personalidad)”, señala Laura Guillén, profesora de Esade. Los ejemplos son abundantes, no hay más que ver a gobernantes como Donald Trump o Vladímir Putin o a ejecutivos como Elon Musk o Marc Zuckerberg. Durante las crisis, la gente tiende a ser más afiliativa y sumisa, mientras que los individuos de la triada oscura mantienen sus ansias de poder y se aprovechan del caos e incluso lo generan. Manifiestan agresividad y dan sensación de tener derecho a todo, según la docente. Su ambición personal está por encima de cualquier cosa.

La vida en edificios a punto de colapsar en Gaza: “Caen trozos de vez en cuando, en mi habitación o en las de al lado”
items.description: Mohammed al Zatma, de 34 años, sale de una habitación y corre hacia el borde expuesto de su apartamento en ruinas, situado en el barrio de Amal, al oeste de Jan Yunis, en Gaza . Sus hijos y los de sus primos están jugando allí, en una parte del edificio que quedó expuesta por un bombardeo israelí: no hay barandilla ni ninguna barrera que proteja a los niños de caer al vacío desde la tercera planta. Al Zatma coge en brazos a su hija menor, Mennatullah, de cuatro años, y la sienta en un sofá raído a varios metros de distancia, lo suficientemente cerca para verla mientras va por los otros niños, pero lo suficientemente lejos para estar a salvo. A sus hermanos, Hossam Eddin, de seis años, y Majd, de ocho, los empuja más hacia el interior. Como este, más de 2.000 edificios en toda Gaza corren riesgo de derrumbe , según la Defensa Civil de Gaza. A mediados de septiembre, en Ciudad de Gaza, se derrumbó un edificio residencial , llamado Al Sa’ada, previamente dañado por la ofensiva israelí. Una veintena de personas murieron sepultadas y decenas más permanecen desaparecidas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: PTI’s protest postponement to double security cost in Islamabad
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The government will pay Rs46.5 million per day to the owners of 1,550 containers arranged to counter the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) protest in the capital. Sources in the police said the amount requested by the capital police for security arrangements to counter the PTI’s protest would effectively double and was likely to cost the exchequer more than Rs1 billion as the political party has postponed the protest rally for about a week. Earlier, PTI had announced a countrywide protest starting on September 27. Following the announcement, the capital police, like their counterparts in Punjab, began preparations and requested Rs820 million to cover the rent of containers, accommodation and meals for the police personnel arriving from Punjab and Sindh. Police yet to decide whether to release containers or retain them in their custody, says All Pakistan Goods Alliance chairman The amount was intended to cover one week, as the police expected the protest and long march, scheduled to begin on September 27, to disperse by October 4. However, with the protest and long march postponed for a week, the expenses are also expected to increase. All Pakistan Goods Alliance Chairman Nisar Hussain Jaffri said the alliance had initially demanded a daily rent of Rs40,000 and Rs20,000 for 40-foot and 20-foot containers, respectively. Later, he said, the demand was revised to Rs30,000 per container for both sizes. After PTI postponed the long march, the police were asked about the containers, he said, adding that the authorities had so far not decided whether to release or retain them in their custody. The sources said that according to the demand the daily rent for 1,550 containers comes to Rs46.5 million, while the rent for one week is Rs325.5 million and for two weeks Rs651 million. The sources said the police had also requested a contingent of 16,000 personnel from the Punjab Police and 2,000 from the Sindh Police. So far, the Sindh Police contingent has reached the capital and is staying at marquees at the Police Lines Headquarters, Faisal Mosque and Community Centre G-13. Three meals a day are being provided to the visiting personnel. The cost of three meals per person is Rs600, meaning Rs1.2 million is being spent each day to feed the 2,000 Sindh Police personnel. The cost of meals for one week is Rs8.4 million and for two weeks Rs16.8 million. Surprisingly, the requested Punjab Police contingent is yet to reach Islamabad. The sources said the 16,000-member contingent was scheduled to reach the capital by the evening of September 25, as the deployment plan was to take effect from the evening of September 26. However, no Punjab Police official had arrived in Islamabad by Friday evening, they added. About 70 coasters, 30 double-cabin vehicles and buses were also arranged to transport the police force between their places of accommodation and designated duty points. The daily rent of a coaster is Rs15,000, bringing the daily cost of 70 coasters to Rs1.05 million. The daily rent of a double-cabin vehicle is Rs10,000, while the 30 vehicles cost Rs300,000 per day. The police also booked 175 rooms in 13 hotels in different sectors for 246 inspectors, 58 deputy and assistant superintendents of police, superintendents of police, 10 senior superintendents of police and eight deputy inspectors general of police. Of the 13 hotels, 157 rooms in 11 hotels were booked for officers from the ranks of inspector to SP. The daily rent for these rooms is Rs754,500, and rent for one week will be Rs5.2815 million. Although the Punjab Police contingent has yet to arrive in the capital, its three-meal daily food bill is estimated at Rs9.6 million. The cost would rise to Rs67.2 million for one week. The rent of the buses arranged to transport the police force, as well as the rent of 18 rooms at two hotels booked for DIGs and SSPs, was not known. Meanwhile, All Pakistan Goods Alliance Chairman Nisar Hussain said the police in Islamabad and Punjab had taken into custody at least 2,700 vehicles along with their three-member crews. Of the total, about 400 vehicles and their crews were still missing, while the crews of the remaining vehicles were being kept at police stations. He clarified that the police had not formally arrested the drivers and other crew members but had stopped them from leaving the police stations except for meals. The police had also confiscated their mobile phones, vehicle documents and keys. The sources said the crews would remain at the police stations until a decision was made on releasing the containers. They were being kept there to drive and move the vehicles, as special skills were required to operate the large container trucks. The containers and vehicles were seized and their crew members detained in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Lahore, Jhang, Hasanabdal, Attock, Kamoke, Taxila, Jhelum, Mianwali, Chakwal, Faisalabad and Gujrat. Of the 2,700 vehicles, 450 were carrying goods, including medicines, food items and chemicals. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: Balochistan farmers postpone march on Islamabad
items.description: • Decision follows provincial govt assurances to address growers’ demands • Kissan Ittehad president calls on CM Bugti to declare agricultural emergency QUETTA: The Pakistan Kissan Ittehad has postponed its long march and sit-in towards Islamabad, which was scheduled to begin from Quetta on Friday, following a request and assurances from the Balochistan government. According to Home Affairs Adviser Babar Yousafzai, a government delegation led by Provincial Minister Ali Madad Jattak met Kissan Ittehad President Khalid Baath. Member of the Balochistan Assembly Mir Jahanzeb Mengal also attended the meeting. During the meeting, the government delegation assured the farmers’ leader that steps would be taken to address the demands of the farming community and fulfil their legitimate concerns. Mr Yousafzai said Khalid Baath acc­e­p­ted the government’s assurances and req­uest and announced the postponement of the long march towards Islamabad. He also assured the government delegation of the farmers’ cooperation. He said the Kissan Ittehad had decided to postpone the march in view of the prevailing national situation and law and order concerns. The home affairs adviser said the dialogue between the Balochistan government and the Kissan Ittehad was an important step towards progress. He added that the provincial government was taking serious measures to address the demands of the farming community. Press conference Earlier, before postponing the protest following a meeting with the government delegation, Mr Baath said at a press conference that a long march on Islamabad had been planned to press for the acceptance of farmers’ and landowners’ demands, including the resignation of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz. He said the protest would continue until their demands were accepted. Mr Baath said farmers’ caravans from across the country would join the Islamabad march. He said the movement aimed to highlight the agricultural problems faced by farmers and address the deteriorating condition in the agriculture sector. He said the farmers would launch a nationwide campaign for their rights and demands and continue their peaceful struggle until the problems facing the agricultural sector were resolved. He said they had serious reservations about Punjab CM Maryam Nawaz’s agricultural policies and were demanding her resignation. He said farmers were the backbone of the country’s food supply, adding that the agriculture sector had suffered severely over the past three years due to what he described as flawed policies. He said rising inflation had made it difficult for low-income people to afford even basic food items, while urgent and effective measures were needed to revive the sector and support farmers. Mr Baath further said the prosperity of farmers was essential for the prosperity of Balochistan and Pakistan. He alleged that bureaucrats were unaware of the problems faced by farmers and landowners and that flawed policies and decisions had harmed the country. He appealed to Balochistan CM Sarfraz Bugti to declare an agricultural emergency in the province and prioritise agriculture over development projects. He said that due to law and order problems in Balochistan, deputy commissioners and assistant commissioners were unable to even reach their offices. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: La resurrección del huevo pasado por agua: de ser la cena de nuestros abuelos al desayuno de los urbanitas
items.description: Fue una de las cenas más populares de quienes fueron niños en los 80, recurso rápido de las neveras con telarañas y solución socorrida donde las haya, de esas que ahora, en la era de TikTok en la que triunfan las recetas que se cocinan en menos de diez minutos y tienen menos de tres ingredientes, podría viralizarse por arte de magia. Y, por supuesto, como sucede con casi todo lo impregnado por esa capa de nostalgia y practicidad, acaba de volver a nuestras vidas. Y es que los huevos pasados por agua, embajadores de la cocina viejuna por excelencia , han resucitado al calor de dos tendencias que copan las cartas de casi todos los locales gastronómicos de primera hora: las proteínas y el café de especialidad. items.title: CNN blocked from Trump trip on Saturday
items.description: CNN reporters have been barred from traveling with US President Donald Trump as planned on Saturday, in a new move by the White House to limit the news network’s access. The president last week sought to ban three US outlets – CNN, MS NOW and Politico – from the White House, accusing them of providing only negative coverage on him. After journalists with the three outlets were blocked from entering the White House complex, a judge ordered their access to be temporarily restored, saying Trump’s move was likely unconstitutional. For Trump’s trip on Saturday to Tennessee, CNN had been scheduled to be the TV network in the press “pool” traveling with him. However, a schedule released by the White House on Friday evening did not list CNN or any of the TV networks in the TV pool rotation. The pool is a rotating group of journalists that travel with the president and provide coverage to other outlets, due to limited space. The White House schedule only listed a “Secondary TV” correspondent and crew: Lindell TV — a staunchly pro-Trump outlet run by his close ally, businessman Mike Lindell. Earlier this week, when CNN’s White House access was still revoked, the top five US broadcasters made a rare joint move to halt pool coverage of the White House in solidarity. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said. CNN declined to comment when reached Friday by AFP. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Vanguard News The post CNN blocked from Trump trip on Saturday appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Iran proposes Hormuz plan, Trump reportedly refuses
items.description: Iran offered a plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, Tehran said Friday, but within hours reports indicated that US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal. The waterway key to the world’s oil supply is central to the conflict between the United States and Iran, which is at a stalemate after nearly seven months. But new mediation efforts at the UN’s gathering of world leaders in New York this week offered some optimism of progress toward a deal. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital shipping channel. “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN. “The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. However, with hours of his comments The Wall Street Journal reported Trump had rejected the proposal, citing US officials familiar with the matter. The report noted that the 80-year-old president was skeptical Tehran would meet his demands and added he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely. Trump also posted an image to his Truth Social platform of a map showing the Strait of Hormuz circled and labelled “Trump Strait.” Earlier media reports suggested the new plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon. Frozen assets It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran. On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview with broadcaster CBS that the ceasefire “process will begin from the very day they accept it.” “We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan…if the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before,” he added. Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands. The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear program. But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway. Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons. Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation. items.title: When cancer fights back: New drug could reopen door to treatment
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe Cancer treatment can become a race against time. A drug works, the tumour shrinks, hope returns. Then the cancer changes. The treatment that once held it back starts losing its grip. Cancer cells find another way to survive, and a battle that seemed to be won begins all over again. Read Also: We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple Scientists at Baylor College of Medicine in the United States now say they may have found a way to disrupt one of cancer’s most frustrating survival strategies. The experimental drug, CS18, has shown early potential to weaken the biological defences that help cancer cells survive treatment and, crucially, make some resistant tumours sensitive to existing drugs again. In laboratory experiments, CS18 restored the sensitivity of lung cancer cells that had become resistant to osimertinib, a drug used to treat certain lung cancers. When the two were combined, more cancer cells died. The researchers also reported reduced tumour growth in animal models, without major weight loss or other obvious signs of toxicity. Published in Science Advances, the findings could point to a new approach to one of the most difficult problems in cancer treatment: drug resistance. However, CS18 is still an experimental compound and has not been established as a cancer treatment for patients and requires further research and testing. For oncologists, treatment resistance remains one of the biggest challenges in cancer care. A drug may work remarkably well at first, but cancer cells can adapt. They can switch on alternative biological pathways, evade the treatment and continue to survive. Eventually, the cancer may return. The study’s corresponding author, Dr. Weei-Chin Lin, professor of medicine, haematology and oncology, and molecular and cellular biology at Baylor College of Medicine, said “Therapeutic resistance is a major obstacle to achieving effective and durable cancer treatments. While some therapies are effective initially, many patients eventually relapse because cancer cells can activate compensatory and convergent biological pathways that allow them to overcome the toxic effects of treatment and survive.” That was the problem the Baylor team set out to tackle. Instead of targeting one cancer pathway at a time, the researchers went after what they describe as a central control point inside cancer cells. Their target was TopBP1 which is involved in several processes linked to cancer growth and survival. The researchers describe it as a biological “switchboard” because it helps regulate multiple pathways at once. They reasoned that disrupting the central control point could make it more difficult for cancer cells to activate alternative mechanisms for survival. CS18 was tested against triple-negative breast cancer, ovarian cancer, lung adenocarcinoma, lung squamous cell carcinoma and acute myeloid leukaemia. The compound also appeared less toxic to non-cancerous cells in the laboratory experiments. The results became particularly interesting when CS18 was combined with cancer drugs already in use. One of the most notable findings involved osimertinib. Some of the lung cancer cells used in the experiments had already developed resistance to the drug. Adding CS18 changed the response. The resistant cancer cells became sensitive to osimertinib again, increasing cancer cell death. The researchers also found that combining CS18 with PARP inhibitors, another class of cancer drugs, produced greater cancer cell killing than either treatment alone. Much more research is needed before the compound can progress through the stages required for human treatment, including clinical trials. The idea is bigger than simply killing cancer cells. It is about attacking the mechanisms that allow them to survive treatment in the first place. If future studies confirm these findings, CS18 could eventually form part of combination therapies designed either to prevent resistance from emerging or to make resistant tumours vulnerable to treatment again. For now, the Baylor findings offer a cautious glimmer of hope in a battle where resistance has often given cancer the upper hand. Cancer can fight back, scientists are now looking for ways to make treatment fight back harder. items.title: Too much light at night may quietly affect your heart
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe If your bedroom isn’t completely dark at night, a new study suggests it may be worth taking a closer look at how much light reaches you while you sleep. Read Also: We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple Research involving more than 11,000 people found that higher exposure to light at night was associated with subtle changes in the heart, including thicker and stiffer heart muscle. The study doesn’t prove that nighttime light causes these changes. It does, however, add to growing evidence that exposure to light after dark may have implications for cardiovascular health. Tonight, switch off unnecessary lights, draw the curtains, cover bright LEDs and put the phone away before bed. Keep the room as dark as comfortably possible. The findings, published September 9 in the European Heart Journal, raise fresh questions about something most people rarely think about: how much artificial light surrounds us after sunset. The research was led by Professor Lu Qi of Tulane University, New Orleans, USA. He noted that previous observational studies had linked nighttime light exposure with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, but much less was known about what might actually be happening inside the heart. “We carried out this research to find out what happens to the heart over time when people are exposed to too much light at nighttime,” Qi said. The study involved 11,071 participants from the UK Biobank. Each wore a light sensor on the wrist for seven days, giving researchers a measure of how much light they encountered during the night. About three years later, the participants underwent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI. The scans gave researchers a detailed look at the structure of the heart and how well it was functioning. The researchers compared people exposed to nighttime light levels above three lux with those exposed to almost no light at night. One of the clearest differences was found in the left ventricle, the heart’s main pumping chamber. Those exposed to higher levels of nighttime light had thicker walls in the left ventricle. As the wall thickened, the space inside the chamber became smaller. The scans also showed that the heart muscle was less able to flex normally with each heartbeat. Reduced flexibility can be an early sign of altered cardiac function. Changes were also found in the right ventricles and left atria, suggesting that the association was not confined to a single chamber of the heart. The heart has to contract and relax with every beat. When the muscle becomes thicker and less flexible, it can become harder for the heart to relax properly and fill with blood. Qi described the structural and functional changes as cardiac remodelling, a process in which the heart changes in response to prolonged stress or injury. “This is the first study of its kind,” he said, adding that cardiac remodelling may initially be the body’s way of adapting to stress but could ultimately weaken the heart and contribute to heart failure. The researchers said the findings add to evidence suggesting that light pollution could be an emerging cardiovascular risk factor. There is, however, an important caveat. The study found an association between nighttime light exposure and cardiac changes. It did not establish that exposure to light directly caused those changes. Other factors could have played a role, so the findings will need to be confirmed by further research. Could a darker bedroom help? An accompanying editorial by Professor Thomas Münzel of University Medical Center Mainz, Germany, and colleagues argues that doctors may need to pay greater attention to how much light their patients encounter at night, particularly those already living with heart failure or atrial fibrillation. They suggested that doctors ask about the sleep environment: how dark the bedroom is, whether the patient works night shifts and how much screen exposure occurs after sunset. The proposed changes are simple and inexpensive. They include blackout curtains, warmer and dimmer bedside lighting, and covering bright standby lights on household electronics. But the issue goes beyond the bedroom. Modern cities remain illuminated long after sunset, with streetlights, buildings, shops, advertising signs and vehicles contributing to the glow. The editorial authors argue that cities can reduce unnecessary exposure through measures such as shielded light fixtures, warmer-spectrum bulbs and dimming or motion-activated streetlights. For individuals, though, the first step may be much simpler. Switch off lights you don’t need. Draw the curtains. Cover bright LEDs. Dim your screens and put the phone away before bed. Then keep the bedroom as dark as comfortably possible. So tonight, take a look around your bedroom. Turn off the lights you don’t need, draw the curtains, cover bright LEDs and put your phone away before bed. Keeping your sleeping space darker is a simple step you can take while researchers continue to study the possible heart effects of nighttime light. Whether such measures can actually prevent heart disease remains to be established. Still, as nights become brighter, researchers are asking a question worth taking seriously: what happens to the human heart when the world around us never quite switches off?
