items.title: X : les États-Unis interviennent aux côtés d’Elon Musk contre l’amende de l’UE
items.description: Le gouvernement américain a officiellement demandé à intervenir dans la procédure engagée par X et Elon Musk contre l’amende de 120 millions d’euros infligée par l’Union européenne. Washington conteste notamment la portée extraterritoriale que pourrait avoir, selon lui, la réglementation européenne sur les entreprises américaines. Nouveau rebondissement dans le bras de fer entre Elon Musk et l’Union européenne. Le gouvernement américain a déposé jeudi une demande d’intervention devant le Tribunal de l’Union européenne à Luxembourg, afin de soutenir les recours introduits par X et son propriétaire contre une décision de la Commission européenne datant du 5 décembre 2025. Cette décision avait infligé une amende de 120 millions d’euros à X et à des entités liées à Elon Musk pour des violations du Digital Services Act (DSA), le règlement européen encadrant les grandes plateformes numériques. Dans sa demande, le gouvernement américain estime que la Commission européenne a cherché à étendre son pouvoir réglementaire à des entreprises américaines qui ne seraient pas présentes ou actives sur son territoire. Le ministère américain de la Justice affirme également que l’affaire pourrait avoir des conséquences plus larges pour les grandes entreprises technologiques américaines opérant dans l’Union européenne. Selon Washington, le maintien de la décision européenne pourrait notamment avoir des implications pour la manière dont les plateformes numériques américaines sont soumises aux règles européennes. Le recours américain porte également sur la manière dont la Commission a considéré les liens entre X, Elon Musk et d’autres sociétés appartenant à l’homme d’affaires. Le gouvernement américain conteste notamment l’approche européenne concernant la responsabilité des différentes entités au sein d'une même structure économique. Une amende liée au Digital Services Act La sanction de 120 millions d’euros constitue la première amende infligée par l’Union européenne dans le cadre de l’application du DSA contre une très grande plateforme de ce type. La procédure européenne concernait notamment le système de certification « bleue » de X, dont les modalités avaient été modifiées après le rachat de Twitter par Elon Musk. Le DSA impose aux très grandes plateformes numériques des obligations renforcées en matière de transparence, de lutte contre les contenus illégaux et de protection des utilisateurs. X et Elon Musk ont engagé des recours devant le Tribunal de l’Union européenne pour demander l’annulation de la décision de la Commission. Le gouvernement américain cherche désormais à intervenir dans ces procédures. Pour Washington, l'enjeu dépasse donc le seul montant de l'amende infligée à X. Le ministère américain de la Justice indique que l'intervention est également motivée par la volonté de protéger les entreprises américaines contre ce qu'il considère comme des mesures réglementaires extraterritoriales. The post X : les États-Unis interviennent aux côtés d’Elon Musk contre l’amende de l’UE appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: 37 miners’ death: CSOs demand mining sector overhaul; illegal operations deepen, fuel revenue flight
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike & Gabriel Ewepu ABUJA — The last thing many of the miners arrested around the Wushishi-Lukoto axis of Niger State could have expected when they were taken into custody was that some of them would not come out alive. Read Also: Full List: 20 NSCDC officers suspended over 37 miners’ death; probe panel members Between September 15 and 16, operatives of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, raided suspected illegal mining sites west of Minna and detained about 65 artisanal miners. By the early hours of September 17, dozens were dead inside an NSCDC detention facility along David Mark Road, Minna. Hospital footage showed 33 bodies in one ward. The Niger State governor subsequently confirmed that 37 detainees had died. The official explanation initially pointed to a suspected disease outbreak, with the bodies sent for medical examination. But survivors gave a different account, describing a severely overcrowded cell in which breathing became difficult. An intelligence assessment reportedly also pointed to overcrowding and inadequate ventilation as the likely causes of the deaths. Whatever the final findings establish, one fact is already beyond dispute; 37 people arrested over alleged illegal mining ended up dead in state custody within one or two days. Some of those arrested were minors or very young people. Amnesty International subsequently demanded an independent investigation into the deaths. By September 18, anger had spilled onto the streets of Minna. Protesters demanded answers. Police used tear gas and, according to some accounts, live ammunition to disperse the crowd. An overnight curfew was imposed, an NSCDC commander was suspended and government announced an investigation. But beneath the immediate questions about detention conditions and responsibility for the deaths lies a much larger question. Why is the Nigerian state so capable of finding the person holding the digger and shovel, yet seemingly less capable of identifying and dismantling the people who finance, buy, transport, and profit from the minerals that the digger and shovel produce? That is the question Minna has forced back into the national conversation. The 37 Who Never Came Out The tragedy has become a grim window into Nigeria’s informal mining economy. The men, boys, and other artisanal miners at the center of the incident were allegedly operating illegally. That point matters because illegal mining carries environmental, economic, and security consequences, and the state has a responsibility to enforce its laws. But the manner in which the enforcement chain operates is now under scrutiny. Dr Andrew Mamedu, Country Director, ActionAid Nigeria, believes the deaths should not be examined only as a detention tragedy. “We must distinguish between the poor artisanal miner digging to survive and the organised interests financing, buying and profiting from illegal mining. The enforcement net should not catch only the poorest person at the bottom while those making the biggest profits remain untouched,” Mamedu said. He put the question even more directly: “Go after the major beneficiaries of illegal mining, not only the poorest people at the bottom of the chain.” That distinction may be crucial to understanding the country’s mining crisis. For the person at the pit, the mineral is a livelihood. Further up the chain, it can become a commodity, an investment, an export and, potentially, a source of considerable profit. The identities and activities of those alleged beneficiaries remain questions to be established through evidence and investigation. But several other civil society organisations insist that enforcement which ends at the mining pit is unlikely to dismantle the wider illicit economy. Philip Jakpor, Executive Director, Renevlyn Development Initiative, RDI, also said security agencies should focus on the bigger players. “Arresting artisan miners trying to eke out a living cannot be a big burst when the big players walk freely on the streets,” Jakpor stated. “We need to know what the young men were mining; who owns the particular sites where they were apprehended or if the deaths were the silencing of pawns to shield some powerful individuals,” he added. The allegation about the deaths being intended to silence anyone remains an allegation and requires investigation. But Jakpor’s underlying question is harder to dismiss: who owns the sites, who finances the operations and who ultimately benefits? The Digger and Shovel are Easy to Find Nigeria does not lack minerals. The country is estimated in the supplied material to have more than 40 commercially viable minerals, including gold, lithium, tin, columbite, limestone, and gemstones, spread across more than 500 locations and 32 states. Yet the economic return from this geological wealth remains strikingly small. The solid minerals sector contributed only 0.72 per cent of GDP in 2023, about N401 billion, while contributing less than one per cent of national revenue. That is the paradox. A country can possess valuable minerals beneath its soil while many of the people living around those deposits remain poor, informal miners operate outside safety standards and the government struggles to capture the full economic value of extraction. The sector has laws. It has institutions. It has licensing arrangements. It has enforcement agencies. It has policy roadmaps and reform announcements. Yet illegal and informal mining remain deeply entrenched. Mamedu argues that the problem is not necessarily the absence of a regulatory framework, but its reach. “The regulatory framework exists, but implementation remains weak,” he said. “Government already has structures for formalising artisanal and small-scale miners, organising them into cooperatives and providing training on safety and environmental protection.” Then comes the question that goes to the heart of the matter. “The real question is: how many miners in rural communities actually feel the presence of that support system?” Mamedu asked. It is a question that turns the usual description of an ‘illegal miner’ on its head. If a miner has no licence, no safety equipment, no training, no environmental safeguards and no reliable access to a legitimate market, arresting him may enforce the law without fixing the system that produced the illegality. “We cannot regulate artisanal mining only with arrests. Regulation must also provide a legal pathway for people to work safely and responsibly,” Mamedu said. That pathway, critics argue, remains one of the missing pieces in Nigeria’s mining economy. Where the Money Disappears The problems extend well beyond artisanal miners. The sector faces allegations and concerns around regulatory bottlenecks, licensing delays, overlapping titles, questionable community consents and weak enforcement. Inadequate geological information makes investment and boundary enforcement harder, while poor roads, power supply and logistics increase operating costs. Financing is another problem for legitimate Nigerian operators. Communities, meanwhile, can be left carrying environmental and security costs without seeing commensurate benefits from the resources extracted around them. The result is a sector caught between formal regulation and an informal economy that remains commercially powerful. The economic consequences are significant. Revenue that could accrue through royalties, taxes and legitimate mineral sales can leak away through illicit channels. Report produced by Nigeria’s extractive industries watchdog NEITI and the Africa Network for Environment and Economic Justice (ANEEJ) with UK government funding also points to concerns about foreign buyers, shell companies, opaque ownership structures, and criminal networks. But the central question remains one of visibility. Who is actually making money? ActionAid’s Mamedu believes the answer should be pursued through the entire chain. “First, Nigeria must know who is mining, where they are mining, what they are producing and who is buying it,” he said. “Government should also follow the money. Do not stop with the young man holding a shovel. Identify the financiers, middlemen, smugglers and powerful interests benefiting from illegal mining,” Mamedu added. He also called for a mineral-traceability system covering extraction, processing, sale and export. Without such visibility, the state may continue to know the location of the pit without knowing the destination of the money. And that is where the governance problem becomes more than an illegal-mining problem. It becomes a question of whether Nigeria actually controls the mineral economy beneath its soil. Poverty at the Pit, Profit Beyond It The human dimension cannot be separated from the economics. Arc Nnimmo Bassey, Executive Director, Health of Mother Earth Foundation, HOMEF, described the deaths as a warning about the human and ecological cost of Nigeria’s extractive economy. The victims, according to reports, were reportedly aged between 14 and 20. Bassey said the country must confront the conditions pushing young people into hazardous mining. “We must stop treating extraction as the pathway to development while ignoring the lives, lands and ecosystems sacrificed in the process. Whether it is oil, gold or critical minerals, an economic model that destroys the ecological foundations of life cannot be the future we seek,” Bassey said. He called for action on poverty, unemployment and the loss of sustainable livelihoods, arguing that communities need alternatives to dangerous informal extraction. Janet Adeyemi, Founder and National President, Women in Mining Nigeria, WIMIN, similarly linked illegal mining to economic desperation. “We cannot continue to use iron fists and lethal containment strategies against young citizens who are driven into mining pits by the sheer desperation for survival. Mining, for these teenagers and young men, is an escape from hunger and extreme hardship,” Adeyemi said. Her position is that the answer cannot be simply more force. “The government must shift its focus from aggressive militarisation to human-centric formalisation,” she said. Awual Rafsanjani, Executive Director, Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre, CISLAC, broadened the diagnosis further. “CISLAC’s research shows that illegal mining and the exploitation of children are being fuelled by deep-rooted poverty, unemployment, poor access to education, insecurity, weak social protection, regulatory failures and inadequate enforcement of mining and child-labour laws,” Rafsanjani said. Those factors mean the young person at the pit is not necessarily where the story begins. For many, the pit may simply be where poverty eventually meets mineral wealth. Can Abuja Really Regulate the Pits? That brings the debate to the Constitution. Against the backdrop of the Minna deaths, Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde called for mining to be removed from the Exclusive Legislative List and placed on the Concurrent Legislative List. Under the 1999 Constitution, mines and minerals fall under federal legislative control. Makinde argues that states, being closer to mining communities, could exercise more effective control if given greater authority to legislate and regulate mining, while the Federal Government retains an oversight role. A bill seeking the constitutional change has passed second reading in the House of Representatives. Any constitutional amendment would still require the prescribed approval process, including support from at least two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly. The proposal raises an important question: would moving authority closer to the communities necessarily make the industry better governed? There is a plausible argument on the other side. States may be closer to mining communities, local conflicts and informal operators. Greater authority could potentially allow them to respond faster and formalise operations closer to the source. But decentralisation would not automatically supply states with geological data, trained mining personnel, laboratories, surveillance technology, environmental enforcement capacity, financing or independent regulatory institutions. If the problem is weak governance, moving responsibility does not by itself guarantee stronger governance. That is why Makinde’s proposal should be viewed within the wider debate about who can actually regulate Nigeria’s mineral wealth effectively, rather than as a standalone solution. A Mineral Economy Without a System Chima Williams, Executive Director, Environmental Defenders Network, EDEN, focuses on the enforcement gap. “The sector suffers from inadequate manpower and training, undermining regulation and policing. Regulations exist but implementation and enforcement are weak,” Williams said. He called for stronger manpower and training, as well as surveillance technologies, drones, helicopters and enhanced cadastral monitoring. The environmental consequences are equally serious. Unrehabilitated excavation sites can endanger people, while chemicals used in unregulated mining can contaminate soil and water. Farmland can be destroyed. Communities can lose livelihoods. The danger, therefore, is not only that Nigeria loses mineral revenue. It can lose farmland, water, public health, community trust and lives. HOMEF’s Bassey cautioned against replacing one extractive problem with another. “Nigeria must not reproduce the history of the Niger Delta by replacing oil with minerals while leaving communities to bear pollution, dispossession, livelihood losses and ecological destruction,” he said. That warning places the mining debate in a broader context. Nigeria wants its minerals to drive economic development, but the question is whether the country can extract that wealth without reproducing the environmental and social costs associated with other extractive industries. The missing pieces are now increasingly clear: effective formalisation of artisanal mining; credible licensing and cadastral systems; reliable geological and ownership data; mineral traceability; financing and safer equipment; infrastructure; environmental monitoring and rehabilitation; community participation; protection of children; stronger inter-agency coordination; and enforcement that reaches the entire value chain. Most importantly, formalisation must mean more than telling a miner to obtain a licence. It must create a realistic route from informality to legality registration, cooperatives, training, finance, equipment, safety standards and legitimate markets. How Long Can FG Look Away? The Federal Government has announced reforms and enforcement measures over the years. The Ministry of Solid Minerals Development’s roadmap acknowledges risks including policy uncertainty, infrastructure gaps and unclear enforcement roles between federal and state authorities. Yet the basic contradictions remain. A sector with more than 40 commercially viable minerals contributes less than one per cent of national revenue. A country with mining laws still has large numbers of informal operators. A government that can raid mining sites still struggles with the question of who finances and buys the minerals. Communities near valuable deposits can bear environmental costs without necessarily receiving corresponding benefits. And young people can be arrested as illegal miners while the larger commercial structures alleged to sustain illicit extraction remain difficult to see. For how long should the Federal Government keep playing the ostrich over the mining industry? The question is not whether illegal mining should be stopped. It should. The harder question is whether arrests alone can solve a problem rooted in poverty, informality, weak regulation, poor traceability and an opaque chain of financial beneficiaries. Mamedu’s prescription is blunt: investigate the deaths, publish the findings, formalise artisanal mining, provide safer equipment and finance, strengthen environmental safeguards and rehabilitate damaged communities. And his final reminder carries particular weight after Minna. “Once the state takes a person into custody, it also takes responsibility for that person’s safety,” Mamedu said. That responsibility does not end with the 37 deaths. It extends underground, to the pits where young people still search for livelihoods, and upwards, through the buyers, financiers and commercial networks that turn what is dug from Nigerian soil into money. The 37 miners may have been the easiest part of the mining economy for the state to find. The harder task is finding out who benefits when the mineral leaves the pit. Until Nigeria can answer that question with evidence, accountability and a system that works from the mining face to the final buyer, it will remain a country extraordinarily rich beneath the soil, yet strangely poor at managing what lies there. And Minna will remain more than a tragedy. It will be a warning about what happens when a state can find the shovels and diggers, but loses sight of the hands counting the money. items.title: Trump rejects Iran's 'seven-day' proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
items.description: US President Donald Trump has rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the ‌Strait of Hormuz and halt regional fighting within seven days, and told aides he expects to resume bombing after November congressional elections, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing unnamed US officials. Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi had told reporters at the United Nations on Friday that Iran has conveyed "a concrete seven-day plan" to the United States through Qatar. The seven-day timeline will start as soon as Washington accepts it, Araghchi said. Under the plan, the United States would need to take certain actions that Iran believes may take four or five days, said Araghchi, adding that on day six, the strait would be open. "And on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects." "I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," said Araghchi. "The choice now rests with the United States," he said. "Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure." Earlier on Thursday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian reaffirmed his country's commitment to dialogue and diplomacy while accusing the United States of repeatedly disrupting the negotiation process. A US official had told Reuters that the US and Iran were having "positive and constructive discussions through the mediators," but Trump was privately skeptical that Iran would meet his demands, the Wall Street Journal report said. He has told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely, the Wall Street Journal said. Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN General Assembly in New York underscored the global stakes of the seven-month-old conflict, which has disrupted oil flows through one of the world's most critical shipping lanes and drawn in regional and world powers. Return to diplomacy? The Iranian seven-day proposal comes after previous attempts at ‌diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes. Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran's conventional forces and damaging Iran's already ailing economy. Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in ​Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack ​that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. All the while, Iranian-backed Hezbollah has been engaged with Israeli forces in Lebanon. With the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government under assault from Yemen's Houthi fighters, and Houthi missiles striking inside Saudi Arabia, allies of ​the kingdom have united to show support. Defense officials of Türkiye and Pakistan, both partners in a joint ​defense pact with Saudi Arabia, met in Riyadh on Friday to review the security situation and discuss intelligence cooperation, military coordination, and integrating forces, the Saudi defense ministry said in a statement. The statement came a day after Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met within the framework of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. The violence in Yemen has prompted a ​new humanitarian crisis, the United Nations children's agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute ​malnutrition among children. (With input from agencies)

items.title: Ohanaeze At 50: Celebrating five decades with ideas, sober reflection
items.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru It was a roll call of eminent Igbo sons and daughters at Dover Hotel, Ikeja, during the week as traditional rulers, political leaders, business captains, and cultural icons all gathered for a different kind of golden jubilee. For its 50th anniversary, Ohanaeze Ndigbo, the apex Igbo socio-cultural organisation founded in 1976, chose intellectual engagement and sober reflection over the usual drums and dances. Present were Abia State Governor, Dr. Alex Otti; Chairman of the occasion, Elder U.K. Eke; His Royal Majesty, Igwe Alfred Nnaemeka Achebe; Eze Kalu Kalu Ogbu IV, Enachioken of Abiriba; former Anambra State Governor, Mr. Peter Obi; Senator Enyinnaya Abaribe; Prof. Okey Anueyiagu, who reviewed the book; Prof. Anya O. Anya; Dr. Joe Okei-Odumakin; Chief Emeka Mba; Chief Dr. Ifeanyichukwu Odii, chief launcher; Ada Agina-Ude; Kanayo O. Kanayo; and many others. The high point of the convergence was the unveiling of a 602-page book, “Ohanaeze at 50: The Burden of Memory, The Politics of Relevance,” written by Agbeze Ireke Kalu Onuma, Executive Director of the Ndigbo Lagos Foundation. The book is a critical biographical reflection on the history, evolution, challenges and continuing relevance of Ohanaeze to the socio-political development of Ndigbo. Its significance is even deeper because the author witnessed the birth of the organisation and has followed its trajectory for five decades. Welcoming guests on behalf of the President-General of Ndigbo Lagos, Chief David Ogbodo said the event celebrates “ideas, knowledge, creativity, perseverance and the power of the written word.” He described the book as more than a collection of pages, but a moment to ask hard questions: Have the objectives of the founding fathers been achieved? How does Ohanaeze compare with similar groups like Afenifere and the Arewa Consultative Forum? He commended the author for “his courage, discipline and commitment, noting that the book “promises to stimulate discussion among readers.” In his remarks, Chairman of the occasion, Elder U.K. Eke, said the book was driven by “an urgent need for institutional renewal.” “After 50 years, Ohanaeze stands at a historic crossroads. The author did not write to flatter our ego, but to provide a diagnostic mirror that challenges us to move from reactive agitation to structured, proactive and strategic regional governance,” Eke said Delivering a speech titled Ohanaeze at 50: A Book That Holds Up the Mirror, Special Guest of Honour, Governor Alex Otti, said the book goes beyond the story of Ohanaeze. “It is often said that a people who do not remember where they came from may struggle to determine where they are headed. This book is much more than a book about Ohanaeze. It is a book about memory, identity, leadership, responsibility and the future of a people,” he said. At 50, an institution deserves celebration, but it also deserves reflection. Rather than merely recounting 50 years of Ohanaeze Ndigbo, the author invites us to confront a more difficult question: What has Ohanaeze become, what should it be, and what must it do to remain relevant to generations of Ndigbo yet unborn?” According to Otti, the book examines Ohanaeze’s triumphs and disappointments, leadership transitions, internal disagreements, relationship with political authority, and its struggle to define its place in a changing Nigeria. “But perhaps the most important contribution is that it refuses to merely celebrate the past,” he noted. “An institution cannot live indefinitely on the strength of its history. Heritage gives an organisation legitimacy, but relevance must be earned continuously.” Otti said the book raises fundamental questions about institutional renewal, generational transition, and the bond between leadership and the people, with a strong message for younger Igbo. “The future of Ndigbo cannot be secured by nostalgia alone. It must be built through institutions that understand the aspirations of young people, embrace technology and innovation, engage the global Igbo diaspora, and translate cultural identity into economic, intellectual and political strength. “As Ohanaeze turns 50, we should reflect on renewal — a point where an institution looks honestly at its past, learns from it, and summons the courage to imagine something greater,” Otti stated. The post Ohanaeze At 50: Celebrating five decades with ideas, sober reflection appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: All Nigeria Editors Confab 2026: We’re building Enugu into South-East economic gateway – Mbah
items.description: By Juliet Umeh For many years, Enugu carried the history and prestige of the old Eastern Region, but Governor Peter Mbah believes nostalgia is no longer enough. His ambition is to build a state that does not merely look back at its past importance but becomes a major economic force in modern Nigeria. Read Also: Editors’ Conference 2026: After 27 years, why democracy still fails ordinary Nigerians — Onaiyekan That ambition was at the centre of his message to Nigerian editors gathered in Enugu, where he declared that a transformation was taking place across the state and challenged journalists not to take his word for it, but to go out, see the projects and speak with the people. Mbah, who spoke at the All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC 2026, said his administration wants to position Enugu as the economic gateway to the South-East, rank it among Nigeria’s top three states by Gross Domestic Product, GDP, and make it a national leader in human development. “What is happening here is, I believe, one of the fastest and most ambitious transformations of any state in modern Nigeria. And the ambition reaches beyond Enugu itself,” he told the editors. “We want this state to become an economic gateway for the South-East, one of Nigeria’s top three states by GDP, and a national leader in human development.” Roads, schools changing communities Mbah pointed to infrastructure as one of the most visible signs of the transformation, saying more than 1,500 kilometres of roads had been constructed or reconstructed across the state. But beyond roads, he said his government was attempting to take development into communities through massive investments in education, healthcare, water and transportation. He cited the delivery of more than 7,000 classrooms and the development of Smart Green Schools across the state’s 260 electoral wards. For Mbah, however, the significance of those projects is not merely in the number of buildings constructed but in how they change everyday life. “A child walking into a digitally equipped school in a community that has been left behind. Healthcare closer to home. A journey to market that will no longer take half the day,” he said, painting a picture of what the investments should mean for ordinary residents. Water supply, which had remained a major challenge in Enugu metropolis for years, also featured prominently in the governor’s account. He said water was returning “at scale” to Enugu city, alongside new transport terminals and Compressed Natural Gas, CNG, buses designed to improve movement within the state. Enugu takes to the skies Mbah also pointed to Enugu Air as another part of his administration’s attempt to reposition the state. With the state-backed airline taking to the skies, alongside other investments in transport and urban development, the governor said businesses were beginning to see Enugu differently – as a place where they could invest, build and grow. He also drew attention to the emerging Enugu Smart City, inviting the editors to visit the development and judge its progress themselves. “Enugu has become a state people are talking about, far beyond our borders. While you are here, I invite you to experience it for yourselves,” he said. Tinubu partnership helping Enugu Interestingly, Mbah did not claim that the transformation was being achieved by the state government alone. He acknowledged what he described as a strong partnership with President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Government, saying increased federal support to states had provided additional fiscal space for investment. He also cited federal interventions in roads, aviation, energy and regional development. According to him, the concessioning of Akanu Ibiam International Airport could further strengthen Enugu’s position as a gateway to the wider South-East. Mbah said: “I have acknowledged that partnership publicly before, and I gladly do so again. The partnership is helping us build at a scale and pace that would once have seemed impossible.” ‘Come and see for yourselves’ Yet perhaps the most striking part of Mbah’s presentation was his invitation to the editors to test his claims themselves. There was still much to be done, he admitted, and his administration was making no claim that every problem had been solved. Instead, he urged the visiting journalists to leave the conference halls, explore Enugu city, travel further into the state and speak directly with residents. “Take some time to explore the city. Speak to the people who live and work here and get a sense of the direction in which Enugu is moving,” he said. It was effectively an invitation to put his administration’s record under the microscope. For Mbah, the Enugu he wants Nigerians to see is no longer simply the historic Coal City, but an emerging economic and investment destination seeking a bigger role in the South-East and Nigeria. And his message to the editors was straightforward: come, look around and judge the transformation for yourselves. items.title: Hybrid vehicle prices slashed
items.description: KARACHI: After a delay of nearly two weeks, assemblers have begun lowering prices for hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) following the reduction in the general sales tax (GST) on vehicles up to 2,000cc, from 25 per cent to 18pc, effective Sept 13. Also on Friday, Mega Motor Company (MMC), BYD’s official partner in Pakistan, announced that “BYD has reached a major milestone of 10,000 vehicles on Pakistani roads, marking the fastest ramp-up by a new-entrant New Energy Vehicle (NEV) brand in the country’s automotive history”. Honda Atlas Cars Ltd (HACL) has revised the prices of HR-V e: HEV and HR-V VTIS to Rs9.299 million and Rs7.299m from Rs10.369m and Rs7.799m, respectively. HACL said the new prices are for a limited time and would be offered on limited stock. New retail prices will be applicable on all orders invoiced on and after Sept 25. Assemblers pass on GST cut after two-week delay According to a circular issued by the Indus Motor Company (IMC), the new prices of Toyota Corolla Cross HEV X and Cross HEV are Rs9.729m and Rs9.299m, respectively, down by Rs570,000 and Rs550,000. Chery Master Director Sales and Marketing Syed Asif Ahmed told Dawn that the government’s decision to settle the general sales tax (GST) issue at 18pc from 25pc on electrified vehicles may revive sales, as consumers had delayed their purchases, waiting for the government’s decision. Under the Automotive Industrial Development Policy (AIDP) 2021-26, which expired on June 30, the GST was 8.5pc on EVs. After the expiry of AIDP, the industry has been waiting for the new policy, which was expected to take effect from July 1, but it has yet to be announced. Assemblers believe that the absence of a clear policy framework had created uncertainty across the automotive value chain, affecting business planning, production scheduling and investment decisions. During the July-August period, several assemblers temporarily deferred vehicle invoicing due to the absence of clarity on the applicable policy and tariff regime. Mr Asif recalled that the 25pc GST caused a sharp drop in demand, leaving a sizable stock of assemblers’ electrified vehicles unsold until mid-September as consumers waited for clarity on the GST issue. “I think sales will return to normal in the coming months,” he said, adding that it is unclear whether GST will drop further or remain unchanged, depending on decisions in the new auto policy. On deliveries and bookings, he said most vehicles from his company and other assemblers will be delivered in the next two months. It also seems that completely knocked-down (CKD) kits are readily available at assemblers’ plants, despite geopolitical tension in the Middle East, as the Iran-US war has plunged the region into turmoil since Feb 28. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: Plateau: Killings, attacks continue despite curfew
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa – JOS The curfew was meant to bring a measure of calm to some of the communities in Plateau State that had, in recent days, been shaken by a fresh wave of killings. Read Also: We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple But barely a day after the Plateau State Government restricted movement between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. in Barkin Ladi, Bokkos and Mangu Local Government Areas, fresh deaths were reported. On Tuesday, gunmen reportedly ambushed security personnel attached to Operation Rainbow along Gagshi Road, killing one personnel, while three civilians were reportedly killed in a separate incident at Rakok, also known as Kafi Abu, in Barkin Ladi. The two incidents, according to separate accounts, brought the reported death toll to four, with the ambush on the security personnel occurring around 4 p.m., before the commencement of the night-time restriction. The incidents have added a troubling dimension to the security crisis: while the government has restricted movement during the night to give security agencies room to stabilise the affected areas, violence has continued to be reported during the day. President of the Berom Youth Moulders-Association, BYM, Barr. Dalyop Solomon Mwantiri, who said he narrowly escaped the ambush involving the Operation Rainbow personnel, described the development as evidence that the security situation was assuming a bigger dimension. “I would have also been involved in that incident if not that God, out of His mercy, saved me,” Mwantiri said. “This security challenge has entered another level. This thing is taking a bigger dimension. This will not be a night attack again. This will not be even during daytime.” A security operative, who spoke on condition of anonymity, also confirmed the ambush. “We just experienced an ambush in which a security personnel attached to Operation Rainbow was killed,” the operative said. At Rakok, community source Lawrence Gyang said three persons were killed while attending the funeral of two people who had allegedly been killed the previous day while travelling to Gashish. The Plateau State Police Command had not responded to inquiries on the incidents at the time of filing the report. A curfew under pressure The Plateau State Government imposed the dusk-to-dawn curfew on Monday, September 21, following what it described as emerging security threats in Barkin Ladi, Bokkos and Mangu. Commissioner for Information and Communication, Joyce Lohya Ramnap, said movement would be restricted from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. until further notice. The government said the measure was intended to maintain public order, protect lives, prevent further breakdown of law and order and enable security agencies to stabilise the affected communities. Security agencies were directed to enforce the order, while motorcycle use was also banned in the affected areas. For residents already living under the shadow of repeated attacks, the announcement offered the possibility of temporary respite. Yet the latest incidents have shown that restricting movement alone does not end the threat. The Tuesday attack along Gagshi Road happened before the curfew began. The reported killings at Rakok also occurred in the broader context of a community gathering for a funeral. And in another incident in Mangu, the Mwaghavul Youth Movement alleged that three men were killed at about 7:39 p.m. Tuesday during the period when movement was already restricted. The separate incidents underline the different challenges facing communities: preventing attacks during the day, protecting residents during the curfew hours and ensuring that those enforcing security measures are themselves not exposed to ambushes. Three killed during curfew in Mangu In Mangu, the Mwaghavul Youth Movement, MYM, said three Mwaghavul men were killed in an ambush at the Kyikyau-Gyambwas boundary in Mangu Halle District at about 7:39 p.m. on Tuesday. The victims were identified as Samson Dachet, 45; Gambo Fwangyil, 50; and Zughumnan Bamaiyi, 35. The movement said the men were among residents keeping watch over their community. In a statement signed by its Director of Public Affairs, Tubwot Joël Sunday, on behalf of its president, Comr. Kyesmang Jonathan Yusuf, the group condemned the incident and called for a review of the curfew. The group questioned how residents could remain safe if armed attackers were still able to operate despite the restriction. It demanded effective patrols, rapid-response capacity, intelligence-led operations and appropriate engagement with recognised community vigilance structures. The MYM said the curfew should not result in law-abiding residents being confined to their homes without adequate protection. Its position has brought the debate over the curfew into sharper focus: whether the restriction should be viewed simply as a limitation on civilian movement or as part of a wider security operation involving surveillance, intelligence and rapid intervention. When the killings continued The Tuesday incidents did not occur in isolation. They followed a succession of attacks that had already claimed several lives across Barkin Ladi, Riyom and Mangu. At least nine persons were reportedly killed in separate attacks between Saturday night and Sunday morning, including five passengers travelling to Gana-Ropp as labourers and two people, including a pastor, who were reportedly killed while travelling to church at Dorowa Babuje. A woman was also reportedly killed at Baten Wereng in Riyom, while another person was reportedly killed at Ratyidi in Fan District. Five of the victims were travelling to Gana-Ropp in search of work. Pyem Youth Leader in Gana-Ropp, Ukasha Garaba, said: “We evacuated the corpses of five persons from Gana-Ropp. They were passengers who were travelling as labourers. “They were simply travelling to their destination when they were attacked. It is painful, and something needs to be done urgently to protect innocent travellers.” Their deaths illustrated how insecurity has transformed ordinary journeys into potentially dangerous ventures. For residents, the fear is no longer limited to travelling at night. A trip to the farm, a journey to the market, a funeral procession or a visit to a place of worship can all become occasions of anxiety. Women and children on the run At Dorowa Bubuje in Barkin Ladi, the human cost of the violence was seen in the evacuation of women and children following reports of gunshots from the direction of Kantoma. Lawrence Shong, a resident, said gunshots who spoke to our correspondent said the gunmen stormed the community and starting shotting. “Women and children were evacuated because of the attack.” The BYM spokesman, Rwang Tengwong, also said women and children were moved to safer locations. “Women and children were evacuated from this place because of the attack,” he said. Military personnel were reportedly deployed to the area, but Tengwong called for sustained security presence to prevent further attacks. The evacuation captures the deeper reality behind the casualty figures. When women and children begin fleeing before an attack is fully understood, it means fear has already taken hold. The market became a killing ground In Mangu, the violence has also reached places that ordinarily serve as economic lifelines. On Friday night, gunmen reportedly attacked a vegetable market in Mangu town, killing three persons and injuring scores. The incident occurred at about 8:30 p.m. as traders and buyers were preparing to close for the day. President of the MDA, Bulus Dabit, said the attackers opened fire on a vehicle leaving the market, killing two women and a young man. Several other people were reportedly injured and referred to the Jos University Teaching Hospital, JUTH, for treatment. George Amos a resident of Mangu said: “The attack was more than another entry in the casualty figures. “It struck at the heart of everyday economic life.” “Markets are where farmers sell their produce, traders earn income and families obtain food “. “When fear empties a market, the consequences extend beyond those directly attacked” he said Even funerals become dangerous The reported Rakok killings have introduced another disturbing element into the crisis. According to the community account, the three civilians were killed while attending the funeral of two people allegedly killed the previous day. For communities already traumatised by repeated violence, such incidents create a frightening cycle, ,People are attacked, Families gather to bury the dead. Mourners become exposed. Another attack occurs And another set of families is left grieving. The bigger Mangu crisis The latest incidents have also renewed attention on the wider security crisis in Mangu. The Mwaghavul Development Association has claimed that more than 750 Mwaghavul people have been killed in attacks since 2023. The MDA also rejected claims that any part of Mwaghavul territory has been legally ceded, sold or transferred. BYM: Curfew must be matched with security The Berom Youth Moulders-Association has called for a broader security strategy alongside the curfew. The group said residents did not simply need restrictions on their movement but effective measures capable of preventing attackers from operating freely. It called for security operations around suspected hideouts and access routes, sustained deployment along vulnerable roads, intelligence-led operations and protection for communities and mourners. “The people of Plateau State are tired of burying their sons and daughters,” the association said. Mutfwang’s assurance Governor Caleb Mutfwang has repeatedly maintained that the state government will continue to protect residents. Speaking at the 2026 Plateau Annual Convention of the General Council of Assemblies of God Nigeria, North East Zone, at Gyel, Jos South, the governor said: “I cannot abandon my responsibility of securing the people of Plateau State. We will protect our people with all that we have, within the ambit of the law.” “Plateau State will not be defeated by violence or the gun” he added. items.title: 6 million citizens registered under PM’s fuel relief scheme: Shaza Fatima
items.description: • Minister says over 6.18m tokens generated, 4.79m redeemed since launch • 24/7 control room monitoring implementation for ensuring transparency and timely resolution of issues ISLAMABAD: Federal Infor­mation Technology and Teleco­mmunication Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said on Friday that around 5.91 million citizens had been registered under the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme since its launch. Addressing a news conference along with Minister of State for Finance and Railways Bilal Azhar Kayani, she said over 6.18 million fuel relief tokens had been generated, of which 4.79m had been successfully redeemed. Reiterating that the government had removed the five-litre limit for motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi following public feedback, she said the ownership requirement had also been remo­ved for motorcycle and rickshaw users who used rented vehicles. She said that amid volatility in global oil markets resulting from regional tensions in the Middle East, the fuel relief scheme was aimed at providing direct and targeted relief to citizens most affected by rising fuel costs. She reiterated that the scheme provided fuel relief to eligible two- and three-wheelers, including motorcycles, Qingqi and rickshaws, as well as cars up to 800cc. The scheme had been designed to ensure that relief reached eligible citizens through a simple, transparent and technology-enabled mechanism. The IT minister also displayed a live dashboard showing the total number of registrations, tokens generated and redeemed, as well as the provincial breakdown of the figures. Token figures The province- and region-wise breakdown of redeemed tokens included 210,032 in Islamabad Capital Territory, 3.07m in Punjab, 1.21m in Sindh, 267,460 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 6,761 in Balo­chi­stan, 23,796 in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and 4,845 in Gilgit-Baltistan. The minister underscored that the figures reflected the broad outreach of the scheme, with eligible citizens across all provinces and regions availing themselves of fuel relief. She said a 24/7 control room at the IT and Telecommunication Ministry was monitoring implementation of the scheme across the country. The control room was overseeing the process from registration and token generation to redemption, with a focus on ensuring transparency and timely resolution of issues. She said citizens facing any difficulty or requiring assistance regarding the scheme could call 9771 or visit the official website pmfuelrelief.pk for information and support. Ms Fatima said provincial governments and their administrations were playing an important role in overseeing the programme. She said around three meetings were being held daily to monitor its implementation, while officials were also present on the ground. She said she had personally visited petrol stations where people were facing problems and observed the implementation of the scheme. Awareness campaigns The minister thanked petrol pump dealers, oil marketing companies and the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) for facilitating citizens under the scheme and urged petrol pump staff to assist eligible people with registration and provide information about the facility. She said the government was conducting awareness campaigns and would also use the media to reach more people, particularly those affected by higher petrol prices. The minister said the government was also monitoring petrol stations through a live GIS map to identify facilities being used and address problems. Regarding older motorcycles, Ms Fatima said she had seen very few cases involving motorcycles registered before 2006. She added that there were some old cars, including Suzuki FX models, but said most of the people targeted by the subsidy were receiving the facility. She said the scheme was continuing smoothly and petrol pumps were being paid within a 24-hour cycle. With input from APP Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: King’s College Concession: Fears, assurances of parents, Old Boys
items.description: By Adesina Wahab That the Federal Ministry of Education signed a concession agreement with the Old Boys Association of King’s College, Lagos to run the school for 50 years is not news, but the manner all other 116 unity colleges have been shut for weeks over the issue has become a matter of asking what the issue really is? Read Also: Rivers 2023 results: Questions on Wike’s account on Atiku, Obi There are 117 unity colleges across the country, four of which are in Lagos State, but parents’ antagonism against the concession is hinged on a number of factors, Saturday Vanguard gathered even as it is clear that the school appears to have been run down.The factors can be termed “fears” that the parents feel are real. On the other hand, the concessionaire are of the view that they have taken adequate steps to take care of the fears. While the Federal Ministry of Education, FME, is also giving the impression that there is nothing to fear. Our fears – Parents The Parent Teacher Association, PTA, of Unity Colleges in the Southwest, led by Mr Ayopo Somefun, supported by his colleagues across the country, expressed the fears of the parents to include: Introduction of outrageous fee regime According to them, examples abound of where public schools were returned to private owners and the next thing was that the schools became elitist. They cited some schools returned by the Lagos State government, incidentally when Asiwaju Bola Tinubu was Governor, to missions and the fees were hiked astronomically. They mentioned instances where parents are now paying close to a million naira per term. Unity college students pay barely N100,000 annually. Elitist nature will rubbish Federal Character Principles The parents are also of the view that when the new operators come in, and the school is turned to an elitist one, children from across the country would not be able to attend again. The admission could be skewed in favour of the big guys in the society. Old Boys should support the college not run in Another point being raised by the parents is that old students are not supposed to take over their alma mater but to support same with facilities, endowment, scholarships among others. They argue that if those who graduated before them had taken over the college, probably many of them would not have had the opportunity to attend it. Public assets should be left for Nigerians to enjoy The PTA opined that if the old boys are so concerned about contributing to lifting the quality of education, they could come together and set up their own school and leave public assets like King’s College for Nigerians to enjoy. Staff will lose their jobs Though it is the FME that is the employer of most workers in the college, except for some engaged by the PTA, the group is saying most of the current workers could lose their jobs, as concessionaire would bring in their own people. Government will concession other schools The PTA is also alleging that the FG has entered into agreement with the World Bank to secure $20 million to concession 20 unity colleges in Nigeria. They are of the view that if the concession of King’s College stands, it would move to other colleges. What we plan to do – Old Boys The King’s College Old Boys Association, KCOBA, under the leadership of Kashim Ibrahim Imam, has repeatedly tried to assuage the feelings of the PTA. The group has held sessions and media interactions explaining what they want to do with their alma mater when they begin to run it. Imam and his team listed what they intend to do to include: We will provide affordable quality education To achieve this, Imam said an endowment fund of N100 billion has been set up. He explained, “From our findings, we got to know that about N2.4 billion is committed to the college annually, while we don’t want to begin to ask where does the money go, we are sure of raising the N100 billion seed fund. Surely, we will invest the money and let us even say in the first few years we are going to spend say up to N4 billion because of the need to put facilities back in shape, the invested fund would continue to bring in profits that will sustain our efforts. So, there is not going to be need for any outrageous fees,” he said. Federal Character Principle will continue Imam explained that the college would still be run with the principles of Federal Character in mind. He said the admission process would take care of that . He added that each state and FCT would be given 10 slots each in the first instance before other slots would be allocated taking note of merit, catchment areas, and others. Our support in the past were rendered futile The old boys expressed frustration that their support in the past amounted to nothing because facilities were not maintained. They recalled air conditioners installed that were damaged barely four months after. An old boy said the tartan tracks laid on the field and the water draining system installed on the football field were damaged when the school authorities started renting the field out for social events. An old boy, Sir Gbolahan Olayomi, mentioned how his effort to support the college with edtech materials was frustrated. He also said the hostels that were renovated and rehabilitated by different sets have become derelict because of poor maintenance. ‘We are not buying the college’ On the allegation that the old boys were planning to buy the college, Imam said as far as King’s College is concerned, there is no willing seller or a willing buyer. He reiterated that the group has no intention of buying the school. We will increase salary not retrench workers Rather than laying off staff, Imam gave the assurance that his group would significantly increase the salaries of workers. He, however, said that would apply to those who want to work with his team. “They are federal government employees, in case there is anybody who does not want to work with us, the ministry will transfer the person to any other unity college nearby. In Lagos, there are three other unity colleges apart from our school.” Nothing stops us from lifting the status of our alma mater On the suggestion that the old boys should go and start their own school, Imam explained that there are many old boys owning schools or working in the education sector, but that does not stop them from lifting the status of the college that made them. “The facilities that are currently run down now will be given great facelift I can assure you that. King’s College is an institution that must not be allowed to be in the parlous state it is now. We only want to give back and not allow that great college to become a very poor shadow of its past glory. It must attain higher glory,” he stated. We will curb admission racketeering An elder statesman, Femi Okunnu, SAN, who is also an old boy, was the first to raise the issue of admission racketeering in the college. Accusing fingers are being pointed at some parents and some school officials. A slot is reportedly sold for as high as N500,000. The development has led to say somebody like Abiodun Emeka claiming to be an indigene of Yobe State. Recently, the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, accused PTA leaders of engaging in it by conniving with some ministry and college officials to do so. The PTA also fired back that they are not admission officers. The KCOBA promised that the admission process would be made fair and transparent and eliminate racketeering. Government can do whatever it likes with its colleges On the allegation of a World Bank loan to concession unity colleges, KCOBA held that the government can do whatever it likes with its schools. Vanguard News The post King’s College Concession: Fears, assurances of parents, Old Boys appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The many sides of Otti: Obi, Tinubu, ‘otumokpo’ and life after power
items.description: By Juliet Umeh There are moments when Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, sounds more like the banker he once was than the politician he has become. Read Also: Rivers 2023 results: Questions on Wike’s account on Atiku, Obi Ask him how Abia could confront billions of naira in inherited obligations while pouring money into roads, hospitals and schools, and he talks about expenditure ratios, financial discipline and cutting the cost of governance. Push him on Peter Obi, President Bola Tinubu and the intrigues of 2027, and another Otti emerges: cautious, deliberate and unwilling to be boxed into declarations he does not want to make. Then comes the humorous side. What is the secret behind the spending? “That’s what I call my otumokpo,” he joked, using the expression for supernatural powers before explaining that there was no magic involved. These different sides of Otti emerged during a wide-ranging interview he granted ARISE Television, where he spoke about Obi, Tinubu, 2027, Abia’s finances, electricity subsidy and life after Government House. Perhaps one of the most revealing moments came when he explained why he remained in the Labour Party, LP, when Obi decided to leave. “You don’t relocate from your house because armed robbers came,” Otti said. According to him, Obi consulted him before leaving. “He came and met with me. And I told him that for me, I was staying back. But he said he was leaving.” Otti said Obi believed LP’s internal crisis would not be resolved while he remained, although the governor thought resolution was already underway. Still, he would not condemn Obi’s decision. “He could have seen what I wasn’t seeing,” Otti said. “I don’t even have superiority of knowledge.” Walking the Tinubu-Obi tightrope Otti’s position becomes more intriguing as 2027 approaches. While maintaining a working relationship with Tinubu, he insists cooperation with the President should not automatically be interpreted as an electoral endorsement. Pressed about suggestions that Southeast governors were backing Tinubu, Otti insisted: “Nobody can speak for me. I’m the one that will speak for myself.” He said he had a Labour Party presidential candidate and declined to reveal who would eventually get his personal vote. On Obi, however, he insisted there was no personal quarrel. “Peter Obi and I are not fighting,” he said, adding that Obi, Atiku Abubakar or any other candidate would be free to campaign in Abia. That is what democracy is about.” ‘I stand by what I wrote’ Otti also stood by his previous account of the funds Obi left after governing Anambra State, an issue that has returned to political debate ahead of 2027. “What I documented in 2020 is factual,” he said. But Otti drew a distinction between the savings he knew about and whatever liabilities may have existed. “I cannot talk about the debts. It’s not within my competence to talk about it.” The ‘otumokpo’ behind Abia If Otti is willing to discuss Obi’s financial record, he is equally eager to put his own before the public. He said his administration inherited about N191.2 billion in different obligations, including contractor debts and pension arrears. Yet his government has continued spending heavily on infrastructure. His “otumokpo”, Otti explained, is financial discipline. We said no less than 80 percent of our budget will go into capital expenditure.” Abia’s 2026 budget is N1.016 trillion, according to the state government. Otti said containing recurrent expenditure leaves the government with resources for roads, hospitals, schools and other infrastructure. “If you don’t manage your costs very well, you will find that year in, year out, you are struggling, you are working hard, you are sweating, but it’s not showing.” ‘Electricity cheaper than darkness’ The same philosophy shapes his position on electricity subsidy. Otti argues that manufacturers need reliable power more than subsidised consumption. “If you have to run a generator, buy the diesel, provide for the maintenance, you will find that you are paying a whole lot more than public power supply. It’s still cheaper than darkness.” But perhaps his most striking declaration was about his own future. There will be no Senate or presidency after Abia, he insists, a position he has reiterated publicly. “Not local government chairman, not Senate, not President. I think I came to deliver a call, and that is what I am doing now. Once I finish it, I will retire.” For a politician who fought repeatedly to become governor, it is an intriguing promise: when the Abia chapter closes, Otti says the political book closes with it. items.title: PM invites Achakzai for ‘direct talks’
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Soon after the opposition annou­nced its decision to extend the date of its long march, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday invited Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mehmood Achakzai for direct talks, apparently in a bid to ensure political stability in the country. According to a source close to the prime minister, PM Shehbaz extended the invitation for dialogue, but no response had so far been received from the opposition leader. “Yes [the PM has invited Mr Achakzai], but nothing yet [from the opposition side],” the source said. A Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) spokesman conf­irmed that the opposition leader had received the prime minister’s invitation. Before the latest invitation, the prime minister had already invited Mr Achakzai on Sept 11 for mandatory consultation on the appointment of a new chief election commi­ssioner (CEC). Prime Minister Sheh­baz, who is currently in the United States to attend the UN General Assembly, is expected to return within a few days. Before the prime minister’s first invitation to Mr Achakzai over the appointment of the CEC, National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq had urged both the prime minister and the opposition leader to sit together for consultations on the appointment of a new CEC. Under Article 213(2A) of the Constitution, the prime minister is required to consult the opposition leader in the National Assembly and forward three names for the appointment of the chief election commissioner to a parliamentary committee, which hears the candidates and confirms one of them. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

items.title: Rivers 2023 results: Questions on Wike’s account on Atiku, Obi
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The 2023 presidential election has thrown up many post-election arguments, but FCT Minister Nyesom Wike’s latest account has opened a particularly revealing window into the calculations of the five aggrieved Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, governors who opposed Atiku Abubakar, and why Rivers State was treated differently from other South-South states. Read Also: Editors’ Conference 2026: After 27 years, why democracy still fails ordinary Nigerians — Onaiyekan Speaking on TVC’s Journalists’ Hangout, Wike said the G5 governors were less concerned about Peter Obi taking votes in parts of the South-South than about preventing Atiku from benefiting from the region’s traditional PDP strength. “How did he (Obi) win? We, in the G5, had our strategy. We said, PDP is stronger in the South-South. And our problem would be Atiku. Therefore, instead of Atiku to take it, let it go to the Labour Party,” Wike said. The political calculation was simple. If the PDP’s traditional strength in the South-South translated into votes for Atiku, it could boost his national tally. But if those votes moved to Obi, Atiku would be denied the advantage. According to Wike, that was precisely what happened in some states. Why Rivers was different Wike said the strategy was deployed in Edo and Cross River, but Rivers was deliberately kept outside it. “We felt that Atiku was more of a factor in that election than Obi. So our strategy was to make sure that you vote for Obi to win in order to deny Atiku the votes,” Wike said. Then came Rivers. “It was only in Rivers, I said, ‘No, Obi would not win here because if he does, it would send a wrong signal somewhere and people would not understand it.’ And we stopped it,” Wike said. That sentence has become the most contentious part of his account. Wike did not explain publicly what he meant by a ‘wrong signal’. That leaves an obvious question hanging: if an Obi victory was considered useful elsewhere because it would deprive Atiku of votes, why was the same outcome unacceptable in Rivers? One possible explanation is the peculiar political importance of Rivers to Wike, but that would be an inference rather than something established by his statement. What Wike’s account does establish is that, according to him, Rivers was deliberately treated differently from other states covered by the G5 strategy. Result that remains contested INEC declared Bola Tinubu the winner in Rivers with 231,591 votes, followed by Obi with 175,071 and Atiku with 88,468. Tinubu’s margin over Obi was 56,520 votes. Those figures have remained contentious. The BBC’s 2023 election project published the declared results using INEC data, while subsequent scrutiny of polling-unit result sheets on the IReV portal generated questions about discrepancies in some Rivers results. But questions about discrepancies are not, by themselves, proof that Wike or the G5 manipulated the election. Wike has also rejected that interpretation of his remarks. On September 23, he dismissed allegations that he rigged the 2023 presidential election for Tinubu as a ‘baseless narrative’, insisting that what the G5 did was political manoeuvring against Atiku. The distinction is important because Wike’s latest disclosure is essentially an account of political strategy. The unanswered issue is whether the strategy crossed the line from political mobilisation into interference with voters’ choices. Demand for answers That is where the controversy has moved beyond the political exchanges. The Centre for Human Rights and Civic Education, CHRICED, has called for an investigation into Wike’s disclosure, asking relevant institutions to determine what the G5 strategy involved and whether it affected the integrity of the 2023 presidential election. CHRICED Executive Director, Ibrahim Zikirullahi, said the disclosure raised a fundamental democratic question. “If state officials can ‘allow’ or ‘prevent’ candidates from winning in their states, then the fundamental principle that sovereignty belongs to the people is gravely undermined,” Zikirullahi said. The organisation argued that elections should not become exercises in which powerful political actors determine which candidate should benefit from voters’ choices. That is the institutional question hanging over Wike’s account: where does ordinary political strategy end and improper interference with the choices of voters begin? When Obi became useful to the G5 There is an irony in the episode. The five governors were PDP members locked in a bitter dispute with their party’s presidential candidate and national leadership. Yet, according to Wike, Obi became politically useful to them in parts of the South-South. He did not have to be their preferred candidate. His votes simply had to come at Atiku’s expense. That makes the strategy less an alliance with Obi than an attempt to deny Atiku the benefit of a region where the PDP had traditionally enjoyed considerable strength. Rivers, however, was the exception. And that exception is what has turned an old election strategy into a fresh political controversy. The question beyond Rivers Social media reactions have since pushed the debate further. Morris Monye wrote on X: “Look at what Wike is saying on national television. Does he not know that suppressing votes of the people is also treason? Just look at that. This makes me so upset. He’s already shared the votes and said, ‘Oh, we won’t see votes in Delta, Edo, etc.’” Another X user, Roy, accused Wike of suppressing the popular will. “When you say you stopped Peter Obi winning Rivers State, you are saying you stopped the will of the people. You used INEC ad hoc staff, law enforcement, dogs, the courts, up to the Supreme Court, to keep Nigeria in oppression. Nothing shouts treason louder than this. But go on, keep talking,” Roy wrote. Those reactions are political opinions, not independent evidence that the 2023 election was manipulated. Arise TV broadcaster, Rufai Oseni, has also widened the argument by questioning whether the political calculations Wike described extended beyond Rivers. “But I’m sure Wike, too, should tell us how we also helped Obi win Lagos, you know, in all of this, because when people talk, they just think that they’re everything,” Rufai said.That was a question, not evidence of a coordinated ntervention in Lagos. But it points to the larger issue raised by Wike’s account: presidential elections are shaped not only by manifestos, rallies and voting-day activity, but also by alliances, regional calculations and political structures operating behind the scenes. Wike has supplied part of that story. He has explained why, according to him, the G5 wanted Obi to take votes from Atiku in some South-South states. He has explained why Rivers was excluded from that calculation. What remains unexplained is what exactly made an Obi victory in Rivers capable of sending the ‘wrong signal’. Until that question is answered, the most revealing part of Wike’s disclosure may not be who won Rivers in 2023, but why he says some votes were politically useful elsewhere, and politically unacceptable at home. Vanguard News The post Rivers 2023 results: Questions on Wike’s account on Atiku, Obi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Attaques terroristes au Sahel : le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè déplore une « caution inavouée » de la communauté internationale
items.description: Le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE, a rencontré Monsieur Alexandre ZOUEV, Sous-Secrétaire général par intérim du Bureau des Nations Unies de lutte contre le terrorisme, le 25 septembre 2026. Cette rencontre a été une opportunité pour les deux hommes, de passer en revue le partenariat et de faire des suggestions pour améliorer ce partenariat entre le Burkina Faso et cette entité onusienne, qui apporte un soutien à notre pays dans la lutte contre le terrorisme, à travers notamment le renforcement des capacités opérationnelles des acteurs chargés de cette lutte. Le responsable onusien a réitéré l’engagement de sa structure à poursuivre l’appui au Burkina Faso, en matière d’enquêtes anti terroristes et d’autres programmes de collaboration. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères a indiqué que le Burkina Faso apprécie la collaboration avec le Bureau des Nations Unies pour la lutte contre le terrorisme. Mais tirant leçon de ce qui n’a pas marché jusque-là, il a souligné la nécessité de mettre l’accent sur le volet prévention pour éviter les recrutements des jeunes dans les rangs des terroristes, et de rallier plusieurs autres acteurs pour aller dans une démarche plus globale dans cette lutte. A cette audience, le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè a exprimé son indignation face à la caution non avoué que la communauté internationale accorde aux groupes terroristes, soit à travers le silence soit à travers l’offre d’espaces d’expression à ces groupes. A titre d’exemple, le ministre des Affaires étrangères est revenu sur la surprise des pays de la Confédération AES, de constater le silence totale de la communauté internationale lorsque le JNIM s’est associé à un groupe séparatiste (le FLA) pour attaquer le Mali en avril dernier. >, a déclaré le ministre Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE.
