items.title: ONU : Le Burkina Faso appelle à faire de chaque pays le maître d’œuvre de sa propre paix
items.description: Lors d’une réunion de la Commission de consolidation de la paix de l’ONU à New York, le ministre burkinabè des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré, a plaidé pour un leadership national dans la conception et la mise en œuvre des programmes de consolidation de la paix. Le Burkina Faso a défendu, jeudi 24 septembre 2026, une approche fondée sur l’appropriation nationale des processus de consolidation de la paix. La position a été présentée au siège des Nations unies à New York par le ministre des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération régionale et des Burkinabè de l’extérieur, Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré, lors d’une réunion de la Commission de consolidation de la paix. Les priorités nationales au centre des interventions Dans sa déclaration, le Burkina Faso a estimé que l’appui international à la consolidation de la paix doit s’appuyer sur un leadership fort des administrations nationales. Selon Ouagadougou, les administrations doivent être placées au cœur de la conception, de la mise en œuvre et du suivi-évaluation des programmes soutenus par les partenaires techniques et financiers. Les priorités nationales doivent, selon cette approche, orienter les interventions afin d’éviter la conception de projets déconnectés des mécanismes institutionnels et des réalités locales. Le ministre a également défendu une définition élargie de l’appropriation nationale. Celle-ci doit permettre aux institutions nationales et locales de définir les priorités, d’orienter les interventions, d’en assurer le pilotage et de contribuer à la pérennisation des résultats. « Les pays doivent devenir les maîtres d’œuvre de leur destinée, de leur propre paix », a déclaré le Burkina Faso. L’expérience du Fonds pour la consolidation de la paix Dans son intervention, le Burkina Faso s’est également appuyé sur son expérience avec le Fonds pour la consolidation de la paix. Le pays a cité les conclusions d’une évaluation indépendante menée en 2025. Celle-ci relève notamment des résultats en matière de renforcement des capacités locales, d’amélioration de la confiance entre les institutions et les populations, ainsi que d’implication croissante des autorités et de la société civile. L’évaluation identifie toutefois des marges d’amélioration, notamment concernant la participation nationale à la conception stratégique des interventions. Elle souligne également que la durabilité des acquis dépend de leur ancrage institutionnel et local. Trois priorités mises en avant par Ouagadougou À partir de cette expérience, le Burkina Faso a identifié trois priorités pour renforcer l’efficacité et la durabilité des actions de consolidation de la paix. Il s’agit d’abord de co-construire les interventions avec les acteurs nationaux et locaux. La deuxième priorité consiste à renforcer durablement les capacités des institutions nationales. Enfin, le Burkina Faso préconise d’inscrire les acquis dans les politiques publiques, afin d’en assurer la pérennité. Pour Ouagadougou, l’appui international doit donc contribuer au renforcement des capacités nationales sans se substituer aux institutions des pays concernés. Le Burkina Faso a conclu en affirmant que la paix durable doit se construire « de l’intérieur », avec l’appui de partenaires engagés aux côtés des États. L’article ONU : Le Burkina Faso appelle à faire de chaque pays le maître d’œuvre de sa propre paix est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: ONU : Le Royaume-Uni sollicite le soutien du Burkina Faso pour des candidatures britanniques aux postes internationaux
items.description: En marge de l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU, le ministre burkinabè des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré, s’est entretenu avec ses homologues gabonaise et britannique sur les perspectives de coopération entre Ouagadougou et leurs pays respectifs. Le Burkina Faso entend renforcer ses relations bilatérales avec la République gabonaise. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré, s’est entretenu avec son homologue gabonaise, Marie-Edith Tassyla-Ye-Doumbeneny, jeudi 24 septembre 2026, dans les locaux des Nations unies à New York. Au cours de cette rencontre, les deux responsables ont salué la qualité des relations historiques entre le Burkina Faso et le Gabon. Ils ont notamment mis en avant les liens humains et fraternels entre les deux peuples, ainsi que la présence d’importantes communautés des deux pays établies de part et d’autre. Les deux parties ont également exprimé leur volonté de consolider davantage les relations bilatérales. Cette dynamique devrait notamment se concrétiser lors de la tenue, en novembre prochain, de la grande Commission mixte de coopération Burkina Faso-Gabon. Cette rencontre devrait permettre aux deux pays de renforcer et d’actualiser leurs instruments juridiques de coopération. L’objectif affiché est de dynamiser davantage l’axe Ouagadougou-Libreville et d’en faire un exemple de coopération Sud-Sud. Dans le cadre de ses activités diplomatiques à New York, Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré a également accordé une audience à Kirsty McNeill, ministre d’État chargée du Développement international du Royaume-Uni. Selon les éléments communiqués par la diplomatie burkinabè, la responsable britannique est venue solliciter le soutien du Burkina Faso en faveur de candidatures britanniques à des postes internationaux. Le ministre burkinabè a indiqué que Ouagadougou examinerait attentivement cette requête. Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré a toutefois souligné la nécessité de renforcer la coopération entre le Burkina Faso et le Royaume-Uni. items.title: Burkina Faso : Les recettes budgétaires atteignent 1 972,85 milliards FCFA au premier semestre 2026
items.description: Au 30 juin 2026, les recettes budgétaires ont dépassé de 21,97 % l’objectif fixé pour le premier semestre, tandis que les dépenses exécutées s’élèvent à 1 832,67 milliards FCFA. Le gouvernement burkinabè a examiné, jeudi 24 septembre 2026, la situation d’exécution du budget de l’État, exercice 2026, au 30 juin. Présenté par Aboubacar Nacanabo, ministre de l’Économie et des Finances, le rapport fait ressortir un niveau de recouvrement des recettes supérieur aux prévisions semestrielles. Au 30 juin 2026, les recettes budgétaires recouvrées s’établissent à 1 972,85 milliards de FCFA, pour un objectif semestriel de 1 617,43 milliards de FCFA, soit un taux d’exécution de 121,97 %. À la même période en 2025, les recettes budgétaires s’élevaient à 1 562,05 milliards de FCFA. 1 832,67 milliards FCFA de dépenses exécutées Du côté des dépenses, le niveau d’exécution des crédits de paiement s’établit à 1 832,67 milliards de FCFA au terme du premier semestre 2026.Ce montant correspond à un taux d’exécution de 46,77 %, sur une prévision annuelle de 3 918,29 milliards de FCFA. À la même date en 2025, les dépenses exécutées s’élevaient à 1 640,39 milliards de FCFA. Plus de 3 300 milliards FCFA encaissés par les comptables du Trésor La situation de la trésorerie fait également ressortir une progression des encaissements. Au premier semestre 2026, 3 306,42 milliards de FCFA ont été encaissés sur les comptes de disponibilités des comptables directs du Trésor. À la même période en 2025, ces encaissements s’élevaient à 2 298,67 milliards de FCFA. Par ailleurs, l’épargne budgétaire ressort à 532,32 milliards de FCFA, tandis que le solde budgétaire s’établit à 59,58 milliards de FCFA. Le gouvernement appelle à poursuivre les efforts Au regard du niveau d’exécution du budget au 30 juin 2026, le Conseil des ministres a félicité les acteurs impliqués dans sa mise en œuvre. Il les a également exhortés à poursuivre les efforts afin de renforcer l’efficacité de l’exécution budgétaire. Le Conseil a enfin marqué son accord pour la transmission du rapport à l’Assemblée législative du Peuple. items.title: We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple
items.description: By Juliet Umeh Michael and Akintomide cannot see, but together they cook, clean, raise their children and battle unemployment as they wait for the teaching jobs they believe could transform their family. For Michael Ogunkanmi, darkness has been part of life for almost as long as he can remember. His wife, Akintomide, also lives without sight. Yet, inside their modest home, the couple are raising three children who can see. Their lives are built around memory, touch, teamwork and an understanding developed over years together. If an item is kept somewhere in the house, everyone knows where it belongs. If either Michael or his wife changes its position, the other must be told. “We do things together,” Michael said. “Even though we cannot see, we do things together. If she is doing something and I don’t know how to do it, she will teach me. That is how we help each other at home.” Now their children are old enough to lend their eyes occasionally. “Sometimes, when there are things we cannot identify, we call the children and ask, ‘What is this?’ and they will tell us,” he said. But long before the children became old enough to help, Michael and Akintomide managed by themselves. “Nobody was helping us,” he recalled. “If I put something in a particular place, I know there is something there. If anybody wants to change it, we will inform each other.” Love found in school Michael, 39, and Akintomide, 34, met in school. Their shared disability became only one part of a relationship that eventually produced three children – two girls and a boy. Their eldest daughter is eight, their son is five, while their youngest daughter is three. The children are sighted, although Michael said the eldest has difficulty seeing objects at a distance. At eight, she is already becoming useful around the house. “She can wash plates and sweep,” Michael said proudly. “Sometimes she can cook rice or beans. Just little things like that.” The children also have dreams far bigger than the circumstances surrounding them. “My first daughter says she wants to become a doctor. The second one, the boy, says he wants to become a lecturer,” he said. Those dreams are precisely what keep their father awake. Not because he doubts his children, but because he worries about whether he will have the resources to give them the education they need. When children return to an empty pot Michael is a trained teacher, musician and special educator, but he has no regular job. For now, he survives mainly by playing drums in a church. Even that income is uncertain. “They used to pay me N20,000, but the payment is not regular,” he said. Sometimes, church members give him N1,000, N2,000 or N3,000 after he plays. “That is what I use to manage,” he said. Managing, however, becomes particularly difficult when three children must eat, go to school and have their everyday needs met. There have been days when the children returned from school and there was simply no food waiting for them. “Sometimes, if they come back from school and there is no food, I will go outside and buy something on credit,” Michael said. “I can buy biscuits for them just to take first. Sometimes one of our neighbours sells raw food, so I go there to buy on credit and later we pay.” The needs never stop “The school is about to resume. They need textbooks, sandals, and another school uniform. All those things, there is no money to get them for now,” he said. Two trained teachers waiting for opportunity What makes the family’s situation particularly painful is that both parents are educated and believe they are capable of working. Michael has a Nigeria Certificate in Education, NCE, having studied Music and Special Education. Akintomide also has an NCE in Social Studies and Special Education. They say they applied for teaching jobs through the Lagos State Universal Basic Education Board, SUBEB, in July last year. According to Michael, they were told they would be contacted. When nothing happened, they returned to make inquiries and were again told to wait for a call. Michael said he was later advised to obtain a recommendation letter, which he did and submitted. “The acknowledgement letter is still with us,” he said. “They said they would call us. They have been calling some people, but up till now, since last year, they haven’t called us. We are still expecting that they will call us.” For Michael, employment is not merely about receiving a salary. It represents security for three children whose futures depend largely on him and his wife. “What gives me concern is this job because I know that if I have a job, things will be easier for me. I can take care of them and cater for them.” He is not asking to abandon his music if he gets employed. Even with a teaching job, Michael says he intends to continue drumming and pursuing other legitimate means of supporting his family. “Even if I have the work, I must still have another work. My handwork and this drumming will support the job. But only the handwork and drumming cannot be enough. That is why I am looking for a job.” Sight lost to measles Michael was not born blind. According to what his parents told him before their deaths, he could see as a baby. His sight was lost following measles when he was about two years old while living with his parents in Badagry. “The problem started when I was two years old. It was caused by measles. My parents told me that I was seeing before,” he recalled. Akintomide’s experience was different. She had sight for several years and was already in primary school when she lost it. “My wife’s sight problem started when she was in Primary Four or Five,” Michael explained. “Her own was caused by measles too.” Their loss of sight did not end their education. It did not stop them from falling in love. And it has not stopped them from raising children. ‘The love is still there’ Poverty and unemployment have tested the marriage, but Michael insists that the affection that broght them together remains. “I still love her. If I didn’t love her, and if she didn’t love me, she couldn’t have stayed with me till now,” he said. Asked what he loves most about his wife, his answer was simple. “I love her because she is very enduring.” Akintomide’s answer about her husband was equally simple: “I like him because he does things for God. He loves me.” Michael has received vocational training in the past, including training in soap-making. Akintomide has also learnt perfume production through an association, but the family says the little start-up materials provided could not sustain a viable business. For now, therefore, their biggest hope remains employment. Asked whether regaining his sight would be the first thing he would change about his life if given the opportunity, Michael paused over the question. “If God can make me see, I will be very happy,” he said. But sight, he added, is not the only path to a meaningful life. “If I can’t see and I am okay, God will provide for me. I know people who cannot see and they are doing well. “Even though I can’t see again, if God blesses me, I can even help the person who can see.” That statement perhaps captures the Ogunkanmis’ story better than anything else.Their greatest demand is not pity. It is an opportunity. Michael and Akintomide want jobs that allow them to use the education they struggled to acquire, provide food without borrowing from neighbours and buy their children’s textbooks without wondering where the next N1,000 will come from. They want their daughter to have a fair chance of becoming the doctor she dreams of becoming, and their son a chance to become a lecturer. Above all, Michael dreams of reaching a point where his family will no longer be the one waiting for help. “God should give us rest of mind and make us better people in life. And when God makes us better people, we too can help others.” he said. For Akintomide, the future is held together by the same faith that has carried the family through difficult days. “We are only depending on God,” she said quietly. We believe that God will help us.” Vanguard News The post We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana : Qui est cette jeune dame tenace qui fait la une de l’actualité ?
items.description: Une vidéo de quelques secondes enregistrée sur le parvis de la Haute Cour d'Accra ce mercredi 23 septembre 2026 a suffi à propulser une jeune agente de l'Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO) au sommet des tendances médiatiques au Ghana. En tentant d'interpeller fermement le député de Manhyia South, Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah, l'enquêtrice s'est retrouvée au centre d'un violent bras de fer institutionnel. Entre accusations de brutalité administrative, craintes d'enlèvement formulées par le parlementaire et défense de l'autorité de l'État par les services de lutte contre le crime organisé, le portrait et l'audace de cette fonctionnaire enflamment désormais le débat public ghanéen. Reconnaissable sur les images à ses lunettes et à son calme apparent au milieu du tumulte, la jeune femme est devenue en l'espace de vingt-quatre heures la figure la plus commentée des télévisions, radios et réseaux sociaux ghanéens. Les faits se sont déroulés à la sortie d'une audience au complexe de la Haute Cour d'Accra. S'avançant vers le député et avocat Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah, l'agente de l'EOCO lui demande de la suivre au siège de l'institution pour être entendu dans le cadre d'une procédure judiciaire. https://netafrique.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AQMUH0GUjti3CChlpx8fOtnTKvkwnEyjZ7mohro2mz7FgZoyr0-0jB2VTjx-aKZ18ikKRjRextr_pR3lylBBVofmp8bTgb1bQDBV-DXJZv-YPw.mp4 La scène bascule rapidement. Pris de court devant les caméras de télévision, le parlementaire repousse l'agente, s'engouffre dans son véhicule de fonction et démarre en trombe, manquant de percuter l'enquêtrice restée sur la chaussée. Filmée sous plusieurs angles, la confrontation s'est propagée comme une traînée de poudre sur JoyNews , GhanaWeb et les chaînes de télévision locales. Depuis cet incident, deux versions irréconciliables s'affrontent sur la scène publique. Prenant la parole lors d'une conférence de presse de l'opposition, le député Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah a justifié sa fuite en affirmant avoir craint pour sa sécurité personnelle. Selon ses propos relayés par le Ghanatimes , l'agente ne se serait pas identifiée dans les règles : « J'ai refusé de la suivre parce que j'ai craint qu'elle ne tente de me kidnapper » , a-t-il soutenu, accusant les agents de l'EOCO d'abus de pouvoir. La réponse de la direction de l'EOCO ne s'est pas fait attendre. Dans un communiqué officiel publié le 23 septembre, l'organisme anticorruption a confirmé la légalité de l'intervention, précisant que le député avait ignoré deux convocations officielles envoyées en février 2026. Selon l'EOCO, l'agente et ses collègues agissaient dans l'exercice strictly légal de leurs fonctions, et l'opération d'arrestation a été interrompue uniquement pour éviter de mettre en danger la sécurité publique face à l'escalade provoquée par l'élu. Au Ghana, le rôle joué par cette jeune agente suscite des réactions passionnées. Pour une partie des observateurs et de la classe politique, la jeune femme est perçue comme le symbole du courage des forces de l'ordre, n'hésitant pas à faire appliquer la loi face aux figures d'autorité politique d'ordinaire intouchables. Ses partisans soulignent qu'elle a fait preuve d'un professionnalisme remarquable en restant impassible face à la réaction physique du député. À l'inverse, ses détracteurs dénoncent une méthode d'interpellation improvisée dans l'enceinte judiciaire, estimant que la jeune femme a pris des risques disproportionnés en se placant à proximité immédiate d'un véhicule en mouvement. Alors que des juristes et éditorialistes débattent sur Kessben TV et Adom FM de la nécessité d'engager des poursuites pour refus d'obtempérer ou de réviser les protocoles d'arrestation de l'EOCO, la jeune dame aux lunettes incarne aujourd'hui le visage d'un État ghanéen en proie à de vives tensions institutionnelles. L’article Ghana : Qui est cette jeune dame tenace qui fait la une de l'actualité ? est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: 2027: Election riggers should go to jail — Obi
items.description: By Anayo Okoli, Dennis Agbo, Chinedu Adonu & Juliet Umeh Presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress, NDC, and former Anambra State governor, Mr Peter Obi, has charged editors and the Nigerian media to guide politicians towards issue-based campaigns ahead of the 2027 general elections. Read Also: Atiku: Produce conviction evidence or… – ADC challenges APC Obi, who spoke while addressing editors at the 22nd All Nigeria Editors Conference in Enugu State, however, began by making it clear that he was not invited to the conference but had come because, as a politician, he believed that wherever people gathered to discuss issues concerning the country, politicians would naturally want to be there. He was also quick to acknowledge that the editors’ conference was not a campaign platform, stressing that he had not come to campaign for the 2027 election but to pass on some messages about the state of the country and the responsibility of the media as Nigeria approaches another election. Obi said he was mindful of the purpose of the gathering and would, therefore, restrict himself to issues he believed were important to Nigeria’s democracy, governance and development. The theme of the conference is “The Ballot, the Media and the Task of Keeping Democracy Alive.” He said editors should challenge politicians whenever they resort to name-calling, personal attacks or other distractions rather than addressing issues affecting Nigerians. “As we approach the election, I have only one thing I will plead that you include in your discussion. We made a choice to be a democratic country, and that choice is a choice that can help our country to grow,” Obi said. “It is important that you help us, the politicians, to ensure that as we approach elections, our discussions, our campaigns, everything we do, is strictly based on issues that will bring good governance, unity, security and prosperity for the country, strictly.” The NDC presidential candidate also urged the media to insist on free, fair and credible elections, particularly by speaking out whenever candidates are prevented from campaigning in any part of the country. He recalled that as Anambra governor, he allowed political opponents to campaign freely in the state, citing instances involving former Lagos State governor, Babatunde Fashola; former President Olusegun Obasanjo; and former Abia State governor, Orji Uzor Kalu. According to him, Fashola once visited Anambra to campaign for Chris Ngige, then a candidate of the Action Congress of Nigeria, ACN, and he provided his official convoy for Fashola while remaining in his office. He said Obasanjo also campaigned for Andy Uba in Anambra in his presence, while Kalu campaigned for Uche Ekwunife. He hosted them to a launch. He stressed that political differences should not result in personal quarrels. “It is the people that we are talking to. So we need that conducive environment to campaign as a country, to make it work,” he stated. On his relationship with Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, Obi dismissed reports of any conflict between them, describing Soludo as a respected elder brother. “There is no issue between me and Soludo. Me and Soludo are close,” he explained, adding that he respects Soludo’s office as governor. Obi also defended his record as governor of Anambra State, particularly concerning the state’s debt profile and savings, saying he left $150 million in savings when he left office. He urged journalists to question politicians directly about their records and claims rather than relying on proxies. “Question us based on our backgrounds. Question us based on what we say. Question us on our qualifications and everything,” he said. The former governor said politicians should be prepared to personally respond to allegations against them, adding that where an allegation was true, the individual should acknowledge wrongdoing rather than deploy supporters to deny it. He further charged the media to scrutinise Nigeria’s governance and development indicators, particularly in healthcare. Obi lamented the decline of major teaching hospitals in the country, saying Nigerians should not be forced to rely on religious centres for treatment because of inadequate healthcare facilities. He also criticised what he described as disparities in healthcare funding, urging journalists to investigate government budgets and question spending priorities. “We must, you people must help us. It’s your country. Help us to stop the abuse, or it will take its revenge on your children,” Obi said. Reacting to questions from the audience, Obi said Nigeria had enough resources to address its major developmental challenges, insisting that the country’s problem was how its resources were deployed. He said, contrary to claims that the country lacked resources to fund critical sectors, billions of naira could be redirected to healthcare, education and other essential services if corruption and waste were reduced. On healthcare, Obi said no teaching hospital was listed as a capital project in the Federal Government’s budget, alleging that none received up to N200 million for capital expenditure. Obi also clarified his position on fuel subsidy, following a question on his alleged disagreement with former Kano State governor, Rabiu Kwankwaso, over the issue. According to him, Kwankwaso had not advocated the outright removal of subsidy but had proposed introducing a different subsidy regime. “What Kwankwaso said is that we will introduce our own style of subsidy. In fact, he didn’t say he would return the subsidy,” Obi said. He, however, maintained that corruption in the subsidy regime had made the system unsustainable. “If you remove the corruption in subsidy, there might not be any subsidy,” he noted, alleging that the subsidy regime had become a major avenue for corruption. Obi argued that savings from the removal of fuel subsidy could be channelled into healthcare infrastructure. On health, he said Nigeria needed about 1,000 kidney centres but currently had fewer than 300, while the country also required about 5,000 dialysis machines but had fewer than 1,000. Using his own estimates, he said establishing 1,000 kidney centres, equipped with five machines each, would cost about N250 billion. He also said Nigeria’s cancer burden required urgent investment, claiming that the country had fewer than 10 functional cancer centres. According to him, establishing 20 cancer centres at an estimated cost of N5 billion each would require about N100 billion. Obi further advocated increased investment in primary healthcare, saying only about 10 per cent of primary healthcare facilities were functional. He noted that Nigeria had 8,809 wards and argued that establishing 10,000 functional primary healthcare centres at an estimated N100 million each would cost about N1 trillion. “Why wouldn’t we take it from our N15.8 trillion — N1 trillion to put healthcare in every ward in Nigeria? We have the money. It is a question of how we use our resources,” he said. Obi also rejected the idea that he was positioning himself against other politicians, saying Nigeria’s leadership challenge affected all political actors. “I am not excluding any politician. I am not excluding myself. We have a problem,” he said. He added: “Nigeria has no problem with our weather, with anything. God blessed us with everything, but our leadership is wrong. And we must correct it.” On food security, Obi cited Bangladesh as an example of a country that had transformed its rice production from dependence on imports to becoming a major producer. He said Nigeria, despite having significantly more land, was still unable to produce enough rice to meet domestic consumption. On the possibility of political cooperation ahead of the 2027 elections, Obi said his focus was on structural reforms rather than personalities or past disagreements. He said Nigeria had about 94 million registered voters, while total votes cast in the last presidential election were about 25 million, representing roughly a quarter of registered voters. According to him, low voter participation was partly linked to citizens’ perception that their votes would not count. “That’s where you come in; that’s where you get to do something. Let’s get those who are not voting to vote. “The day our votes count, that will change,” he told the editors. Obi said having several candidates contesting elections was not necessarily a problem, provided the electoral process was free, fair and credible. “What we are asking is, in 2027, let’s have free, fair, credible elections,” he said. He also said electoral malpractice should attract criminal sanctions. “I can state here today, I know I’m not going to have the opportunity, but if I have the opportunity, anybody who rigs the election will go to jail,” Obi said. He stressed that his political activities were driven by his desire to see Nigeria function better. “I am not desperate to be President. I am desperate to see Nigeria work. Our commitment is to Nigeria, to work for a better Nigeria, where things work for everybody,” he said. Tunde Rahman warns against fake news Also speaking, the Special Adviser to President Bola Tinubu on Media and Publicity, Tunde Rahman, said the media had a critical role to play in ensuring that Nigerians were adequately informed ahead of the 2027 general elections. He said the emergence of artificial intelligence, fake news and deepfakes had made the work of journalists more difficult, warning that misinformation could outpace official information during elections. According to him, “Everybody can sit on WhatsApp and announce fake election results. Only you can debunk it. Police lies with facts and propaganda with professionalism,” stressing that the media must protect its credibility ahead of the 2027 elections. “Let us not allow cliques to kill credibility. The media should not be pro-APC, pro-Labour Party or pro-PDP. It should be pro-Nigeria, pro-truth and pro-people. If the balance is clean and the media is straight, democracy will not just survive in Nigeria, it will thrive,” he said. The presidential spokesman said the Tinubu administration inherited an economy that was “on life support” but had embarked on bold reforms which, he said, were beginning to yield results. Speaking earlier, a foremost legal scholar, Prof. Auwal Yadudu, spoke on issues that could engender voter apathy. He listed them to include lack of or failure of good governance; violence, thuggery and intimidation during elections; as well as incompetence of the electoral management body. Also, in his paper, former Managing Director and Editor-in-Chief of The Guardian Newspapers, Martins Oloja, cautioned against reporting terrorism without adequate verification of the real situation. According to him, reporting terrorism without adequate verification and accuracy could turn such reports into tools for terrorism itself. Vanguard News The post 2027: Election riggers should go to jail — Obi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027 Polls: Lawyers raise alarm over threats, intimidation
items.description: By Dayo Johnson , Regional Editor, South West The polity is already awash with threats of violence and intimidation against those who do not support the ruling All Progress Congress. Few days ago, Chairman of Esan West Local Govt Area of Edo state threatened a hotel hosting Nigeria Democratic Congress meeting that any building hosting any other party apart from APC would be bought down. Read Also: From Obasanjo and Tinubu camps to Atiku’s war room, by Emmanuel Aziken He also went to Ekpoma motor park where he ordered that any commercial driver wearing any other cap other than APC cap would be barred from entering the park. In Abuja, a council chairman told the residents who would not support the APC to relocate from the Federal Capital territory while in Borno, a commissioner threatened that any resident who dared to oppose the ruling party would be flogged. Across the states, thugs have disrupted political gatherings, attacked the people and destroyed property. Concerned lawyers in the country have therefore raised the alarm over the threats and attacks ahead of the January general elections. They warned that such violence can plunge the nation into a state of chaos and this portends a great danger for our democracy. Threatening citizens’ freedoms erode confidence in election result before ballot — Ahia A Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), Mr Kenneth C. Ahia, said: “Demolishing a hotel for hosting an opposition meeting, forcing drivers into party caps, banishing residents from the FCT, threatening floggings, or vowing to remove elected council chairmen who fail to ‘deliver,’ all violate Sections 34, 40, 41 and 42 of the Constitution, which protect the dignity of the person, the rights of assembly, association and movement, and freedom from discrimination on account of political opinion. “The Supreme Court has also settled that no governor can remove democratically elected local government councils. An election remains meaningful only when citizens can campaign, speak and vote without fear. “When officials threaten those freedoms, they discourage participation and erode confidence in the result before a single ballot is cast. Every reported threat should be investigated fairly, and any official found to have abused public power should face appropriate consequences. Leaders of all parties should make clear that votes must be won by persuasion and performance, never by coercion. “Those in power must also remember that power is transient. Years ago, the PDP held sway across the country and acted with impunity; today it is the APC. No party holds power forever, and there is always a time for reckoning.” It’s a reflection of our democracy is degenerating — Akinlaja Another SAN, Mr. Dayo Akinlaja, insisted that Nigeria should have grown beyond politics of bitterness and intolerance. He said: “It is clear beyond any measure of doubt that all these threats are highly unconstitutional, illegal, unfortunate and disturbing. They have no legitimate space in a proper democratic culture. It is a pointer to the fact that our democracy is not improving but degenerating. Over these years, we should have gone beyond this level of intolerance and incivility. Issues, not threats, should define electioneering campaigns. “Sadly, issues are relegated to the background. Fear Mongering is elevated in their place. The situation is tragic, and that is even an understatement.” Infringing on people’s rights to choose unconstitutional, actionable —Akpan For an Abuja-based senior lawyer, Mr. Nkereuwem Akpan, threats emanating mostly from states controlled by the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) constitute an electoral offence. He said: “This ugly trend by supporters of the ruling APC is a cause for concern. I say so because a multi-party democracy such as ours thrives where there is a constitutional guarantee of freedom of choice and the right to self-determination. “Even under military rule, we had options to choose from. Recall that Gen. Ibrahim Babangida gave us the choice between the National Republican Convention (NRC) and the Social Democratic Party (SDP). That was the basis on which we had Chief Moshood Abiola going up against Alhaji Tofa. Again, during the General Sani Abacha years, we had a slew of political parties to choose from. I think the APC must learn from the history of our recent past, from the tragedy that befell the PDP. I remember a time, about 15 years ago, when the PDP was the biggest political party in the whole of Africa. “In fact, members of the PDP became so boisterous, unruly and careless that one Ogbulafor came out on national TV boasting that the PDP would rule Nigeria for sixty years. In those days, you were either PDP or you were wasting your time. It took Nyesom Wike, working from within the ranks of the PDP, to destroy it. Democracy thrives on the choice that the electorate is able to make at the polls every four years. “The APC was an outsider until 2015 and cannot be greater than the masses. It goes without saying that ours is a constitutional democracy founded on the principle of one man, one vote, where the right to cast a vote for a candidate of one’s choice is a fundamental right. Any attempt, before, during, or after the elections, to infringe on this right to choose is clearly unconstitutional and actionable in the law courts. Secondly, it will also constitute an electoral offence to attempt to stifle freedom of choice or to discriminate against a person on the basis of party membership or political affiliation. “These are the very foundations of our democracy. In other jurisdictions, the police would have arrested, prosecuted and jailed anyone engaged in this conduct, but they won’t, because orders will come from Abuja to truncate the case”. Doomsday beckons if political actors don’t comply with the laws — Chief Nwachukwu For his part, another senior legal practitioner, Chief Chukwuma Nwachukwu, said: “All I can see in the above scenarios is the impunity and arrogance of our politicians, especially those of the ruling party. It is important to state that no one is above the law, and by virtue of Section 1(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended), all authorities and persons are subject to the grundnorm and all laws of the land, without exception. “Chapter Four of the Constitution preserves the fundamental rights of citizens, and such rights cannot be tampered with, except in accordance with the provisions of the law. No party member or government official has any right whatsoever to infringe on the guaranteed rights to freedom of association, freedom of movement, etc and, more especially, the right to life of a fellow citizen, under the guise of politics. “The various criminal laws make provision for offences and the punishments therefore, and it is the duty of the relevant law enforcement agencies to carry out their statutory functions in preserving public order. Furthermore, the Independent National Electoral Commission should, as a matter of urgency, read the riot act to political office holders, regardless of their party leanings and affiliations, on the importance of desisting from inflammatory rhetoric as we approach the general elections, so as not to overheat the polity and destabilise the upcoming elections. “As for the issue of imposing huge sums of money as fees for the erection of campaign billboards, I do not see the necessity of imposing a prohibitive sum different from what is generally applicable to other advertisements. This is a deeply tense period in our national life, and if political actors don’t comply with the laws of the land, doomsday beckons”. Political intimidation transforms elections into marketplace of fear — Evans Ufeli Another lawyer, Evans Ufeli said, “Threats by public officials against citizens, workers, traders, civil servants, or businesses because they support opposition parties strike at the foundation of constitutional democracy. Under the 1999 Constitution, Nigerians enjoy rights to freedom of expression, peaceful association, political choice, and protection from discriminatory treatment. “These rights are not gifts bestowed by office holders; they are guarantees that restrain the power of the state and its agents. From an electoral law perspective, intimidation is especially grave where it is intended to compel a person to vote, abstain from voting, abandon a political party, or support a preferred candidate. The Electoral Act 2026 criminalises undue influence and conduct involving threats, coercion, violence, or the threat of injury, loss, and harm designed to distort a voter’s free choice. A threat to terminate employment, withdraw government services, close a business, deny contracts, or unleash security agencies against perceived opposition supporters may therefore amount to more than reckless political speech. “Where evidence establishes intent and action, it may trigger electoral offences, abuse of office allegations, civil claims for fundamental-rights enforcement, disciplinary sanctions, and in appropriate cases criminal liability. Political intimidation transforms elections from a contest of ideas into a marketplace of fear. A voter who fears losing a job, a licence, personal safety, or access to public services cannot be said to be exercising an entirely free franchise. “Such a climate suppresses turnout, entrenches incumbency, weakens opposition mobilisation, and erodes public confidence in election outcomes. A public office is a trust, not a weapon. The survival of credible elections depends on ensuring that no Nigerian must choose between political conscience and personal survival. Credibility of the electoral process at risk — Femi Aborisade Mr Femi Aborisade argued that; “These developments are a very dangerous sign for our democracy. They amount to an unacceptable attempt to constrict the democratic space and intimidate citizens into political conformity. Democracy is founded on the freedom of citizens to make political choices without fear, coercion or intimidation. “Nobody should be threatened or punished simply because he or she chooses to support a political party different from the party in government. What we are witnessing is particularly disturbing because some of these threats are reportedly coming from public officials who ought to be protecting the rights of citizens, irrespective of their political affiliations. A public office must never be used as an instrument of political coercion. “Government officials have a constitutional duty to protect citizens, not to dictate their political choices or threaten them with reprisals for exercising their democratic rights. Political competition should be about ideas, policies, programmes and the records of those seeking public office. Where intimidation replaces persuasion, democracy is inevitably weakened. “If this pattern continues unchecked, it could create an atmosphere of fear in which citizens become reluctant to participate openly in political activities or express their genuine preferences. That would have serious consequences for the credibility of the electoral process.” Threats against opposition anti-democratic — Dr Omare Dr Eric Omare, former President, Ijaw Youth Council (IYC) worldwide contended that: “The verbal threats by members of the ruling APC against opposition party members pose a threat to peace and security going into the 2027 general elections. There is no legal basis for those threats. “In a multi-party democracy, people have the right to support the political party and candidates of their choice; hence, the threats are anti-democratic. I would advise the security agencies to take proactive steps to nip such threats in the bud and address their potential effect on the peaceful conduct of the 2027 general elections.” APC’s strong-arm posture, recipe for anarchy ahead 2027 elections — Clarkson On his part, Amaebi Clarkson, argued that: “It is disheartening when public officials and supposedly elected representatives speak in such an unbridled manner. It reveals how far we have descended into lawlessness. Their unguarded utterances give the impression that the country is governed by the rule of men rather than the Constitution. “Chapter 4 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, is clear on the unfettered rights of the people. Section 40 specifically echoes the freedom of association and the right to peaceful assembly. This is an inalienable right that cannot be circumvented by anybody, including the President. “Our democracy is anchored on a multi-party system which gives the people a wide spectrum to choose their political party and who to vote for. The ruling APC, which came to power in 2015, benefited from these democratic tenets when the people voted out the then ruling PDP government. The APC’s strong-arm posture is a recipe for anarchy in the forthcoming elections. But this government should be reminded that Nigeria is not a banana republic but a country steeped in the rule of law.” It portends a great danger for our democracy — Oviawe A Port Harcourt based lawyer, Amarachi Owhoeli also said: “This portends a great danger for our democracy. Sadly, this is a recurrent phenomenon during electioneering periods. We have seen similar threats like this in Lagos State and other states in Nigeria during the 2023 general elections. It is sad that these politicians and their thugs will still go ahead to carry out their threats and the security agencies will not do anything about it. “Every Nigerian citizen is free to campaign and vote for a candidate of their choice; if anybody threatens or coerces them from freely doing so, then that person ought to be arrested and prosecuted accordingly, no matter his position or qualifications. “Threats of violence like this and actual violence can plunge the country into a state of chaos, because nobody has a monopoly on violence. I will advise the security agencies to swiftly move in and invite the culprits responsible for these threats, make them sign an undertaking not to carry out those threats, so that if these threats later materialize, they will be held responsible for their unguarded utterances.” INEC must create a level playing field — Akiki George Akiki, Ex Chairman of the NBA Young Lawyers Forum, Calabar Branch, stated that “one of the features of democracy is a free, fair and violence-free election, devoid of duress, vote buying, threats, and ballot snatching. Nigeria has been a democracy for over 27 years and should by now have moved past situations where voters are threatened by political thugs. “During the 2023 elections a woman was harassed, molested, and beaten by thugs at her polling unit, as reported in the media. The country’s constitution guarantees freedom of choice of political affiliation and membership under Sections 39 and 40, while Section 77 guarantees the freedom to vote and choose representatives. Furthermore, such actions amount to electoral offences punishable by law. “Therefore, INEC, as the election umpire, has a duty to put up modalities that will encourage a level playing ground for all political parties to participate in elections, while security agencies have a role to ensure that voters and election participants do not suffer any elements of coercion, threat, or duress.” On his part, John Ola Mafo said: “The combined reading of all the threats, barking, howling and vituperations from Edo to Ebonyi, Abuja to Bornu, gives a picture of APC as a political family at the breaking point, weighed down by desperation, frustration and the fear of the unknown. “Nigeria is not a Banana Republic and certain inalienable rights are granted by the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria (as amended), which includes Section 34 on Dignity of Human Person, 35 on Right to Personal Liberty, 38 on Freedom of Thoughts, Conscience and Religion, 39 on Right to Freedom of Expression and the Press, 40 on Right to Peaceful Assembly and Association, and 41 on Freedom of Movement”. Mr Tajudeen Olutop, former Chairman, Nigeria Bar Association, Owo Branch “No citizen should be intimidated, assaulted, denied access to public facilities or forced to relocate merely because of his or her political preference. Nevertheless, such inflammatory statements are not entirely new in Nigerian politics. At different times, politicians belonging to various parties have employed similar language when their parties controlled the machinery of government. “They are often part of political manoeuvring, propaganda and attempts to create an exaggerated impression of dominance rather than policies capable of lawful implementation. However, these statements should not be treated lightly. Even when the speakers have no genuine intention or legal capacity to carry them out, such rhetoric can embolden overzealous supporters, heighten political tension and undermine public confidence in the electoral process. “Public office holders must therefore exercise restraint and remember that government institutions and public spaces belong to all Nigerians, irrespective of political affiliation. Ultimately, elections are determined by the freely expressed will of the electorate not by threats, intimidation or coercion”. Similarly, Chief Ola Amure said: “The reported threats from some government officials reveal a dangerous attempt to turn political competition into an exercise of power, intimidation and coercion. A government has a responsibility to protect the rights of its citizens, not to threaten them for belonging to, supporting, or voting for another political party. “The right to vote, freedom of association, freedom of expression and the right to participate in political activities are not privileges granted by the ruling party. They are fundamental democratic rights. What happens when a commercial driver is denied access to his livelihood because of the political cap he wears? What happens when a hotel owner is threatened because he provides a venue for a lawful political meeting? What happens when an elected council chairman is pressured to deliver votes for a particular party under threat of removal? These are not merely political disagreements. They raise questions about the use of public authority, the protection of livelihoods, electoral fairness and the rule of law. The 2027 elections must not become a contest of intimidation, coercion and the abuse of state power. They must be an opportunity for Nigerians to freely choose their leaders based on policies, performance, character and their vision for the future. “The opposition must not be denied the right to campaign. Citizens must not be forced to support a political party. Public resources and government institutions must not be used as instruments of political punishment. A democracy is measured not only by the ability of the ruling party to win elections, but also by its willingness to respect the rights of those who disagree with it. Moruff Balogun, Former Vice Chairman, Nigerian Bar Association, Ijebu Ode Branch “The more important question is what happens to an election when those who control public institutions begin to communicate to citizens that their political choices may have consequences. Politicians have always used strong language during election campaigns. The more serious concern is that some of these statements are coming from people who occupy public offices and therefore have access to governmental authority and resources. One may dismiss some of these statements as political rhetoric. But when similar statements begin to emerge from different jurisdictions, the issue becomes more fundamental. It creates the possibility of a political environment in which citizens do not merely ask, “Who do I want to vote for?” but also, “What will happen to me if I vote differently? “That is where the concern for democratic freedom arises. A democracy is not defined merely by holding an election on a particular day. It requires citizens to be able to make political choices freely. If a trader fears that his business may be affected because he supports the opposition, if a transport worker believes that displaying the wrong political symbol could cost him access to his livelihood, if a public servant thinks that his position depends on delivering votes for a particular party, or if an ordinary resident feels that supporting the opposition could make him unwelcome in his own community, then the ballot may remain secret while the political environment itself becomes coercive. “The 2027 election should not only answer the question of who will govern Nigeria. It should also test whether our political institutions are mature enough to permit citizens to disagree with those in power without being treated as enemies of the State. In his own submission, Mr Bukola Onifade said: “The problem with our democracy is the lack of respect for the rule of law. Public office holders and politicians generally are not giving enough regard to the constitution which is very dangerous for the development of our democracy and allowing such to continue without check can truncate democracy in the country. “It is unlawful for anyone to resort to threat as a means of campaigning or canvassing votes or to even threaten others from canvassing for votes in any part of the country. The moment we allow the threat to become part of our democracy, we are heading for anarchy and we must use legal means to stop the country from falling into that ditch. We need to preach political tolerance – Bewaji Dr Wunmi Bewaji, a Solicitor of the Supreme Court of Nigeria and former Minority Leader of the House of Representatives, described the threat as excessive enthusiasm, stressing the need for tolerance in the country. He said, “I rather see this as an isolated manifestation of excessive enthusiasm and that is not to be confused for illegality. “Every now and then you find over-zealous officials making statements, which when you look at it, is not really more than an over-zealous pursuit of a legitimate political objective, which is not a crime. I think the focus should be on how to promote political tolerance by all sides, because we will be missing the point if the focus is only on the ruling party, because every government official within their terrain would want to implement one policy or the other that will not be favourable to the other party. So, even within the same party, you can have evidence of intolerance. “For instance, you find a situation where after people have pasted their posters all over the place, exuberant party supporters would go about to pull down billboards to tear posters belonging to the opposition. So, I think we need to preach political tolerance.” Mr Chika Eze, said “The Electoral Act 2026 is quite explicit. Section 97 prohibits a political party, candidate, aspirant or any person or group from directly or indirectly threatening another person with force or violence during a political campaign in order to compel support or prevent support for a candidate. Section 130 also addresses conduct around polling units, including possession of offensive weapons or conduct calculated to intimidate voters. “More importantly, Section 132 criminalises the use or threat of force, violence or restraint, as well as threats of injury, damage or harm intended to influence how a person votes or whether that person votes at all. It also covers conduct that prevents a political aspirant from freely campaigning or mobilising support. Therefore, incidents involving alleged threats or intimidation should not simply be viewed as political rhetoric. Where the facts establish the elements of an offence under the Act, the appropriate authorities have a legal basis to investigate and prosecute. “The real issue is enforcement. The law must be applied consistently, evidence must be properly preserved, and investigators must establish who made the threat, what was threatened, the electoral context and whether the conduct was intended to influence voting or political participation. Where there is evidence of sponsorship or direction by others, investigators should also examine that chain of responsibility rather than stopping with the person who physically carried out the act.” Election law expert, Mr Emeka Nwosu said, “The problem is not necessarily the absence of laws; it is the failure to consistently move cases from allegation to investigation, investigation to prosecution and prosecution to conviction. In many instances, evidence is not properly preserved, investigations are delayed and cases lose momentum before they reach a decisive stage. “A functioning enforcement chain requires specialised investigators who understand electoral offences, proper documentation and preservation of evidence, timely legal advice, dedicated prosecutors and courts or tribunals capable of handling electoral cases expeditiously. There must also be clear institutional responsibility for tracking each case from the point of complaint to its final determination. Most importantly, prosecution must not be selective. Whether the offender is a political heavyweight, a party operative or an ordinary voter, the law should apply equally. Without credible enforcement and consequences, electoral offences will continue to be viewed by some actors as risks worth taking.” According to Mr Chinedu Okafor, “The 2027 election must not become another contest where violence, intimidation and misinformation determine the outcome. Security agencies must be professional, neutral and firm in dealing with anyone who attempts to disrupt the process, irrespective of political affiliation. Political parties and their candidates must also understand that elections are not a do-or-die affair. They must campaign on issues, respect the rules and accept the outcome where due process has been followed. “Citizens, too, have a critical role to play by refusing to participate in violence, vote buying, hate speech or the spread of unverified information. A credible and peaceful election is a collective responsibility. If the security agencies do their job, political actors play by the rules and citizens protect the integrity of their votes, Nigeria can have an election that strengthens rather than weakens public confidence in democracy.” Dapo Akinrefon; Samuel Oyadongha; Rotimi Ojomoyela; Ikechukwu Nnochiri; Shina Abubakar; Ozioruva Aliu; Ike Uchechukwu; Davies Iheamnachor; James Ogunnnaike; Adeola Badru; Juliet Umeh & Gift Chapi-Odekina also contributed to this report . Vanguard News The post 2027 Polls: Lawyers raise alarm over threats, intimidation appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Burkina Faso : De nouvelles règles pour l’évaluation des fonctionnaires d’État
items.description: Le Conseil des ministres a adopté un décret qui précise les modalités et critères d’évaluation des fonctionnaires d’État et introduit plusieurs dispositions nouvelles. Le gouvernement burkinabè a adopté, jeudi 24 septembre 2026, un décret portant modalités et critères d’évaluation des fonctionnaires d’État. Ce texte vient en application de la loi n°081-2015/CNT du 24 novembre 2015 portant statut général de la fonction publique d’État. Il vise à renforcer et à harmoniser le dispositif de gestion de l’évaluation des agents publics. Le nouveau décret regroupe dans un seul texte les différentes modalités relatives à l’évaluation des fonctionnaires d’État. Il prévoit notamment la possibilité pour un responsable hiérarchique de procéder à la notation d’un agent lorsque son supérieur hiérarchique immédiat est défaillant. Le texte encadre également la situation des fonctionnaires nommés en cours d’année ou relevés de leurs fonctions. Ceux-ci peuvent être évalués à leur nouveau poste lorsque la durée d’occupation de celui-ci atteint six mois. Le décret élargit par ailleurs les dispositions relatives aux situations particulières. Un fonctionnaire qui, pour des raisons de force majeure, n’a pas pu cumuler six mois d’occupation de son poste pourra ainsi être pris en compte dans un cadre adapté. D’autres dispositions concernent les fonctionnaires bénéficiant d’une mise à disposition auprès d’une fédération, d’une confédération ou d’une centrale syndicale. Dans ce cas, une note forfaitaire peut leur être attribuée. Le texte prévoit également l’attribution d’une note forfaitaire lorsqu’une reconstitution de carrière concerne un fonctionnaire qui n’a pas effectivement travaillé pendant la période concernée. À travers ce décret, le gouvernement entend renforcer le cadre réglementaire applicable à l’évaluation des fonctionnaires d’État. Le regroupement des modalités d’évaluation dans un même texte doit notamment permettre de disposer d’un dispositif plus harmonisé pour la gestion et le suivi de la carrière des agents publics. L’article Burkina Faso : De nouvelles règles pour l’évaluation des fonctionnaires d’État est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Paris : décès de l’ancien Premier ministre Sidya Touré à l’hôpital américain
items.description: L’ancien Premier ministre et président de l’UFR -aujourd'hui dissout- Sidya Touré est décédé ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026 dans la capitale Française, Paris des suites de maladie, a appris cette nuit Guineenews de sources familiales. Le décès a eu lieu aux environs de 23 heures GMT(1 heure heure locale) à l’hôpital américain de Paris où il était alité depuis près de deux semaines. Déjà malade à Abidjan depuis plus de trois mois, Sidya Touré est arrivé à Paris dans un état critique, selon nos sources. Ancien Premier ministre sous le régime de Lansana Conté, Sidya Touré avait quitté la Guinée au lendemain de la prise du pouvoir par l’armée en 2021 pour s’exiler en Côte d’Ivoire. Avant son entrée en politique en Guinée, il avait notamment servi en Côte d’Ivoire comme directeur de cabinet d’Alassane Ouattara, alors Premier ministre ivoirien et actuel président de la République de Côte d’Ivoire. Sidya Touré a également été Haut Représentant du président Alpha Condé. Au cours des dernières décennies, il s’est imposé comme l’une des figures majeures de la vie politique guinéenne. Il s’est éteint à l’âge de 81 ans. De la haute administration à la Primature Né en 1945, Sidya Touré a effectué une importante partie de sa carrière professionnelle en Côte d’Ivoire, où il s’est notamment illustré dans les milieux économiques et administratifs. Son parcours prend une dimension nationale en 1996 lorsque le président Lansana Conté lui confie la mission de former le gouvernement. Le 9 juillet 1996, Sidya Touré est nommé Premier ministre de la République de Guinée. Il devient ainsi le premier titulaire de la Primature après plusieurs années d’interruption de cette fonction. Il restera à la tête du gouvernement jusqu’au 8 mars 1999, date à laquelle il est remplacé par Lamine Sidimé. Son arrivée à la Primature intervient dans un contexte particulièrement difficile, marqué notamment par les conséquences de la crise économique et financière et les tensions politiques et sociales qui traversaient le pays. Dans un entretien accordé à Guinéenews en 2018, Sidya Touré était revenu sur les circonstances de sa nomination. Il expliquait avoir été reçu par le président Lansana Conté dès mai 1996 pour échanger sur la situation économique, financière et militaire du pays. Selon son propre témoignage, les discussions engagées au cours des mois suivants ont progressivement conduit à la décision de restaurer la fonction de Premier ministre. Un Premier ministre marqué par les réformes Durant son passage à la Primature, Sidya Touré revendiquait une méthode fondée sur la réforme administrative et économique. Des sources consacrées à son passage au gouvernement lui attribuent notamment des initiatives ayant contribué à l’amélioration de la desserte en eau et en électricité à Conakry ainsi qu’à des réformes économiques et financières. Sa période à la Primature est également associée aux efforts de la Guinée pour améliorer ses relations avec les institutions financières internationales et obtenir un allègement de sa dette dans le cadre de l’initiative en faveur des pays pauvres très endettés. Mais au-delà de son bilan gouvernemental, Sidya Touré va surtout marquer durablement la scène politique guinéenne après son départ du gouvernement. De la Primature à l’opposition Après son départ de la Primature, Sidya Touré s’engage progressivement dans l’opposition. Il devient le président de l’Union des forces républicaines (UFR), formation politique qui s’impose au fil des années parmi les principaux partis de l’opposition guinéenne. Sa trajectoire politique va dès lors être étroitement liée aux grands rendez-vous électoraux et aux différentes crises politiques que connaît la Guinée. En 2010, Sidya Touré est candidat à l’élection présidentielle. Il termine troisième au premier tour avec 13,62 % des suffrages, derrière Alpha Condé et Cellou Dalein Diallo. Il conteste initialement certains aspects du processus avant d’accepter finalement les résultats après leur confirmation par la Cour suprême. Le traumatisme du 28 septembre 2009 L’un des épisodes les plus marquants de son parcours politique reste la manifestation du 28 septembre 2009 au stade du même nom à Conakry. Sidya Touré figure alors parmi les principaux responsables de l’opposition mobilisés contre une éventuelle candidature du chef de la junte de l’époque, Moussa Dadis Camara, à l’élection présidentielle. La manifestation est violemment réprimée. Des dizaines de personnes sont tuées et de nombreux responsables politiques et militants sont blessés. Sidya Touré lui-même est grièvement blessé à la tête au cours des événements. Cet épisode restera l’un des moments les plus dramatiques de sa carrière politique et de l’histoire récente de la Guinée. Une voix constante dans les débats politiques Au fil des années, Sidya Touré s’impose comme l’un des interlocuteurs réguliers des médias guinéens et internationaux sur les questions de gouvernance, d’économie, de démocratie et de développement. Dans ses nombreuses interventions publiques, il défend notamment une vision de l’État fondée sur la rigueur dans la gestion publique, les réformes économiques et le respect des institutions. Son passage à la tête du gouvernement sous Lansana Conté lui conférait également une position particulière dans les débats sur les différentes périodes de la gouvernance guinéenne. Dans un entretien accordé à Guinéenews en 2020, il avait notamment livré son appréciation de la gouvernance de Lansana Conté et évoqué plusieurs épisodes politiques auxquels il avait été directement associé. Les dernières années loin de la Guinée Les dernières années de la vie politique de Sidya Touré ont été marquées par son éloignement de la Guinée. Après le coup d’État du 5 septembre 2021 ayant renversé Alpha Condé, le leader de l’UFR s’est installé hors du pays. Dans une interview accordée à Deutsche Welle, il expliquait alors les raisons de son absence et évoquait ses préoccupations concernant les conditions de son éventuel retour en Guinée. Cette période d’éloignement n’a cependant pas mis fin à son engagement politique. Sidya Touré continuait à intervenir régulièrement sur l’évolution de la situation nationale et à défendre les positions de sa formation politique. Une disparition qui intervient après celle de plusieurs cadres de l’UFR La disparition de Sidya Touré intervient quelques mois seulement après celle de Bakary Goyo Zoumanigui, autre figure historique de l’UFR et ancien vice-président de l’Assemblée nationale. Bakary Goyo Zoumanigui est décédé à Conakry le 7 juin 2026. Il était considéré comme l’un des piliers historiques de l’UFR et un proche collaborateur de Sidya Touré. Quelques jours avant la disparition de Sidya Touré, l’ancien député et ancien responsable de l’UFR Babara Fofana était également décédé à Conakry. La disparition successive de plusieurs responsables historiques constitue donc un nouveau coup dur pour les anciens compagnons politiques de Sidya Touré. La Guinée face à la disparition d’un homme d’État Ancien Premier ministre, candidat à l’élection présidentielle, chef de parti et figure historique de l’opposition, Sidya Touré aura occupé pendant près de trois décennies une place particulière dans la vie publique guinéenne. Son parcours aura traversé plusieurs périodes de l’histoire récente du pays : la présidence de Lansana Conté, les années de transition militaire, l’élection présidentielle de 2010, les violences politiques de 2009, les années Alpha Condé et la transition ouverte après le coup d’État de septembre 2021. Au-delà des appréciations politiques parfois divergentes portées sur son action, son décès marque incontestablement la disparition d’un acteur qui aura profondément participé aux débats sur l’avenir politique, économique et institutionnel de la Guinée. À 81 ans, Sidya Touré laisse derrière lui une longue carrière au service de l’État et de la politique, ainsi qu’une formation politique dont il aura été, pendant des décennies, le principal visage.

items.title: Trump dit que la visite de Xi a été "très positive pour les deux pays", l'Iran abordé
items.description: Le président américain Donald Trump a qualifié vendredi la visite d'Etat de son homologue chinois Xi Jinping de « très positive pour les deux pays » et dit avoir parlé avec lui de la guerre en Iran. « Je pense que nous avons fait des progrès énormes, très positifs pour les deux pays », a déclaré Donald Trump vendredi matin depuis la Maison Blanche, où il recevait autour d'un thé Xi Jinping et sa femme Peng Liyuan, en présence de la Première dame Melania Trump, au dernier jour de cette visite fastueuse. Le président chinois a lui mentionné la possibilité de deux autres « occasions » de rencontrer Donald Trump d'ici fin 2026, au sommet de l'APEC en Chine mi-novembre et au sommet du G20 en Floride en décembre. Plus tard dans la matinée, au cours d'une visite des Archives nationales à Washington avec Xi Jinping, Donald Trump a répondu par l'affirmative à la question de savoir si les deux présidents avaient abordé le sujet de la guerre en Iran. Interrogé sur des progrès éventuels concernant la réouverture du détroit d'Ormuz, il a répondu: « je pense que ça va très bien se passer. » La veille, Xi Jinping a déclaré que Washington et Téhéran devaient résoudre leurs différends « le plus rapidement possible » par la négociation, selon des propos rapportés par l'agence d'Etat Chine Nouvelle. La Chine, alliée de l'Iran, subit les retombées du conflit déclenché par le milliardaire républicain. Xi Jinping a été reçu avec des égards très appuyés par Donald Trump, qui a assuré avoir bâti une relation de « grande amitié » avec son homologue chinois. Ce dernier a profité de sa venue à la Maison Blanche pour plaider la coexistence pacifique entre les deux superpuissances rivales, tout en réaffirmant ses lignes rouges sur Taïwan. Cette visite d'Etat de trois jours a connu jeudi son apogée mondaine avec un dîner de gala auquel étaient conviés, côté américain, les patrons des plus grandes entreprises, avec un accent particulier sur la tech. The post Trump dit que la visite de Xi a été "très positive pour les deux pays", l'Iran abordé appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .
