items.title: He entered at eight. He is now 16: Ghana’s children growing up in prayer camps
items.description: At eight years old, Hafiz Abdallah was taken to Nyinbonya, a prayer camp in Paga, near Ghana’s border with Burkina Faso. He is now 16. For eight years, his mother says, her son has lived at the facility without a clinical diagnosis. When his behaviour becomes erratic, she says, he is chained. “He doesn’t even speak, stands often in his own world,” she said. “But this helped me a lot because I am very much assured that he will not wander off and end up getting hurt or killed.” Hafiz became increasingly difficult to manage after the death of his twin brother. He destroyed things, once stole a neighbour’s chicken and often attacked his mother. She said she did not understand what was wrong with him. “I tried herbal remedies and spent money I did not have. Over eight years, my savings are exhausted.” “Where else do I turn to? I put my faith in Allah,” she said. Her story points to a wider problem: for some Ghanaian families, the first response to unexplained or disturbing behaviour is not a mental-health clinic but a church, prayer camp or traditional healer. Clinical psychologist and University of Ghana lecturer Emmanuel Asampong says this is partly rooted in how illness is understood. “We have usually, if you like, relied on what we would say is a biopsychosocial approach to seeking health,” he said. “When things happen to people, and they are not able to explain it easily, then they are quick to attribute it to some spiritual dimension.” For children whose conditions require professional assessment, that can mean being treated elsewhere — sometimes for years. Inside Nyinbonya At Nyinbonya, children and adults were seen walking barefoot. Some appeared malnourished and disassociated. A child believed to be no more than 10 was being held tightly by an adult. Staff were seen pinching and slapping patients to make them behave or stop screaming. Three visibly naked people were also seen walking around the facility. Access was tightly controlled. To enter, the reporter had to pretend to be visiting a patient. A caregiver, who spoke anonymously, said the facility was doing its best and could accommodate almost 200 patients. Hafiz’s mother said keeping him there gave her some reassurance that he would not wander into danger. But the arrangement has also meant that a child who entered at eight has spent half his life at the facility without the clinical diagnosis his mother says she never knew how to obtain. When trauma is mistaken for possession Sarah Adjei was seven when she was sexually assaulted by a family acquaintance. Afterwards, she developed severe distress, waking at night, screaming and sweating. Her parents took her to a church to pray because they believed she had a spiritual problem. She remained there for years. “I was subjected to intense prayer, healing and deliverance every day,” Sarah recalled. “We would fast. I remember the first time I fasted was when I was nine years old. I fasted for 24 hours.” Now 21 and studying psychology at the University of Ghana, Sarah believes she needed professional mental-health support. “What happened to me was unfortunate, and I think I could have gotten better help than I did in a mental health institution or a health professional than the church,” she said. She stressed that she still believes in prayer. “I don’t believe the solution is completely to reject faith because spirituality is deeply important to recovery for many Ghanaians,” psychiatrist Dr Abigail Harding of Korle Bu Teaching Hospital said. “But we have to insist that this recovery must never come at the cost of an individual’s human rights or their dignity.” Harding said unusual behaviour in Ghana is often interpreted as witchcraft, a curse or possession rather than a medical condition. The result, she said, is that some people turn first to prayer camps and deliverance centres, where some facilities lack trained mental-health professionals. She said practices such as chaining, forced fasting and isolation can further traumatise patients and delay effective treatment. “Mental illness is a medical condition, point blank, and as such the treatment should be humane; it should be evidence-based and definitely should be aligned with Ghana’s mental health acts,” she said. The problem is not only belief. It is access. Sarah’s mother, Mary Adwoa Adjei, said she initially believed her daughter’s condition was spiritual. “I actually thought it was a spiritual problem because I’m a very, very spiritual woman,” she said. But when asked why she did not take Sarah to a mental-health clinic, her answer revealed another barrier. “I actually didn’t know where to go, where the mental health clinic was or the number of mental health clinics we had in the country,” she said. She first tried a herbalist before taking Sarah to church. Her experience illustrates why simply telling families to seek medical care may not be enough. Dr Josephine Stiles Darko, deputy head of communications at Ghana’s Mental Health Authority, said the country does not have enough mental-health professionals. She said there are a little over 80 psychiatrists in the country, with most based in Accra. The solution, she said, is to bring mental-health care closer to communities. “You don’t have to travel all the way to Accra, especially for those outside Accra, because most of the few psychiatrists we have are in Accra,” she said. “The Mental Health Authority and Ghana Health Service, with support from the World Health Organisation, are training district health personnel so that some conditions can be identified and treated at primary level, with severe cases stabilised and referred to specialist facilities.” She added that the Authority will soon conduct specialist outreach clinics, taking professionals into selected districts and handing patients over to local health workers for continued care. A system that can work with faith Asampong says the answer is not to pretend religious and traditional providers do not exist. “People go to them anyway, whether we like it or not,” he said. He compared the approach to the way traditional birth attendants were brought into Ghana’s health system and trained to recognise warning signs and refer patients. “I think that is the approach we need to use for mental health,” he said. “We need to bring on board all these relevant stakeholders because people go to them anyway.” Harding said some churches already refer severe cases to psychiatrists and psychologists and invite clinicians to train prayer teams in mental-health first aid. She also pointed to the M-HEALER project, which trains traditionalists and prayer-centre operators as part of efforts to foster collaboration. “Ultimately, we do need stronger regulation of faith-based centres, more public education and more accessible psychiatric services,” Harding said. “When people understand that faith and medicine can coexist, that you can pray and still take your medication, we’ll see better outcomes for people living with mental illness in Ghana.” What the law promises Ghana’s Mental Health Act, 2012 (Act 846), does not leave people with mental-health conditions without legal protection. The Act establishes protections for people receiving mental-health care, including children, and provides for humane treatment, dignity and the least restrictive you environment. It also regulates restraint and establishes Mental Health Visiting Committees to inspect facilities, receive complaints and examine conditions, including at spiritual mental-health facilities. For children, the Act says psychiatric treatment should, as far as possible, take place in the least restrictive environment and that children admitted for treatment should be separated from adults and have their developmental needs addressed. Restraint is permitted only in tightly defined circumstances involving imminent danger, rather than as a routine form of management. But the existence of these protections does not automatically mean they are reaching every child. Darko acknowledged that Mental Health Visiting Committees do not yet exist everywhere they are supposed to. “I have to admit we don’t have it all around the country like it’s supposed to be, but we have started and are gradually picking up,” she said. She said the committees visit places where children with mental-health conditions are managed and check whether facilities are acting according to the law and in the best interests of patients. “If something is not going right and they have to, they give their reports, they comment on it, they come back to make sure that you are doing the right thing,” she said. The Authority could not provide a figure for registered or accredited prayer camps and spiritual healing centres under its oversight. That leaves an important accountability question: how many such facilities are operating, which ones are subject to oversight, how often are they inspected, and what happens when children are found in unsafe conditions? Making the protections usable Lawyer Lady Ann Essuman says part of the problem is that families do not know what legal avenues are available. She described a previous case in which her firm obtained an involuntary court order so a child could receive treatment at Korle Bu. “The rights are available to people,” she said. “That is why I’m advocating more on how policy should be generated so that people can understand better.” She said families, police officers, or concerned citizens can seek intervention where a person may pose a danger to themselves or others, subject to the legal requirements. Her argument is not that faith should disappear from Ghanaian life. Instead, she says churches and other religious institutions need to stop treating every mental-health condition as exclusively spiritual. “The church now has to have the responsibility of not over-spiritualising everything,” Essuman said. She also supports greater integration between faith and medicine. “The more work we do in promoting this advocacy, the better we destigmatise the field, and we integrate faith and science to give people the care they need,” she said. What would change for children like Hafiz? The experts interviewed for this story point to a system that does not have to choose between faith and medicine. It can educate families about mental illness and where to find help. It can train pastors, prayer-camp workers and traditional healers to recognise warning signs and refer people for professional assessment. It can expand mental-health services at district and primary-care level, so families do not have to travel to Accra. It can strengthen inspection of spiritual mental-health facilities and ensure that children are seen privately and their rights protected. And it can make legal remedies understandable and accessible to families. Darko said implementation of the Mental Health Act remains an ongoing process. “There is still a deficit,” she said. “We are hoping that going forward with the advocacy from journalists like yourself, the visiting committee, and all those things, the tribunal being established, people will know that there are legal repercussions to some of these things.” For Hafiz, those protections have so far remained largely abstract. He entered Nyinbonya at eight. He is now 16. His mother says he has never received a clinical diagnosis. And after eight years, the question is no longer simply why families turn to prayer camps. It is whether Ghana’s health, social welfare, and oversight systems can reach children before they spend their childhoods inside them.

items.title: Police municipale de Ouaga : Intervention contre un réseau clandestin de fabrication et de reconditionnement de boissons alcoolisées
items.description: Le mardi 22 septembre 2026, suite à une dénonciation, la Direction de la Sécurité Publique (DSP) a mené une intervention dans l’arrondissement n°06 de la Commune de Ouagadougou, visant un réseau présumé impliqué dans des activités clandestines de fabrication et de reconditionnement de boissons alcoolisées au sein d’une cour. Les vérifications effectuées sur les lieux ont notamment permis de constater la présence de différentes boissons alcoolisées, dont du pastis, faisant l’objet d’un procédé présumé de fabrication et/ou de reconditionnement. Au cours de cette intervention, environ 500 bouteilles de boissons, ainsi que des fûts, des cartons contenant des boissons et divers matériels utilisés dans le processus, ont été saisis. Des personnes ont également été interpellées pour les besoins de la procédure. La Police Municipale remercie les populations pour leur vigilance et leur collaboration. Elle les encourage à poursuivre la dénonciation de tout fait ou comportement susceptible de porter atteinte à la sécurité, à la salubrité et à la santé publiques. La Police Municipale, toujours plus proche de vous ! items.title: ‘Development must not always begin from Accra’ — Anwelle Foundation launched in Jirapa
items.description: The Paramount Chief of the Jirapa Traditional Area, Naa Di-Naa Donlabong III, has called on residents and natives of Jirapa living outside the community to take greater responsibility for its development instead of relying solely on the government. He made the call at the launch of the Anwelle Foundation in Jirapa in the Upper West Region, where he urged citizens to bring their resources, expertise and networks home to help tackle poverty and youth unemployment. “Development does not always have to begin from Accra. It can begin here. It can begin from a young man who refuses to give up on his community; it can begin from a woman farmer, a teacher, a student, a philanthropist, or from the traditional palace. And sometimes, it can begin with nothing more than a decision to care,” Naa Di-Naa Donlabong III said. The foundation is focused on addressing resource gaps in rural communities through interventions in education, youth empowerment, sustainable livelihoods and rural development. The Paramount Chief said sustainable development required communities to look beyond government for solutions and encouraged sons and daughters of Jirapa across the world to return with their capital, academic knowledge, professional expertise and networks. Naa Di-Naa Donlabong III also defended the recent decision by the Jirapa Traditional Council to confer a chieftaincy title on social media influencer Parrot Mouth, who was enskinned as the Jirapa Development Social Media Influencer Chief. He said the move reflected the need for traditional institutions to adapt to modern communication platforms and use them to promote the community. “The palace must not become disconnected from the tools of the modern world. A story about Jirapa can travel across the world before the Traditional Council has finished its meeting,” he said. “We cannot complain that the world is not hearing about Jirapa and, at the same time, reject those who have the capacity to make the world listen to us.” Founder and Chief Executive Officer of the Anwelle Foundation, Frank Anwelle, said his decision to establish the charity was influenced by his own experience of receiving educational support at a critical stage of his life. He said many talented young people in rural communities miss opportunities simply because they do not have access to information or financial support. “At a critical moment in my life, someone saw potential in me and opened a door. But support was largely a matter of chance,” Mr Anwelle said. “Sometimes, scholarships exist, but the brilliant student in the village never hears about it. The Anwelle Foundation exists to close that gap. Help should not be hidden; opportunities should not be accidental.” The foundation had undertaken a number of interventions before its formal launch, including emergency support for students affected by the Jirapa Senior High School dormitory fire, the distribution of sewing machines to vocational trainees and the drilling of boreholes to provide communities with access to clean water. One beneficiary, Abdul Karim Hakim, a Level 400 Bachelor of Science in Computer Science student at the University for Development Studies, recounted how the foundation supported his university education. Mr Hakim, a native of Walewale, said Mr Anwelle met him while he was working as an apartment security guard in Dansoman, Accra, in 2022 to raise money for his tertiary education. He said the foundation subsequently covered his tuition, accommodation and living expenses throughout his four years at university. The foundation also announced plans for an automotive apprenticeship programme in partnership with industry operator Johani Annie. Under the initiative, selected young people from Jirapa will receive technical training at automotive branches in Tamale, Sunyani and Accra. The foundation plans to establish an automotive workshop in Jirapa after the training to provide employment opportunities for the beneficiaries. The Upper West Regional Minister, Charles Lwanga Puozuing, commended the initiative and personally donated GH¢20,000 to the foundation. He encouraged stakeholders to develop integrated agricultural value chains covering production, processing, storage and market access to make farming more attractive to young people. Mr Puozuing, however, cautioned residents against placing excessive demands on the new foundation, warning that such expectations could undermine its ability to operate sustainably. “When one person undertakes to help, we shouldn’t break the fellow’s back,” he said. “In Jirapa, we are over 200,000 natives. If one person comes to support and our demand seems to quadruple because there is an Anwelle Foundation, the foundation will collapse before we get the necessary impact.” Leader of the People’s National Convention (PNC) and Bimoba Youth Chief, Bernard Anbataayela Mornah, also donated GH¢5,000. He urged political actors not to view youth-led development initiatives through partisan lenses or undermine them through what he described as the “Pull Him Down” syndrome. Board Chairman of the Anwelle Foundation, Prof Williams Angko, said the name Anwelle translates from the local dialect to mean “no one should be left behind”. He pledged that the foundation would operate according to principles of transparency, non-partisanship and merit-based assistance. “The board will ensure that every resource entrusted to us is used transparently and reaches out to those in need—not those who are related to us. Everybody is our relative,” Prof Angko said. The launch also attracted international participation, including Daniel N. Kolubah, Presidential Envoy for Trade, Investments and Special Duties of Liberia, for whom Mr Anwelle serves as Special Aide for Ghana. Mr Kolubah urged African leaders and development organisations to focus on measurable community impact rather than the number of programmes they announce. “The true measure of leadership lies not only in what we achieve for ourselves, but also in the opportunities that we create and the lives that we positively impact,” he said. Chairman of the occasion, Prof Osumanu Issaka Kanton, said the foundation’s success would ultimately depend on sustained work in communities. He called on the Jirapa Municipal Assembly, traditional authorities and development partners to collaborate with the foundation in addressing poverty and other development challenges in the area.

items.title: Editors’ Conference 2026: After 27 years, why democracy still fails ordinary Nigerians — Onaiyekan
items.description: By Juliet Umeh For 27 uninterrupted years, Nigerians have lived under elected governments. They have queued under scorching sun and rain to vote, watched presidents and governors come and go, and seen disputed elections move from polling units to courtrooms. Read Also: All Nigeria Editors Confab, 2026: Before ballot box, Africans already knew democracy — Achebe Yet, for the ordinary Nigerian, John Cardinal Onaiyekan believes a fundamental question remains: Has democracy really put the people at the centre of governance? At 82, the Archbishop Emeritus of Abuja has witnessed Nigeria’s journey through colonial rule, independence, military governments and civilian administrations. His conclusion is sobering: having democracy is one thing; making it work for ordinary people is another. “I speak as an 82-year-old Nigerian who has seen this nation going up and down with hopes of greatness that have continued to elude us,” Onaiyekan told editors at the All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC 2026, in Enugu. For him, the true test of democracy is not merely how many elections have been conducted or how long civilians have remained in power. It is whether the government serves the people. When citizens become pawns Nigeria has achieved something that once seemed difficult: more than a quarter-century of uninterrupted civilian government. But elections alone, Onaiyekan argued, do not make democracy meaningful. He said: “Democracy must be governance for the good of the people. The leaders must be serving the interests of the governed, and people must be at the centre of governance – what we call the common good.” It is, he said, “the kind of democracy that Nigerians have been dreaming about.” Yet, that ideal is tested whenever elections become primarily struggles among politicians for control of power Onaiyekan accused some politicians of adopting a “do-or-die” attitude because political office brings wealth and influence. “In all this, the people hardly count at all,” he said. “Rather, they are just pawns on the political game.” That is perhaps one of the contradictions of Nigeria’s democracy: the citizen who is supposed to be its most powerful participant can become its least influential actor. Who owns the vote? Since Nigeria returned to civilian rule in 1999, successive elections were expected to strengthen democratic institutions. “We have had several elections since 1999. It is difficult to believe that we have been making progress. In fact, it seems that the quality of the elections has been reducing from one election to the other, and this is not good news at all,” he said. His concerns range from the conduct of politicians to the independence of INEC, deployment of security agencies and role of the judiciary. But he reserved one of his sharpest questions for politicians who boast that they will “deliver” entire states to preferred candidates. “Where is the freedom of the people of the state to vote according to their individual consciences?” he asked. “Or does the governor intend to vote for everybody in his state?” Behind that question lies another: Who owns the vote – the citizen who casts it or the political structure claiming to control it? Ballot box or courtroom? Onaiyekan also questioned the growing prominence of courts in electoral outcomes. “The judiciary is not to determine elections about who wins, but rather to adjudicate disputes when they arise. “If elections were well conducted, there ought not to be any need for judicial cases.” But Nigeria, he observed, has increasingly witnessed electoral battles moving from polling units to tribunals. “Our experience in the recent past has almost become that we have been witnessing a situation where our elections are being determined not at the polls, but in the courts by the tribunals.” For voters who queued to exercise their franchise, such prolonged disputes can raise questions about where electoral power ultimately resides. ‘Power belongs to the people’ For Onaiyekan, Nigeria’s democratic journey must eventually return to its simplest promise: government exists for citizens. He said: “In political terms, we say that power belongs to the people. By that, we mean that it does not belong to the political leaders and office holders.” He also rejected arguments that Nigerians should simply wait for democracy to mature over generations. “We must never give up our efforts to keep pushing for a government of the people, by the people, for the people. “We cannot accept the specious argument that democracy has taken centuries to build in some nations, and that so we should wait for hundreds of years to achieve our own. “We have the experience of history, and we cannot be re-inventing the wheel.” After 27 years, therefore, Nigeria’s democratic challenge is no longer merely keeping soldiers out of government or conducting another election. It is ensuring that the ordinary Nigerian who stands in a polling queue truly has a stake in determining how the country is governed. “The ultimate objective,” Onaiyekan said, “is to install a government that is freely chosen by the people and that works for the common good of the people.” Until that promise reaches the ordinary citizen, Nigeria’s democracy, in Onaiyekan’s reckoning, remains unfinished. Vanguard News The post Editors’ Conference 2026: After 27 years, why democracy still fails ordinary Nigerians — Onaiyekan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: « On a réussi à dompter les latéraux burkinabè » : Les révélations de Gernot Rohr après le nul à Ouagadougou
items.description: Ancien sélectionneur des Étalons désormais aux commandes des Guépards du Bénin, Gernot Rohr a réussi son retour au Stade du 4-Août de Ouagadougou en arrachant un point précieux (1-1) lors de la 1re journée des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Contestant vivement le penalty accordé au Burkina Faso en première période, le technicien franco-allemand a salué la réaction d'orgueil et la discipline tactique de son groupe au retour des vestiaires. En conférence de presse, le patron du banc béninois a détaillé la manière dont ses joueurs ont neutralisé les couloirs burkinabè pour réaliser un « bon coup » stratégique en terre adverse. Le scénario de la première mi-temps semblait pourtant donner raison au public du Stade du 4-Août, poussant derrière des Étalons dominateurs. À la 17e minute, une main béninoise dans la surface de réparation a incité l'arbitre à accorder un penalty, immédiatement converti par Franck Lassina Traoré pour ouvrir le score. Une décision arbitrale que Gernot Rohr a fermement remise en cause devant les médias à l'issue de la rencontre. « Le penalty ne devait pas être sifflé parce que quand le ballon touche une partie du corps avant de toucher la main, on ne siffle pas penalty. Il y avait injustice » , a martelé le sélectionneur des Guépards. Loin de se laisser abattre par cette ouverture du score précoce, le technicien a transformé cette frustration en levier psychologique pour remobiliser ses troupes. « La meilleure façon de montrer son mécontentement, c'est de jouer. Et on a joué » , a-t-il souligné avec fierté. Rentrés aux vestiaires avec un but de retard, les Béninois ont reçu des consignes claires de la part de leur entraîneur pour corriger leurs erreurs initiales. « J'ai dit à mes éléments à la mi-temps : « calmez-vous » » , a conféré Gernot Rohr. Constatant que les Étalons ont baissé d'intensité physique et de rythme en seconde période, le coach béninois a ajusté son dispositif pour fermer les espaces. Le réajustement s'est avéré particulièrement payant dans la fermeture des couloirs, où les latéraux burkinabè posaient d'importants problèmes durant le premier acte. « On a été dominés en première période. Les Étalons ont baissé en deuxième période. Les enfants ont su réagir et ont égalisé… On a réussi à dompter les latéraux burkinabè en 2e période. On s'est créé des occasions » , a analysé avec précision l'ancien sélectionneur du Burkina Faso. La domination tactique du Bénin en seconde mi-temps s'est concrétisée à la 66e minute par l'obtention d'un penalty, transformé avec sang-froid par Tosin Aiyegun pour rétablir la parité (1-1). Fidèle à ses déclarations d'avant-match où il affirmait qu'un nul lui conviendrait parfaitement, Gernot Rohr a savouré ce partage des points obtenu au terme d'un match maîtrisé. « Le coup le plus parfait était de gagner. Mais ce nul est également un bon coup… Mes jeunes joueurs m'ont procuré du bonheur » , a conclu le sélectionneur du Bénin. Grâce à cette réaction de caractère orchestrée par leur entraîneur, les Guépards quittent Ouagadougou avec un point capital dans la course à la qualification du groupe F. items.title: All Nigeria Editors Confab, 2026: Before ballot box, Africans already knew democracy — Achebe
items.description: By Juliet Umeh Long before ballot papers, polling booths and electoral commissions became features of Nigeria’s political life, communities gathered to deliberate, question those who exercised authority and arrive at decisions affecting their collective existence. Read Also: 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians There were no voter cards or electronic accreditation machines. Yet, according to the Obi of Onitsha, His Royal Majesty, Igwe Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, beneath those traditional systems lay an important democratic principle: power required the consent and participation of the people. For Achebe, therefore, democracy should not simply be regarded as a foreign political idea handed down to Africans. Its fundamental values, he argued, have deep roots in indigenous African society. Speaking as chairman of the All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC, in Enugu, Achebe reached into Igbo traditional governance to make his point. “In our Igbo tradition, the Obi does not rule by decree. He rules in council, in dialogue, in the constant testing of truth against the wisdom of elders and the voice of the people. “Igbo democratic instinct is ancient. Even kingship here has always been checked by the community, by consultation, by honest speech,” he said. It was a striking intervention at a conference devoted to the ballot, media and survival of democracy. Democracy beyond election day Modern democracy is commonly associated with periodic elections, political parties, legislatures and constitutions. But Achebe’s argument goes deeper: these institutions may be modern, but the underlying idea that leaders should listen to the people is not necessarily new to African societies. He declared: “The ballot box, in this sense, is not an import grafted onto our soil. It is a modern vessel for an old African value, which states that legitimate power flows from the consent, the voice, and the informed judgment of the people.” That distinction is significant. It suggests that the real test of democracy is not merely whether citizens queue every four years to cast ballots, but whether their voices continue to matter after the votes have been counted. Achebe, who reflected on Nigeria’s journey from independence through military rule to democratic government, described the country’s democracy as a continuing project rather than a finished achievement. “I have watched Nigeria’s journey from the optimism of independence, through the turbulence of military rule, into the fragile and still-unfinished project of democratic self-governance,” he said. His message was that democracy requires constant protection. “Democracy is not a monument we erect and then walk away from,” Achebe warned. “It is more like a fire lit to keep the house warm. It must be tended, fed, protected from wind and rain, or it dies quietly in the night while everyone believes it still burns.” Consent must be informed But Achebe also identified a complication in the principle of popular consent. For the people’s choices to confer meaningful legitimacy, he argued, those choices must be informed. “Consent is only meaningful if it is informed,” he said. That is where he placed journalism at the heart of the democratic process. “The ballot is the citizen’s voice. The media is the mirror by which that citizen sees the world clearly enough to know what to say with that voice. “When the mirror is cracked, or worse, deliberately distorted, the citizen no longer votes from truth but votes from illusion.And a democracy built on illusion is not genuine democracy but drama. It becomes a theatre,” he said. For editors gathered in Enugu, the traditional ruler’s argument effectively connected two institutions separated by centuries: the village council where voices were heard and the modern newsroom through which citizens receive information. In both, he suggested, honest speech matters. When the people stop mattering Achebe’s reflection also raises a larger question for Nigeria: if consultation, consent and accountability are deeply rooted values, why should democratic participation begin and end at the polling booth? His description of traditional leadership offers an interesting contrast to any system in which obtaining political office is treated as sufficient authority to govern without listening. Even an Obi, he stressed, is subject to restraints. “Even kingship here has always been checked by the community, by consultation, by honest speech.” It is perhaps one of the most important messages from his address. Democracy may have acquired modern institutions and technologies, but its survival still rests on an old and remarkably simple principle: those who govern must remain connected to those they govern. And citizens, in turn, must have truthful information with which to judge them. That explains why Achebe charged journalists not merely to report democracy, but to help preserve it. “In the face of challenges, politicking, electioneering and partisanship, you must stand upright for democracy and the nation. “Even if politicians, electoral body, institutions, and other things fail, you must be the ultimate last man standing in the task of defending democracy,” he told the editors. From the traditional council to the modern ballot box, Achebe’s argument is ultimately about the same thing: power derives its legitimacy not simply from those who wield it, but from the people whose consent gives it meaning. items.title: FACT-CHECK : Élisabeth Ndiaye n’est pas décédée, la confusion vient de la disparition de sa sœur Hélène Harley
items.description: Une fausse information annonçant le décès d’Élisabeth Ndiaye, figure emblématique du journal télévisé au Sénégal, circule sur les réseaux sociaux et a été relayée par certains médias. En réalité, la personne décédée vendredi matin à Paris est sa sœur, Hélène Harley, âgée de 93 ans, ancienne speakerine et grande voix de Radio Sénégal. Ce qui est affirmé Des publications diffusées sur les réseaux sociaux, reprises par certains médias, annoncent le décès d’Élisabeth Ndiaye, ancienne présentatrice vedette du journal télévisé de la télévision nationale. Cette information est fausse. Ce que révèle la vérification La personne décédée à Paris est Hélène Harley, sœur d’Élisabeth Ndiaye. Un décès confirmé par sa famille. Âgée de 93 ans, elle a marqué l’histoire de la radio sénégalaise par sa voix et ses journaux parlés. En 1964, Hélène Harley intègre l’Office de Radiodiffusion Télévision du Sénégal (ORTS) en tant que speakerine. Au fil des années, elle s’impose comme une figure emblématique du paysage audiovisuel national et une journaliste reconnue de Radio Sénégal, marquant plusieurs générations d’auditeurs. Élisabeth Ndiaye, une figure de la télévision sénégalaise Élisabeth Ndiaye dont la ressemblance avec sa grande soeur est assez frappante, pour sa part, est une figure majeure de la télévision sénégalaise, qu’elle rejoint en 1970. Présentatrice vedette du journal télévisé, elle a marqué plusieurs générations de téléspectateurs avant de quitter le petit écran en 2001. En 2023, la Convention des jeunes reporters du Sénégal lui a rendu hommage pour son parcours à la télévision nationale. En mars 2026, Le Soleil la citait encore parmi les pionnières ayant marqué l’histoire de la présentation du journal télévisé au Sénégal. Un démenti relayé par Adama Sow Le journaliste et analyste des médias sénégalais Adama Sow, spécialiste des questions numériques et ancien présentateur de magazines télévisés, a également publié un message pour démentir cette fausse information sur le décès d'Elisabeth Ndiaye, relayée par plusieurs médias. Verdict : une confusion entre deux sœurs La vérification permet de distinguer clairement les deux informations : Élisabeth Ndiaye n’est pas la personne dont le décès est annoncé. C’est sa grande sœur, Hélène Harley, qui est décédée à Paris. C.G. DIOP

items.title: Éliminatoires CAN 2027 : Le Burkina Faso déçoit et concède le nul face au Bénin (1-1)
items.description: Ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026, au Stade du 4-Août de Ouagadougou, les Étalons du Burkina Faso ont concédé un match nul décevant (1-1) face aux Guépards du Bénin lors de la première journée des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Bien lancés en première période grâce à un penalty transformé par Franck Lassina Traoré, les hommes d'Amir Abdou se sont complètement effondrés au retour des vestiaires, concédant l'égalisation sur penalty par Aiyegun Tosin. Entre choix tactiques poussifs et colère noire du sélectionneur national, ce partage des points précoce prive le Burkina Faso d'un départ idéal et contraint l'équipe à réagir au plus vite. L'atmosphère s'annonçait festive dans un Stade du 4-Août chauffé à blanc à 19 heures pour l'entrée en lice des Étalons dans le groupe F des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Dès les premiers instants, les Burkinabè ont affiché leurs intentions offensives, notamment sous l'impulsion d'Issa Kaboré dont le débordement tranchant a obtenu un corner dès la première minute de jeu. Dominants et entreprenants, les locaux ont concrétisé leur supériorité à la suite d'une faute de main béninoise commise dans la surface de réparation. Dernier arrivé au regroupement, Franck Lassina Traoré a pris ses responsabilités en transformant sereinement le penalty accordé par l'arbitre, libérant les travées du stade à la 20e minute. Face à des Guépards timorés durant le premier acte, la sélection burkinabè a conservé la maîtrise du ballon et s'est procuré d'autres occasions franches, comme cette frappe soudaine d'Ousseni Bouda détournée en corner juste avant la pause. À la mi-temps, le tableau d'affichage indiquait un avantage logique de 1-0 en faveur des Étalons, la défense béninoise montrant des signes évidents de fébrilité. La suite des événements a viré au chemin de croix pour le public ouagalais. Dès le retour des vestiaires, les Étalons ont étrangement baissé de rythme, devenant passifs, déboussolés et incapables d'imposer leur jeu. Profitant de cette apathie, les Guépards du Bénin ont pris possession du cuir, imposant un pressing étouffant et poussant la défense locale à multiplier les pertes de balle. Furieux sur sa ligne de touche, le sélectionneur Amir Abdou s'est agité en vain face à l'impuissance de ses joueurs. La punition est intervenue à la 66e minute lorsqu'une faute sur Tamimou Ouorou a offert un penalty au Bénin, immédiatement converti par Aiyegun Tosin pour remettre les deux formations à égalité. Symbole du désarroi burkinabè, Axel Taonsa — entré à la pause à la place de Rachid Kouda — a été rappelé sur le banc à peine 26 minutes plus tard pour laisser sa place à Elohim Kaboré. Les remplacements ultérieurs de Lassina Traoré, Ismaïla Ouédraogo et Edmond Tapsoba n'ont pas permis d'inverser la vapeur, laissant le sélectionneur béninois Gernot Rohr savourer un point précieux qu'il avait lui-même qualifié d'objectif idéal la veille. À l'issue du coup de sifflet final, l'amertume et la frustration ont supplanté la ferveur initiale au Stade du 4-Août. En conférence de presse, le sélectionneur Amir Abdou s'est montré particulièrement incisif envers la prestation de son groupe, déclarant : « La deuxième mi-temps ne reflétait pas du tout la physionomie de la première. En deuxième période nous sommes restés dans les vestiaires » . Le technicien a pointé du doigt les faiblesses techniques et le manque d'engagement : « J’avais pourtant averti les joueurs. J’ai senti un peu de fatigue et de réticence. Nous avons perdu la maîtrise du match… Je n’ai pas vu des joueurs conquérants capables d’aller chercher la victoire » . Tête de série du groupe F, le Burkina Faso abandonne précieux deux points à domicile derrière la Mauritanie, victorieuse de la Centrafrique (3-1). Conscient de l'urgence de la situation, Amir Abdou a conclu sur une note de fermeté en prévenant que son équipe avait « grillé un joker » et qu'elle devra faire preuve « de maturité et d'abnégation » lors de ses prochaines sorties pour espérer valider son billet pour la CAN 2027. L’article Éliminatoires CAN 2027 : Le Burkina Faso déçoit et concède le nul face au Bénin (1-1) est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Ouagadougou : Quand la pluie obéit aux ordres de Waong Sougr Naaba !
items.description: Selon plusieurs témoins, le Waong Sougr Naaba aurait effectué des prières traditionnelles alors que la pluie menaçait la cérémonie d’ouverture du festival, avant que les précipitations ne cessent brusquement. Une scène particulière a marqué la cérémonie d’ouverture du festival Kienfague Zamnogo, le 24 septembre 2026. Alors que la pluie s’abattait sur le site de la cérémonie, le Waong Sougr Naaba, chef coutumier, aurait entrepris une série de gestes et de prières traditionnelles afin, selon les témoins, de permettre à l’événement de se poursuivre dans de bonnes conditions. D’après plusieurs personnes présentes sur les lieux, le chef coutumier se serait d’abord accroupi pour murmurer quelques paroles. Il aurait ensuite levé les yeux vers les nuages tout en psalmodiant des prières traditionnelles. Toujours selon les témoignages recueillis, la pluie se serait arrêtée peu après ces gestes, permettant à la cérémonie de se poursuivre. La scène aurait suscité les applaudissements et les réactions enthousiastes de l’assistance, certains participants interprétant l’arrêt soudain de la pluie comme le résultat de l’intervention du chef coutumier. L’article Ouagadougou : Quand la pluie obéit aux ordres de Waong Sougr Naaba ! est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: From Obasanjo and Tinubu camps to Atiku’s war room, by Emmanuel Aziken
items.description: Atiku Abubakar’s choice of leaders for his 2027 presidential campaign tells a larger story than the announcement of a campaign council. Its chairman, Kashim Ibrahim-Imam, was once firmly identified with Olusegun Obasanjo. Its deputy chairman, Nasir El-Rufai, served on a panel that examined allegations against Atiku during his bitter struggle with Obasanjo. Both later moved through the political camp that brought Bola Tinubu to power. Now they are to help Atiku defeat him. Read Also: 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians The appointment of Ibrahim-Imam is an illustration of how far Nigeria’s political relationships can travel. At the start of the Fourth Republic, Obasanjo made him presidential liaison officer to the Senate. It was a delicate assignment: relations between the presidency and the legislature were already fraught. Ibrahim-Imam was accused of involvement in moves against Senate President Chuba Okadigbo and declared unwelcome at the National Assembly. The accusation did not establish his guilt, but it reinforced his reputation as an unwavering Obasanjo man. That association carries particular irony for Atiku. His partnership with Obasanjo ended in one of the Fourth Republic’s most enduring political feuds. Only this year, the former president again described choosing Atiku as his vice-president as a mistake. One of the politicians who built his early career close to Obasanjo is now entrusted with directing Atiku’s bid for the office they once occupied together. Ibrahim-Imam’s own ambition was to govern Borno State. He won the Peoples Democratic Party ticket in 2003, but Ali Modu Sheriff—“SAS” to his political followers—defeated him on the opposition All Nigeria Peoples Party platform. Ibrahim-Imam tried again in 2007. Sheriff beat him again and completed two terms as governor. For an Obasanjo loyalist flying the president’s party flag, the double defeat was a bruising lesson in the limits of presidential proximity. There have long been suggestions that Sheriff enjoyed a separate relationship with Obasanjo through his father, who was said to have carried out contracts during Obasanjo’s military administration. Such accounts help explain the intrigue that surrounded the Borno contests. They do not prove that Obasanjo secretly worked against Ibrahim-Imam. The electoral record is clear enough: twice the president’s party candidate confronted Sheriff; twice he lost. Thereafter, Kashim remained in the political background from 2007 for more than a decade. It is alleged that in that period he quietly formed an alliance with Asiwaju Bola Tinubu, and that it was on that basis he received one of the few appointments President Muhammadu Buhari gifted to Tinubu. It was no small job. The chairmanship of the Tertiary Education Trust Fund, TETFund, was one of the juiciest positions on offer during the Buhari years. Kashim was among those considered for running mate to Tinubu in the run-up to the 2023 election, but he lost out to his fellow Borno man and namesake, Senator Kashim Shettima. There were insinuations that he was not happy with it. Tinubu tried to mollify him by nominating his 25-year-old son as chairman of FERMA, but that nomination drew a national outcry and was withdrawn. For whatever reason, Kashim then withdrew from the Tinubu space and subsequently emerged in the ranks of the opposition, and then in Atiku’s ADC. El-Rufai’s history with Atiku is more personal. In the early Obasanjo years, he headed the Bureau of Public Enterprises under a privatisation programme supervised by Atiku as vice-president. They had worked together before becoming adversaries. The break became consequential during the Petroleum Technology Development Fund affair. In 2006, Obasanjo established an administrative panel to review allegations involving Atiku. When the Obasanjo government exited and he fell out with the successor, he quickly pitched camp with Muhammadu Buhari and reinvented himself as a son of the former military head of state. He won the governorship of Kaduna State on the coattails of the Buhari phenomenon in 2015 and served out two terms of what many still call one of the most divisive administrations in the history of the state. At the peak of Buhari’s power, and with Tinubu in seeming decline, El-Rufai took up tirades against Tinubu and at one point came to Lagos to lecture political actors on how to overthrow political godfathers. Shockingly, by 2022, El-Rufai was among the northern APC governors backing a southern successor to Buhari. He then supported Tinubu’s candidacy against Atiku in 2023. A place in Tinubu’s government appeared to follow. Tinubu nominated El-Rufai as a minister, and El-Rufai spoke of plans for the power sector. The Senate withheld his confirmation, citing security clearance. El-Rufai later said Tinubu had changed his mind about appointing him. The contents of the cited security concerns were not publicly settled, and the competing accounts offer no firm basis for claiming who engineered his exclusion. The partnership ended; El-Rufai moved into opposition politics. There is a further complication for Atiku’s campaign. El-Rufai remains in custody while facing trial over alleged money laundering and conversion of public property. Those allegations are unproven. His circumstances nevertheless raise a practical question about how a deputy chairman can help coordinate a national campaign while unable to move freely. Atiku’s team calls its structure lean: Senator Austin Akobundu will manage campaign operations through six directorates and 30 directors. Its two political leaders bring formidable experience, along with the baggage of the governments and rivalries that shaped them. The appointments show Atiku’s willingness to reconcile with old opponents. The test will be whether Ibrahim-Imam and El-Rufai can offer voters a convincing reason for their new alliance—and a governing purpose that reaches beyond removing Tinubu. items.title: Atiku: Produce conviction evidence or… – ADC challenges APC
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike The African Democratic Congress, ADC, Presidential Campaign Council has challenged the All Progressives Congress, APC, to produce any court judgment convicting former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the allegations being levelled against him by the party, accusing its spokesman, Felix Morka, of turning allegations into verdicts. Read Also: 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians The Council said Nigerians were less interested in political insults than in answers to the pressures they face daily, from the cost of food and fuel to transport and electricity. In a statement by its Director of Strategic Communications, Phrank Shaibu, the Council said Morka could raise questions about Atiku’s record but could not present allegations as established convictions. “Morka has become an untutored spin doctor for a party caught in the conundrum of a sinking regime,” Shaibu said. He challenged the APC spokesman to identify the court and produce the judgment if he claimed Atiku had been convicted of corruption. “Morka may raise each matter. He may not strip away the report’s distinctions and present the resulting fiction as a judgment against Atiku,” Shaibu said. The Council then turned the APC’s attack on Atiku’s suitability to manage public funds against President Bola Tinubu, citing the United States forfeiture proceedings involving $460,000 from an account in Tinubu’s name. Shaibu said the proceedings and associated financial records raised questions about transactions involving Tinubu and individuals named in the case. “A bank introduction. A transfer. A cheque. A company. Tinubu should explain those transactions and why the same names kept appearing around his finances,” he said. The Council also cited the US litigation over access to FBI and other investigative records concerning Tinubu, arguing that Nigerians should be allowed to see the relevant documents, subject to lawful protections. “Morka’s colleagues will rush to tell Nigerians that a search result is not a conviction. Nobody has said it is,” Shaibu said. He said the distinction did not erase the questions surrounding the records. “Yes, the case before the court concerns access to records. The records concern an investigation. Both facts can be true at once,” Shaibu said. The post Atiku: Produce conviction evidence or… – ADC challenges APC appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians
items.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri As campaigns for the 2027 general elections heat up, former President Goodluck Jonathan has warned politicians to play according to the rules, saying it would be wrong for candidates to maneuver the system just to win an election. Read Also: 2027: I’ll lead Tinubu’s campaign team in FCT, Rivers — Wike Jonathan’s admonition appears to counter President Bola Tinubu’s earlier remark that “all is fair in politics.” Delivering a goodwill message at a public lecture held to mark the 80th birthday of a former Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Mr. Kanu Agabi, SAN, ex-President Jonathan, who voluntarily conceded defeat to the opposition party in 2015, maintained that politicians cannot justify every action taken to win an election by simply describing it as politics. According to him, electoral contests must be governed by established rules, and politicians should not treat the quest for victory as justification for misconduct. He said: “In politics, it is a disaster. People do stupid things, also even criminal things, and they will tell you it is politics. It is not politics. Politics has rules. “Politics is like a soccer match. You play according to the rules, and that is why the courts step in to mediate if you go against the rules. Otherwise, you can do anything and win an election and walk away.” The erstwhile president also stressed that the anti-corruption fight in the country requires more than laws and enforcement agencies, emphasising that enduring change would depend on building a society where ethical conduct is valued above wrongdoing. “The challenge before Nigeria is not simply to make laws against corruption. It is to build a culture in which ethical conduct becomes the norm, where public office is treated as a trust, and where institutions are strong enough to uphold accountability. “We cannot continue to claim that private corruption will just keep going around in circles. It cannot go anywhere until we develop that culture, and nobody does wrong willingly,” he added. Recalling an experience in Rwanda, Jonathan said the country’s social values discourage public officials from accepting gifts that could be considered inappropriate. He said the experience demonstrated how deeply rooted social norms can influence public conduct beyond what formal laws prescribe. “I gave this to my aides to give to the people who take care of me. If you give me a hotel room where nobody can see anybody, where it is free, they say it is not the culture of Rwanda to accept the little gift — just a gift,” he said. Meanwhile, he stressed that key institutions in the country, especially the judiciary, have an important role to play in ensuring accountability when rules are violated. “All of us Nigerians have a major role to play if we want to suppress corruption, not just the bodies established by law to discipline and punish those who do it,” he stated, even as he urged politicians to exhibit higher moral standards. Vanguard News The post 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Journées nationales d'engagement patriotique : Une exposition gouvernementale pour rendre compte des réalisations de la RPP
items.description: Le gouvernement annonce la phase 2 de la 3ᵉ édition (la première phase s'est tenue du 26 mars au 09 avril 2026) des Journées nationales d'engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC), du 2 au 16 octobre 2026. Cette deuxième phase est placée sous le thème « Produisons burkinabè, consommons burkinabè ! », avec au programme, diverses activités, dont une exposition gouvernementale des réalisations et acquis de la RPP. L'information a été donnée ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou à travers une conférence de presse animée par le ministre de la justice et des droits humains, Me Rodrigue Bayala, et le ministre de la communication, de la culture, des arts et du tourisme, porte-parole du gouvernement, Gilbert Ouédraogo. Quatre ans après le sursaut patriotique du 30 septembre 2022, situent les conférenciers, le peuple burkinabè a fait un choix clair de reconquérir sa souveraineté, en comptant d'abord sur ses propres forces et bâtir, ici, le Faso de la dignité. Instituées par un décret du 3 avril 2024, les Journées nationales d'engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC) sont désormais l'école pratique du Manifeste de la révolution progressiste populaire, lancé le 26 avril 2026, déroule le ministre de la justice et des droits humains, Me Rodrigue Bayala, livrant la déclaration liminaire. Les JEPPC sont, poursuit-il, organisées en deux phases au cours de l'année, du 26 mars au 9 avril, puis du 2 au 16 octobre ; elles convertissent les valeurs cardinales du peuple : patriotisme, intégrité, discipline, solidarité, esprit de sacrifice en actes concrets et vérifiables. Ainsi, du 2 au 16 octobre 2026, sur toute l'étendue du territoire, dans les 17 régions et dans les missions diplomatiques, « le peuple sera à l'œuvre à travers les activités suivantes : montée du pavillon national et diffusion du message du camarade président du Faso, port de tenues traditionnelles, journées de salubrité et participation aux chantiers Faso Mêbo, dons de sang et contributions au Fonds de soutien patriotique, conférences sur le civisme et le civisme économique jusque dans les yaars, foires et dégustations de mets locaux (nationaux) ». Le 15 octobre sera consacré à l'hommage au président Thomas Sankara et la « Nuit des Étoiles du Faso » distinguera, le 16 octobre, les meilleurs exemples d'engagement citoyen. « Le visiteur verra la Révolution en actes : pavés produits en direct sur le chantier-démonstration de Faso Mêbo, motos des FDS (Forces de défense et de sécurité) et des VDP (Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie) réparées par le Service national pour le développement, constat d'accident simulé par drone, technologies issues de nos laboratoires, métiers à tisser du Faso Dan Fani, village de la production pénitentiaire, archives de la Défense, de la diplomatie et du Mémorial Thomas Sankara. Chacun des huit jours de l'exposition portera un message : ‘'Le peuple debout rend compte'' (2 octobre) ; ‘'Faso Mêbo : la Patrie se construit de nos mains'' (3 octobre) ; ‘'La diaspora et l'AES : le Sahel debout'' (4 octobre) ; ‘' Santé souveraine et protection sociale'' (5 octobre) ; ‘'Du champ au marché'' (6 octobre) ; ‘'Éduquer, former, employer'' (7 octobre) ; ‘'Made in Burkina'' (8 octobre) ; ‘'Gouvernance, justice et finances publiques'' (9 octobre, clôture). À l'Allée des services au peuple, de 9 heures à 18 heures, le citoyen repartira avec quelque chose entre les mains : document d'identité délivré par l'ONI, e-casier judiciaire, e-certificat de nationalité, e-permis de communiquer, e-RCCM, immatriculation au RAMU, adhésion au BBDA, dépôt de demande de carte de presse, dépistage et don de sang. Il pourra consommer burkinabè au Village des mets et produits nationaux et à l'expo-vente, vibrer chaque soir au Village culturel du patriotisme et contribuer à Faso Mêbo », détaillent les conférenciers. Lire aussi : Journées nationales d'engagement patriotique 2026 : La consommation locale érigée en fierté nationale L'innovation majeure de cette phase est, déclarent les ministres, l'exposition gouvernementale des réalisations et acquis de la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP), du 2 au 9 octobre 2026 au SIAO, au sein du pavillon du Soleil levant et sur l'esplanade extérieure. Elle sera ouverte le 2 octobre à 9 heures. Elle sera une vitrine, et surtout un exercice de redevabilité (le gouvernement rend compte, devant le peuple, de quatre années de Révolution). Il s'agira, de façon concrète, de montrer l'innovation (au moins une innovation datée de la période, conçue ou maîtrisée au Burkina Faso, présentée en fonctionnement et expliquée par un agent) ; présenter du concret (au moins un objet, un ouvrage ou un document original produit entre septembre 2022 et octobre 2026, accompagné d'un chiffre daté et vérifiable) ; offrir des services au peuple (au moins un acte utile rendu sur place pendant les huit jours, un document délivré, une inscription enregistrée, un droit ouvert, un conseil formalisé) ; communiquer par la démonstration (au moins une démonstration à heure fixe, annoncée à l'entrée du stand on fabrique, on répare, on soigne, on cuisine, on tisse, on instruit un dossier devant le public). « Devant notre peuple, chaque ministre répondra de ce que son département a fait de la confiance qui lui a été donnée », ont annoncé ces membres du gouvernement. Pour rappel, l'objectif général des JEPPC est d'amener les citoyens à s'approprier les valeurs de patriotisme, de civisme et de citoyenneté et à développer des réflexes d'engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne en faveur de la paix, de la cohésion sociale, de la défense de l'intérêt général et de la construction de la nation. O.L Lefaso.net

items.title: Tinubu-Must-Go poll puts Atiku ahead of Obi, others for 2027
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi An online poll organised by the Tinubu Must Go TMG movement, asking Nigerians who among the leading presidential candidates they would vote for in the 2027 presidential election, has returned former Vice President and African Democratic Congress ADC presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, as the most preferred choice. Read Also: 2027: I’ll lead Tinubu’s campaign team in FCT, Rivers — Wike The poll, which ran for 24 hours from September 24 to 25, attracted a total of 109,799 respondents. Of that figure, 80,809 votes, representing 73.6 per cent, went to the Atiku/Amaechi ticket, while 24,519 votes, representing 22.3 per cent, went to the Nigeria Democratic Congress NDC ticket of Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso. The remaining 4,471 respondents, representing 4.1 per cent, voted for other candidates in the poll. According to a statement by the pollsters, the margin held steady from early in the exercise. “Approximately seven minutes after voting commenced, the figures stood at about 76.6 percent in support of the Atiku/Amaechi ticket and 20.9 percent for Obi/Kwankwaso,” the statement read. It added that “as participation expanded dramatically, the percentages settled and remained remarkably consistent.” The TMG movement, which is promoted by Abba Hikima, has grown in reputation for its opposition to the Tinubu administration over hardship occasioned by its economic policies. The group noted that a comprehensive report documenting the methodology, participation growth, timestamp analysis, reach, limitations and organisational significance of the exercise would be published in due course. items.title: Force internationale à Gaza : Le Maroc et le Kosovo en première ligne pour le déploiement
items.description: La mise en place de la Force internationale de stabilisation à Gaza entre dans une nouvelle phase, avec l’engagement annoncé de plusieurs pays et la préparation du déploiement de premiers contingents militaires. Le Maroc figure parmi les pays appelés à participer à cette formation avec un premier contingent de 500 soldats marocains et kosovars dont le déploiement est actuellement préparé, selon le général américain Jasper Jeffers, commandant de la Force internationale de stabilisation à Gaza (ISFA). « Nous avons effectué plusieurs missions de reconnaissance sur le terrain dans le secteur de Rafah, dans la bande de Gaza. Nous avons également formé et équipé notre force avancée, composée d’unités militaires regroupant 500 soldats du Kosovo et du Maroc, en vue de leur déploiement à Gaza », a déclaré le militaire américain lors d’une réunion à New York du Conseil de la paix pour Gaza. Lors de cette réunion consacrée à faire le point sur les efforts de reconstruction de ce territoire palestinien, le commandant américain a détaillé les principales étapes de cette opération, qui prévoit notamment le déploiement progressif de forces internationales, la formation de nouvelles unités de sécurité et la mise en œuvre d’un plan de désarmement dans la bande de Gaza. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans un dispositif plus large porté par le « Conseil de la paix » pour Gaza, qui associe également des volets sécuritaire, institutionnel et humanitaire. Le Maroc avait officialisé en juillet 2026 son accord de participation à cette force internationale, dans le cadre des efforts visant à accompagner la mise en place d’un nouveau dispositif de sécurité dans la bande de Gaza. Le général américain a rappelé qu'un an auparavant, « la Force internationale de stabilisation n’était même pas un concept, et l’idée de créer une nouvelle force de sécurité à Gaza était inconcevable ». Et de se féliciter qu'actuellement d’autres forces venues d’Albanie, du Kazakhstan et d’autres pays ont rejoint ladite force, et la construction des infrastructures de la base temporaire destinée au premier contingent de 500 soldats a déjà été effectuée. Il a expliqué que la prochaine étape consistera à garantir le déploiement de la force internationale, avec une expansion continue, et à mettre en œuvre le plan de désarmement secteur par secteur, tout en adoptant une approche visant essentiellement l’ensemble de Gaza. « Cela facilitera la prise en charge des responsabilités par le comité national compétent et garantira l’existence d’un mécanisme permanent et continu de vérification », a-t-il estimé. Le général a également annoncé la réception de plus de 250 000 demandes d’adhésion à la police qui sera présente a Gaza, soulignant que 19 candidatures ont été vérifiées et leur formation initiale a débuté. « En ce qui concerne le désarmement, nous travaillons activement à l’élaboration d’un plan militaire et technique pouvant être mis en œuvre progressivement, secteur par secteur » , a estimé le responsable militaire américain en insistant sur le défi que cela représentait. « L’ampleur du problème est énorme », a-t-il noté en expliquant que la complexité revient notamment aux nombreux tunnels kilométrique et aux nombreuses installations ainsi que les armes présentes sur le territoire. Lors de cette réunion, Jared Kushner, gendre du président américain Donald Trump, a estimé que « les efforts consacrés à la création du Conseil de la paix, de la Force internationale de stabilisation et du comité national chargé de Gaza contribuent à établir une plateforme permettant enfin au peuple palestinien de Gaza de se concentrer sur l’amélioration de ses conditions de vie et le développement de son quotidien, tout en donnant à ceux qui souhaitent vivre en paix la possibilité de le faire ». Et d'ajouter: « Nous espérons que cela montrera aux Israéliens qu’il existe un espoir de paix et de coexistence. Mais nous avons compris dès le premier jour de notre travail que la notion de confiance n’existait pas. C’est pourquoi ce projet repose désormais sur des incitations et des mesures concrètes, afin que chacun sache ce que l’on attend de lui et comment parvenir à notre objectif ». Pour sa part Tony Blair, ancien Premier ministre britannique et membre du conseil exécutif du Conseil de la paix chargé de Gaza, a déclaré qu' » il est question de créer une Palestine libre, mais pour les Palestiniens qui vivent à Gaza, ils n’ont pas besoin d’un slogan, ils ont besoin d’une solution. Pour que Gaza soit libre, elle doit vivre en paix avec ses voisins et avec elle-même ». The post Force internationale à Gaza : Le Maroc et le Kosovo en première ligne pour le déploiement appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Le Tribunal de commerce suspend la sanction visant les établissements Aboubacar Charfo Gagara…
items.description: Le contentieux opposant l’opérateur économique Aboubacar Charfo Gagara au ministère du Commerce et de l’Industrie connaît un nouveau rebondissement. Saisi par le conseil de l’opérateur économique, le juge des référés du Tribunal de commerce a ordonné la suspension de la décision portant interdiction temporaire de l’exercice de la profession commerciale ainsi que la fermeture des boutiques et magasins des établissements Aboubacar Charfo. Cette décision intervient après l’adoption, le 3 septembre 2026, d’un arrêté ministériel suspendant pour une durée de trois mois les activités commerciales des établissements concernés et ordonnant la fermeture de leurs différents points de vente. La mesure administrative s’appuyait notamment sur l’article 42, alinéa 3, de la loi n° 2019-56 du 22 novembre 2019 portant organisation de la concurrence au Niger. Dans son ordonnance, le juge des référés a ordonné la suspension de l’exécution de la décision administrative contestée. Cette mesure permet aux établissements Aboubacar Charfo de reprendre leurs activités commerciales, sous réserve des voies de recours prévues par la loi. Le tribunal a également assorti son ordonnance d’une astreinte de 25 millions de francs CFA en cas de retard dans son exécution. Cette disposition vise à garantir l’application diligente de la décision judiciaire et à prévenir toute entrave à la reprise des activités de l’opérateur économique. Pour la défense d’Aboubacar Charfo, cette ordonnance constitue une décision favorable dans le cadre de la procédure engagée contre la mesure administrative. Elle ne préjuge toutefois pas de l’issue éventuelle du litige au fond. Ce différend intervient dans un contexte de renforcement du contrôle des prix et de régulation du commerce des produits de grande consommation, notamment le ciment. Le ministère du Commerce et de l’Industrie avait présenté la suspension des établissements Aboubacar Charfo comme une mesure destinée à lutter contre les pratiques spéculatives et à préserver l’accès des consommateurs aux produits essentiels. Cette affaire met ainsi en évidence la nécessité de concilier le pouvoir de l’État de réguler le marché et de sanctionner les éventuels manquements avec le respect des droits de la défense, des garanties procédurales et de la liberté d’entreprendre. L’article Le Tribunal de commerce suspend la sanction visant les établissements Aboubacar Charfo Gagara… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .
