items.title: Burkina Faso : le retour des pluies relance les espoirs pour la campagne agropastorale 2026-2027
items.description: Les pluies sont revenues dans plusieurs regions du Burkina Faso apres plusieurs semaines de deficit hydrique qui avaient fait craindre une baisse des rendements agricoles. Du 21 au 23 septembre, des precipitations parfois abondantes ont contribue a rehumidifier les sols et a soutenir les cultures dans plusieurs communes agricoles. Le ministere burkinabe de l'Agriculture a indique que, dans les provinces du Ziro et de la Sissili, les cumuls avaient atteint 68,2 mm a Cassou, 52 mm a Gao, 46 mm a Boura et 38 mm a Leo dans la nuit du 21 au 22 septembre. D'autres regions du pays ont egalement enregistre des precipitations importantes, avec des cumuls allant notamment de 38 mm dans le Goulmou a 56 mm dans le Djoro, a Gueguere et a Iolonioro. Selon les previsions de l'Agence nationale de la meteorologie du Burkina Faso, la periode du 21 au 27 septembre devrait rester « tres humide », avec des cumuls pouvant atteindre 50 mm, voire davantage, dans plusieurs localites. Ces pluies ravivent l'espoir de sauver pres de 20 000 hectares de cultures, avait indique le ministre de l'Agriculture, Ismael Sombie, lors d'une tournee de suivi de la campagne agricole effectuee a la mi-septembre. Le ministre a toutefois souligne que, malgre le deficit pluviometrique observe ces dernieres semaines, les progres enregistres en 2026 dans l'extension des superficies emblavees n'etaient pas remis en cause. Le gouvernement burkinabe a par ailleurs assure qu'il poursuivait le suivi de l'etat des cultures afin d'evaluer l'impact des recentes precipitations sur la campagne agricole. Les autorites burkinabe avaient fait etat, en août dernier, de resultats juges historiques dans le cadre de l'offensive agropastorale et halieutique 2023-2025, portant sur plusieurs filieres vivrieres ainsi que sur les productions animale et halieutique. Fort de ces resultats, le gouvernement a lance, le 30 juillet, une nouvelle initiative baptisee « Offensive agropastorale, hydraulique et halieutique 2026-2028 », avec pour objectif de renforcer l'autosuffisance alimentaire du pays.

items.title: What Annie Dillard Left Out
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. Annie Dillard, who recently died at 81, understood that even in suburban landscapes, one could experience the transcendence and solitude of nature. Reading Diana Saverin’s Atlantic essay about Dillard’s great nature writing made me remember the joy of exploring the wetlands behind my elementary school on the outskirts of Denver, where cottony cattails burst open, crayfish scuttled in the creek, and I could spend hours gazing into a bush, attempting to catch sight of the fairies I was sure lived inside. First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The confrontation that broke New York Six hard-to-find books worth reading The book claiming to teach couples how to select their baby’s sex “Pinballing,” a poem by Jan Beatty In her classic book Pilgrim at Tinker Creek , for example, Dillard describes being “knocked breathless by a powerful glance” in an ordinary Virginia backyard: Gazing at a cedar tree outside a home in her neighborhood, she suddenly experienced it as “charged and transfigured.” But her work suggests that to be deeply in nature is to be in some way separated from other humans. Perhaps this is one reason, as Saverin writes, that Dillard’s personal relationships are largely absent from her writing. That’s true in my memories of the wetlands, too: I must have been able to hear passing sirens, or see airplanes overhead, but my memories involve no such intrusions. In fact, I barely remember my fellow students. I know they were there; I remember cajoling one to examine my beloved shrub turned fairy palace. But the images feel solitary. Dillard captured exactly this sense of observational aloneness. I suspect such selective attention occurs for the same reason that, while looking at a work of art closely, you may cease to notice the museumgoers around you. To view something intensely is to blur your own boundaries, such that you become as much the thing you watch as the person you are. I understand why, for Dillard and some of her fellow nature writers, other people can be difficult to bring into the frame. They’re an interruption: As soon as someone says your name, you’re no longer immersed. But Saverin, who deeply loves Dillard’s work, still wonders what else she might have achieved by bringing a bit more of human presence into her considerations of the natural world. “Part of the pain of losing someone, and perhaps especially a favorite writer,” she writes, “involves losing what they didn’t choose to make during the time they had.” Jill Krementz The Enduring Mystery of Annie Dillard By Diana Saverin Dillard kept much of her personal life carefully outside the scope of her nonfiction. Read the full article. What to Read Yesterday’s Burdens , by Robert M. Coates If Coates survives in historical memory, it’s as a Lost Generation footnote—the man who first introduced Ernest Hemingway to Gertrude Stein. This is an unfortunate legacy, though, for an audacious American literary experimenter whose 1926 debut, The Eater of Darkness , was called “the first Dada novel in English.” Because Coates worked for three decades as The New Yorker ’s art critic, something of a painter’s visual language is found in his strange, oblique sentences. My favorite of his novels is Yesterday’s Burdens , of which Stein was an admirer. (“It is so exciting because it is modern,” she declared.) The novel follows the restless Henderson, a young man who wanders Manhattan, visiting speakeasies and crashing parties to keep despair at bay. Coates absorbs the city’s fabulous energies and arranges the tumult into rich, cubist sketches that reproduce overlapping advertising slogans, subway signs, motor cars, and overheard conversations. After being out of print for decades, Yesterday’s Burdens was resurrected in 2020 by Tough Poets Press. Rife with formal oddities and stylistic verve, this masterpiece captures New York in language that still feels fresh nearly a century later. — Dustin Illingworth From our list: Six hard-to-find books worth reading Out Next Week 📚 The Floating World , by Ben Eastham 📚 Bad Boy for Life: The Rise and Fall of Sean Combs , by Cheyenne Roundtree 📚 To Jerusalem and Back: A Personal Account , by Saul Bellow Your Weekend Read Illustration by Matteo Giuseppe Pani / The Atlantic. Source: Getty. America’s Hypocritical Take on Intellectual Property By Alex Reisner Encyclopedia Britannica , the publisher of Chicken Soup for the Soul , and Strike 3, an adult-film company, may not seem to have much in common. But they all agree on one thing: They want payment for the use of their work in training AI models. In the past year, each of them has brought a lawsuit against the big AI companies, claiming that their content was used to train models without permission. Read the full article. items.title: Poutine : la Russie était prête à reprendre les négociations après les législatives, mais Kiev a ciblé Moscou
items.description: « Ils doivent ressentir les ripostes de l'armee russe et comprendre que toutes leurs provocations, leurs tentatives d'aggraver la situation sont absolument inutiles, qu'elles ne deboucheront sur aucun resultat concret et ne feront qu'aggraver leur situation. » Depuis Saint-Petersbourg, ou se tenait ce 25 septembre le XIIe Forum international des cultures unies, Vladimir Poutine a renvoye les dirigeants kieviens a leurs responsabilites dans l'absence de pourparlers de paix. « En effet, nous avons dit qu'il etait peu probable que des negociations soient possibles avant les elections a la Douma et que nous serions prets a reprendre ces contacts par la suite », a declare le chef d'etat russe, apres une allusion aux declarations de Volodymyr Zelensky, selon lesquelles une reprise de pourparlers directs avec la Russie etait envisageable des le mois de septembre, apres les legislatives du 18-20. « Qu'est-ce qui s'est passe depuis ? », a interpelle le president russe, avant de rappeler que dans « la nuit du 19 au 20 septembre, le jour principal du vote, une tentative a ete faite pour effectuer une frappe massive contre Moscou. Premierement, plus de 1 600 drones sont pratiquement entres dans la zone de Moscou ». Attaques ukrainiennes : la Russie a « commence a repliquer sur chaque point » Vladimir Poutine est egalement revenu sur les attaques visant des bureaux de vote et des membres de commissions electorales. Plus tot dans la journee, devant la Douma, la presidente de la Commission electorale centrale, Ella Pamfilova, avait cite les noms de six membres de commissions electorales qui ont ete tues par des attaques ukrainiennes dans le cadre de ces elections legislatives. Le president russe a egalement rappele les nombreuses attaques contre les navires « aussi bien russes que battant pavillon etranger » en mer Noire, ainsi que la campagne « 40 jours » de frappes, dont s'etait enorgueilli Volodymyr Zelensky sur les reseaux sociaux fin juin. « Toutes ces actions ne font qu'empirer leur situation », a fustige le chef d'etat russe. « Les pistes d'une eventuelle reconciliation et les propositions de reprise des negociations sont bien sur la table et restent realisables », a-t-il poursuivi, « mais apres tout ce qu'ils ont fait, nous allons bien reflechir a ce que nous devrions entreprendre en reponse ». Vladimir Poutine a assure que les forces russes avaient « commence a repliquer sur chaque point ». « De toute evidence, les ripostes de l'armee russe se sont averees tellement douloureuses et devastatrices pour l'ennemi que celui-ci remet activement sur la table la question d'une treve sur plusieurs plans : le volet energetique, c'est-a-dire qu'ils sont desormais prets a ne plus frapper nos raffineries, et le volet aerien, en proposant un arret mutuel des frappes », a-t-il souligne, en reference aux declarations de Volodymyr Zelensky quant a un « moratoire energetique » et les appels du president francais Emmanuel Macron a un « double moratoire », tant sur l'energie qu'en mer Noire. Quant a ceux qui, en Europe, brandissent le spectre d'une attaque russe, « nous n'avons aucun plan de ce genre et surtout aucune raison, aucun motif d'aggraver la situation avec l'Europe », a reaffirme le president russe.

Trois sujets ont marque cette semaine : Le reamenagement technique du gouvernement intervenu le 15 septembre 2026 ; Les enjeux lies aux droits numeriques et a la lutte contre la desinformation en Afrique de l'Ouest et au Sahel ; Les preparatifs de la rentree scolaire 2026-2027 au Niger. Pour commenter et analyser ces sujets, Moctar Hamadou recoit : Maimouna Djado , journaliste independante. Abdoulaye Soumana , journaliste independant. Ousseyni Issa Djibo , journaliste.

items.title: What Do We Do About the Cameras Everywhere?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Meta has been selling millions of its camera-equipped glasses, making all of us fodder for content creation—when we’re on the street, at the store, and in our workplaces. Host Charlie Warzel talks with the Verge reporter Mia Sato about how regular people are being affected as these glasses increase in use, the backlash to Flock cameras, and what happens when we’re always being recorded. The following is a transcript of the episode: Mia Sato: I think Meta is kind of like perpetually getting in its own way. You know, it just can’t seem to figure out how to have people soften up to the company. And that’s why you see this rollout just being like a complete disaster, really. Charlie Warzel: Hey there, quick question. Is it a bad thing if people start referring to your AI-powered face computer as “pervert glasses”? I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re talking about Meta smart glasses and the slow and steady erosion of our public expectation of privacy, and whether or not Americans are actually mounting a genuine backlash to the surveillance state. Big tech companies have been trying to crack spatial and face computing for a long time. Arguably the most notable example was Google Glass, a Star Trek –looking headset that was, technologically speaking, pretty impressive, but cost about 1,500 bucks and mostly just repulsed people. The prototype program for Google Glass fizzled out, but not before I tried a pair 13 years ago, visiting Google’s headquarters one day. Google Glass may have failed, but it did produce the most cursed photograph that exists of me. Plenty have tried to make smart glasses a thing. Snapchat released its first version of its spectacles in 2016, but the product just didn’t really catch on. And that’s in part because the technology wasn’t quite there, or it was wonky or cumbersome, or there wasn’t enough memory or storage. And then, in 2021, Meta released its smart glasses. Its first collaboration was with the sunglasses company Ray-Ban. And Meta’s proposition here was that the glasses looked a lot more like actual glasses. Initially, the camera could record about 30 to 60 seconds of video, and the glasses let people listen to music or take calls, and the videos that were captured could be shared across Meta’s platforms, like Instagram and Facebook, using a special stories app. And from the launch, two things happened. First, the glasses caused a somewhat expected controversy around privacy, like all these devices tend to do. But second, the glasses were successful. People bought them. And for creators, especially, the product was something between a gimmick and a genuinely new, useful camera tool. And so Meta decided to invest in them. In 2023, they infused the glasses with AI software that allowed the glasses to describe what a user was looking at in their field of vision. Very fancy. And all the while, Meta has tried to dodge controversy, around whether the glasses will eventually deploy facial-recognition technology and over what data the company retains or uses to train its large language models. And for a while, the glasses were mostly just this. It was a curio used by creators and mostly despised by privacy advocates. But all that has really changed over the past year. In 2026, the glasses had become more popular and more prevalent, and there have been more examples of people abusing them. People filming women on the street for pickup-artist videos. Strange black markets popping up to hack cameras so that the recording light doesn’t show. And as more people wear the glasses, more people are concerned that they’re being surreptitiously recorded at sporting events, at dinner parties, at the store; maybe even being recorded while having sex. And this negative reaction, which started on social media, has spread thoroughly throughout popular culture. This summer, the late-night host Jimmy Kimmel referred to Meta’s device as “pervert glasses.” And yet the glasses keep selling. Celebrities are attaching their names and likenesses to them, and the abuses continue to pile up. And so it all seems like we are headed toward a genuine reckoning for both Meta, but all of us really. What is really going on here? Are these glasses here to stay? Are they impacting the lives of regular people? People who are just trying to go about their days and do their jobs? What happens to all of us in a world where we’re always being recorded? And crucially, what can you do if someone comes up to you on the street wearing a pair of these glasses? Mia Sato is a reporter and features writer at The Verge who has reported extensively on the ways that these glasses are upending people’s lives. What I like about her work is that it’s always situated on the ways that emerging technologies affect regular people. And so she joins me now to talk about all of this. Mia, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Sato: Thank you for having me. Warzel: So before we get into the current state of the Meta Glasses, the cameras everywhere, the panopticon world that we live in, I wanted to walk just a little bit through the history of these glasses with you. Kind of get your reaction to some of it. And this all starts on my birthday, September 9th, 2021. Facebook launches the glasses. Did you expect them to take off? I mean, this is—I’ll just put myself out there. I, at every moment with a facial wearable technology, like a camera-on-your-face kind of situation, I always expect it to fail. I mean, everyone was very excited about Apple’s Vision Pro a couple of years ago, and I was just like, I don’t think we’re ready for it yet. But like—did you expect this to be an actual product category for Meta that was gonna work, or did you sort of feel like it was destined for the same dustbin? Sato: I think at the time, and what I still believe, is that this will not be adopted in the way that Meta says it will or hopes it will. And to me, the most straightforward reason is that not everyone wants to wear glasses. Like, sometimes people don’t want something on their face. And this was kind of the thing that I couldn’t get over with the Vision Pro and other headsets and stuff is like—that’s a really big barrier to entry. Having something on your head, having something on your face that covers, you know, your hair, your makeup; like, there are all sorts of weird human things that that is just like a barrier, literally. Warzel: So I’ve picked out a couple of events here that I think are related in the history of these glasses. And the first is in 2024, Meta confirmed to TechCrunch that images and videos shared with Meta AI—for an example, the look and ask features—may be used to improve Meta’s AI models. So these glasses, you know, the input outputs are going to be used to train artificial-intelligence systems. The second is in April 2025, in an email to glasses owners, Meta said that AI features, including Meta with a camera, would be on by default—and that voice recordings would be stored by default, with no opt-out. This year, confusingly, Meta tells The Guardian that, “unless users choose to share media that they’ve captured with Meta or others, that media stays on the user’s device. And when people share content with Meta AI, we sometimes use contractors to review this data for the purpose of improving people’s experience. We take steps to filter the data and protect people’s privacy.” These feel like important revelations to me, because so much of the concern about these glasses is that they’ll be used to surveil others. But isn’t it just as important of a story how much these glasses are surveilling their owners? Sato: Totally. You are giving up an incredible amount of information about yourself and what you do every day simply by maybe wearing these glasses. And I think, you know, there’s obviously the fears around how other people—who are sort of unwitting participants in your glasses journey—how their information is being captured and stored and used later. But it’s kind of incredible to me that with this sort of back-and-forth flip-flopping, more glasses users aren’t asking, like: I just wore them all day. What do you know about my life? That’s a huge reason why I personally wouldn’t use these glasses. Because I am like—there are some things that I actually would prefer Meta not know about me. They know a lot already. But there’s some stuff that I would like to keep for myself. Warzel: Right. And so, okay, this brings us to earlier this year, February 2026. And The New York Times publishes a report that I think cast the company in as poor a light as I’ve ever seen an internal memo cast on a tech company. The story alleges that Meta is talking internally about adding facial recognition back into its glasses. And the Times gets a hold of a document from May of the previous year, which described these plans to release Name Tag, which is its codename for a facial-recognition product. They plan to release it to attendees of a conference for the blind, which the company didn’t actually do. But this was part of what they were gonna do. And there’s a line from the internal memo that made news, which is: “We will launch during a dynamic political environment, where many civil-society groups that we would expect to attack us would have their resources focused on other concerns.” That’s according to a document from Meta’s Reality Labs, which works on hardware including smart glasses. I just want, first, to get your reaction to that. Like what are people supposed to make of that? That this company that is making this stuff is hoping that people will be busy enough attending to the other horrors of the world so as not to focus on the actual product that they’re rolling out. Like—tell me what to make of that. Sato: I mean, we have so many gadgets and tech that is beyond what people could have imagined we had, right? We have computers in our phones, and that is amazing. And I think we kind of skip over the fact that the idea of glasses that can record people around you and maybe even recognize who they are is literally like the spyglasses of the kids’ movies that I watched growing up, right? Like, that’s like Spy Kids —would love to have glasses that can record your whole day, and you can ask them later what you saw. As Meta, some leaked plans have suggested Meta’s working on, or recognize the people around you. So the capability is so sci-fi, futuristic spyware that I just want to make sure we take a moment to be like: This is really crazy technology that we’re talking about. And the point about accessibility—the role of glasses in disability spaces, this is something that Meta has harped on quite a bit. And it’s true, and my colleagues at The Verge have done great work about how these tools can be used for accessibility purposes. But there’s a pattern of Meta kind of putting them into these spaces and almost trying to deflect from the larger privacy and surveillance concerns that people have, including people who are disabled. Like, disabled people also deserve privacy. So there’s a real push and pull between, like, “What can these glasses be used for?” and “What settings could we use, could we put them in?” Versus, like, “What is the worst version of how someone could use this technology?” Which is always going to be the thing that the public thinks about. Like—what danger does this pose to me, to my kids, to my life day to day? And you know, right now, a lot of the news stories that we’re reading, and the story that I wrote, was about some of the people who are doing the worst version of that. So it’s sort of like a shadow cast over Meta and this new line item that they hope will become a major part of how people interact with their company. Warzel : And this, to me, this idea of “We wanna launch during a period of time when people—but especially like, you know, civil-liberties groups—aren’t gonna be paying as much attention about this.” To say nothing of taking advantage of horrific world events or political events? It suggests that they know this is creeping people out, to some degree. That, to me, feels like they have lost in that sense the cover of saying, No, no, no—we think this is just going to be a great thing for the world. Like—everyone should want these, and they’re gonna empower people to do great things. Sato: It’s also, you know, a reality that Meta is feeling the heat for these glasses. Like they are synonymous and some people have called them “pervert glasses” or “glasses for creeps,” right? Like, the rollout is so messy. It’s such—it’s really just not a good look. And I think Meta, just even zooming out from the hardware stuff, Meta has lost a lot of public trust over the last decade, and over the last like five years. And it’s facing all of these battles. Not just that people think the glasses are creepy, but that it’s facing all these court cases. And it’s being sued by parents and states for, you know, its products and how it harms young people— Warzel: And losing— Sato : —and losing. And so this idea that, Now, let’s give this company glasses that can recognize faces, or can record your entire day and spit it back out to you. When you ask the AI questions, like, that is just a nonstarter for a lot of people. And I think Meta is kind of like perpetually getting in its own way. You know, it just can’t seem to figure out how to have people soften up to the company. And that’s why you see this rollout just being like a complete disaster, really. Warzel: So just wanna say in response to that Times report, Meta issued a statement and said, “We’re building products that help millions of people connect and enrich their lives. While we frequently hear about the interest in this type of feature”—meaning facial-recognition stuff—“and some of these products already exist in the market, we’re still thinking through options, and we’ll take a thoughtful approach if and before we roll anything out.” That was in response to the February stuff. How damaging do you think that instance was to the reputation of this gadget? Like, do you think that really stuck through to people? Like, those types of things are the reason why you have folks like Jimmy Kimmel calling these pervert glasses? Sato : Yeah, I think it’s the big part. Because, again, it’s one thing to have glasses. It’s one thing to have a phone that can record video. It’s one thing to have glasses that can record video, and it’s an entire other thing to have glasses that can scan your face and tell the wearer who you are, right? Like, it is such an escalation of the technology. And I will say that a lot of the—some discussions about this technology, you know, it can be rife with misinformation and misunderstanding. But I think this idea that, “Well, it’s only, you know, a stone’s throw away to put facial recognition in these glasses”—this seemed to sort of confirm those fears that people hold. What is the worst possible thing that these glasses could do? Well, maybe recognize—if you are a creep wearing these glasses, you can find women on the street and try to identify them, right? Like, that is sort of like the worst-case scenario, the thing that people fear the most. And when things like this leak, it sort of confirms underlying fears, or underlying assumptions that people had that had not been confirmed previously. So I think it was a major part of it. Warzel: So Meta has not released facial-recognition software. In June of this year, though, Wired reported that Meta discreetly moved to infuse facial-recognition tech into its smart glasses, as evidenced by a piece of code discovered in the Meta AI app by Wired journalists. It’s an unreleased feature. So, as we stand, they don’t have facial recognition yet. But do you think that, based off everything you just said—like the reports, the backlash—the feeling that it is, like, you know, having facial recognition is crossing the Rubicon, right? But it’s also like the killer application for this, right? As like the people who are evangelists for this product see it as, you know, this sort of sci-fi endgame, right? Of being able to look all this stuff up, to have the computer on your face that can really process and index all this information. Like, do you think that it’s coming for these glasses? Or do you think that it’s like a bridge too far right now, ’cause it’s like the No. 1 thing that also creeps people out? Sato: Yeah. I mean, it’s hard to say, because I know Meta comms and PR people were really getting into it over the Wired story. They were really upset about it. But there’s a reason they’re working on it. You know, and it’s hard to put that aside. It is clearly, I think, a bridge too far for a lot of people, for a lot of the public. Even the glasses themselves seem to be a bridge too far. And we can talk a little bit about how, after my story, the reaction was so unified in a way that I have not seen for many pieces that I’ve written. People hate it. And so if you’re Meta looking at, you know, the reaction to the glasses themselves and then sort of the uproar with the facial recognition, you have to slow the roll a little bit. So it doesn’t surprise me that they tried to sort of weasel out of it a little bit—like, This is not shipped . Like, you know, we work on things all the time. But at the same time, it is something in development. And there have been other leaks about what type of capabilities they might envision the glasses being infused with. So like one, I believe the Financial Times reported about always-on smart glasses where they’re not actively, you know, capturing video with the privacy light that they have right now—but that every couple seconds they’re taking a photo, and they’re capturing audio. And you can query Meta AI and say, like, you know, What was that restaurant that I walked by earlier? So these are all things that the company is thinking about that they might consider releasing in the future. So yeah; I don’t know. I think the question is more like: When will Meta read the room that this is all too much for for a lot of people? Warzel : Yeah. The idea of taking the photo every few seconds, I mean, that just feels like the largest possible data liability that a company could possibly present itself with. Just especially with—I think some people think of these two as like sunglasses, right? And obviously they make Meta sunglasses, through Ray-Ban, through Oakley, other people. But also, some of these are just clear-frame glasses that, like, people have on all the time, right? Sato: Yeah. Yep. Warzel: So, okay. These glasses have been out in the world for a while. A lot of creators, a lot of normal people, are using them in honestly pretty expected ways, right? And then there’s the creepy stuff. And a lot of that has really come out over the last year. So how, in your reporting and stuff you’ve come across, how are people abusing them? Sato: It’s really weird. They will wear the glasses. Like, some bad actors, let’s say, will wear the glasses into a store and harass the workers who are working there. They might sort of be recording them without the person realizing, and they’re pulling some sort of prank. I use the word prank really loosely. It’s not funny, which is a big problem. But you know, they might ask the price of an item over and over and over. And the person will answer; the worker will answer. And they’ll be like, Well, no, I’m saying: What is the price? What is the price of the item? And this goes on for minutes. They might pretend to be like a rude employee where they’re like getting in the way of other customers, just to get that reaction. And so it makes the worker the butt of the joke. So there’s that genre, right? Harassing people while they’re at their job, and they can’t say no. Warzel: And this is the reporting that you just did for The Verge where you went and spoke with a number of people who have had these exact instances, right? That happened to one of the people you spoke with. What ended up happening there? Like, what was the fallout from that? Sato: So the worker that I spoke with that this happened to went home after their shift. They were obviously very shaken up, and one of their bosses found these videos on social media, posted to social media on TikTok and Instagram. And combined, these videos had more than half a million views. They were, you know, viral by a lot of people’s standards. And they were trying to sort of get them removed. Finally, when I reached out to Meta and asked about them, they removed the entire Instagram profile that had, you know, done these videos. But it sort of creates, you know, a heightened fear, a new fear for workers where they could go into their job and try to help a customer and end up being in a video where they are taken advantage of for content. And Meta—I should say that Meta says that type of content is not allowed on its platforms. It doesn’t want secret recordings of people. It doesn’t want videos that are harassing of people. And so when I asked the company about it, they did say it violated their bullying and harassment policy. But this type of content is very easy to find online. Warzel: The prank genre is a staple here. Can I—I wanna keep on this. Because the story that you wrote for The Verge about this, obviously, as you said, it really resonated with lots of people. But what were some of the other examples? Because I think it’s really helpful to have them out there, these individual use cases. Sato: Yeah. There are some more I guess relatively innocuous worker examples; I spoke with workers. So one person works at a very touristy place in Seattle. And she is a young woman and said the adoption of these glasses just skyrocketed, very quickly. It was like she was seeing these glasses every day, multiple times a day, and now she says she sees like 10 people an hour come into her workplace wearing Meta Glasses. And it’s a touristy place, so there’s always been recording. But now she kind of described it to me as like, You can tell that they’re wearing glasses, and sometimes you can tell that they’re recording. But you can’t really tell what they’re recording, because, you know, it’s eye level. So they’ll be looking around, but what they’re capturing is much broader than just exactly where they’re looking. And she hasn’t been harassed, but she was like: I’m a shorter woman, and when men come in wearing them and record me, they’re looking down at me. And it really feels like they’re looking down my shirt—that they’re recording down my shirt. So there’s this general sense of like—I don’t know what this video is being used for. Are they gonna make a vlog about it? Are they gonna put it in their food review or, you know, tour or vacation blog? Like, who knows? But I all I know is that I’m in a bunch of people’s videos, and I find that really weird. Warzel: I think when we talk about these glasses, the idea of surveillance is this amorphous concept, right? You’re filming people without their consent. But there’s a piece in your story where you write that, in the case of these businesses, store employees are also handling sensitive data at their jobs, right? And this includes things like customers’ names, email addresses, credit-card information. And it strikes me that—I mean, this is obvious, but like surveillance is about so much more than people, right? It is also about everything else that is being consumed, and whether that is for, you know, either public consumption or a stranger’s consumption. What else aren’t we thinking about when it comes to the fallout of these cameras just being everywhere? Sato: I think that this is sort of maybe a drier fallout, but like—the liability that so many people are opening themselves and their employers and everyone else up to when you have a camera attached to your face. So like one of the examples I include in the story is a woman who was working at a grocery store. And her boss came in one day wearing Meta Glasses, and she was very worried obviously about the safety of customers—if they were being recorded by these glasses. Or you know, kids coming in. But a big part was: You are handling customers’ credit cards. You know you can, in their loyalty program, you can see their name and their email address and their phone number, and stuff like that. And so I think a big sort of underappreciated part of this is that when you have glasses attached to people’s faces, you are collecting a lot of data that you probably are not supposed to be collecting. And a privacy and law expert was kind of saying to me, like—the more you collect, the greater the risk is of leaks and misuse. Right. You are just opening yourself up to so much potential liability. That the store, you know, without a specific policy against these glasses, is just kind of throwing your hands up and saying, like, Yeah, my workers can wear these . And it’s just like—are you thinking about how to explain to customers down the line if there is a data breach, if there is a leak on Meta’s side, that their credit-card information is in that too? Warzel: Amidst all of this, Meta announced this summer, as you alluded to there, that it’s gonna ban some of that content that’s filmed with the company smart glasses on Instagram. And you wrote a piece arguing: “Meta just created a moderation nightmare for its smart glasses.” Walk me through why it’s a moderation nightmare. Sato: A lot of content on the internet depends on taking advantage of other people. And it’s unfortunate, and it’s not fair, and that is the way it is. And you know, when Meta first announced, like: We won’t allow these worker-harassment pranks —or like, another genre of Meta Glasses content is men going up to women and trying to do pickup lines on them to see how they react. Meta said: We don’t want this on Instagram. We don’t want this on on Facebook. Warzel: Cool. Sato: But the reality is that, even without the glasses, this type of content was being created. And it was abusive and harassment then, too. But Meta was, you know, like—all that content exists everywhere. And I think about all of the different environments where someone is being recorded without their knowledge. One example that I immediately thought of was like the people who walk through homeless encampments, or, you know, areas where there’s maybe open drug use, and they record it. Sort of almost like—it’s a very extractive type of content, where you’re making it for people to gawk at. And that type of content, as far as I can tell, is allowed on these platforms, because I see it all the time. And if we are taking a stand against content that takes advantage of other people, or records them without their consent or their knowledge, surely a lot more will fall under this category. And I don’t really see any evidence that Meta is taking action on that. In fact, even the content that explicitly they said they would remove, like the pranks, it took a random tech reporter to ask the company about it to ban this account that had hundreds of thousands of followers, and hundreds of thousands of views. So, you know, my argument there with the moderation question is: Where is the line for so much other content, other than the couple that we’ve raised? What is allowed, and what isn’t? Because in some ways, a big part of social media is recording people without their consent. It’s like a massive—you know, recording Karens or like ”People of Walmart,” right? To use a throwback. A lot of content is about strangers. And you never go up and say, “Hey, do you wanna be in my video?” You’re just taking photos; you’re just taking recordings of them. And so I found that moderation decision really interesting. To me, it read more like: Don’t make us look bad on our own platforms by using these glasses that are already incredibly unpopular. Don’t put the bad stuff on Instagram. Warzel: What was Meta’s response to this reporting that you’ve done recently around these glasses? Sato : They have given the same canned answer to a lot of reporters who have written stories about Meta Glasses and their misuse. Meta basically told me, you know, we have built privacy into these glasses from the ground up. They have the LED light that indicates when it’s recording, right, like on the lenses. And they also said that they had been banning certain hashtags from being recommended that are like associated with the content. So like #riz, you know, for these pickup-line videos, or #coldapproach, I think, was another hashtag that they said that they had kind of blocked. And of course they did say, you know, We’re taking down this content; we’ve taken down thousands of pieces of this content; and we’ve banned big accounts with millions of followers who had been posting this content. So, you know, their response to a lot of the criticisms or the reporting is often like: Well, there is this LED privacy light built into them, and we take it seriously. And they’ve made certain software updates where if the camera detects that you’ve covered the light, supposedly it will stop recording. I think, you know, it’s a rolling update, so maybe it’s not applied to all glasses right now. And people are obviously always trying to find ways around it. But they’ve tried to make it so you can’t tamper with the light, so that people don’t know when you’re recording. Warzel: It seems like a bit of an arms race, right? Because there’s been reporting in places like The Guardian and other outlets that follow people who run businesses essentially that help, you know, jailbreak these devices, right? To disable the red light, which obviously is against Meta’s terms of service. That’s not what they want people to use, but I think it’s worth noting here that there’s just like this entire economy built around trying to make these even more surreptitious than they already are. You know, what really strikes me about what you’re reporting on this subject is that Meta has created essentially a first- and second-order problem, right? In the first, they’ve done arguably more than any other company to create this culture of social-media clout and engagement chasing: the pranks and other things for views, this whole content-creation ecosystem. Like, they didn’t set the terms of that at Meta, but Facebook is the OG social network, right? They helped build that world that we’re all living in, the content landscape. And then they drop this product into it—a product that is tailor made for these types of creators and these types of people, to be used in these environments. And they’re now using it to turn people’s lives into content in a way that’s even more focused than, you know, the camera phone. And I’m curious, like: Where’s this all going? Like, what is the end goal here for Meta with these things? Sato: Well, I think—you know, Meta is an ads business. So presumably, the more information they have about what you do all day and what you see all day, the better their targeted ads will get. I assume that they’re thinking about how to monetize this. The other thing is like Meta—for as central as it’s been to social media for 20 years—in recent years, they’ve also really been playing catch-up, right? Like, TikTok changed the game, and Meta changed its business around TikTok. And so what Meta has always been concerned about is scale. It has more users in TikTok, more content. And what it needs is people on its platform in different ways. And I think there’s sort of a catering to that type of creator. Creators who can amass views, even if people don’t really like their content or, you know, people find it sort of morally objectionable. And so I think, you know, there’s a reason why creators were some of the first people to adopt these glasses. Because who else is recording all day? Who else is recording their interactions? The people that do use them, it creates a frictionlessness for content creation. And so I, you know, have to assume that a big part of these glasses is that they want creators livestreaming, for example, right? Like, streaming is a huge part of the online ecosystem. Ads, obviously, I assume they’re working on ways to incorporate that, or to try to monetize it in the future. And it’s strange, because I think it is really butting up against a real social backlash around being watched. And I think it’s interesting that, you know, this is happening at the same time when there’s like nationwide outrage over Flock cameras. I think these two are intrinsically related. You know, they’re coming from the same frustration of the feeling that you cannot escape the grips or the eyes of these huge, behemoth tech companies. And so yeah; I’m curious at what point Meta, you know, sort of decides to go all in or to pare things back. Like, it wouldn’t be the first time that Meta tried something and then it didn’t work, right? Its namesake was a complete flop, the Metaverse. At what point do they sort of feel the public outcry is too much to bear? I think they’re obviously taking a pretty defensive posture and trying to assuage some of these fears, but there’s sort of an incompatibility that I see between the public reaction and Meta’s plans. Warzel: There’s a lot I wanna unpack there. I think before we get into a little more of the broader backlash against surveillance, you know, we have: This summer Meta announced announces its new line of glasses, and Kylie Jenner is the face of that campaign. And there’s a line from Taylor Lorenz, a tech reporter who writes a Substack. She wrote this July: “Influencers are declaring a hot surveillance summer. West Village fashion girlies are posting AI glasses selfies, and for thousands of people, cameras on your face have officially gone from creepy to chic.” And I’m curious if that is, in your understanding, a bit of a micro-phenomenon thing, something that’s already burned out. Like, are these glasses actually popular? Are non-influencer types wearing them? I mean, my understanding is that they’re hard to keep in stock, you know, and Meta has sold millions of pairs of glasses. Like it’s hard to deny, and they’re the market leader, right? Like when you talk about smart glasses, it’s Meta. Sato: I think, you know, the example of the West Village girlies wearing the Kylie Jenner glasses. That was actually kind of smart on Meta’s part, because they made the glasses cute. Like, not everyone wants to wear the classic Ray-Ban shape, and the sort of design element was a step up. I guess I would question whether that is just an isolated phenomenon in these small pockets of types of creators, versus like—I don’t know that they’re convincing their followers to go out and buy them, which is sort of the whole point. A lot of the influencer marketing with these glasses; they sent them to influencers. And I had seen a few videos of even content creators that I follow, and the comments are not good. You know what I mean? Like, their followers are mad at them for taking a Meta Glasses brand deal. So I think it’s sort of hard to gauge. Meta obviously wants it to be part of your work life, your social life. You know, just going around listening to music. They talk a lot about, like, you can listen to music too, and take calls and stuff. But I do think this is kind of the direction that tech companies are thinking. Apple, you know—there’s been leaks of Apple working on earbuds that have cameras on them. Which, if glasses were a problem, earbuds will really make people upset. So it’s definitely a trend that other companies are wading into. I just wonder, you know, how long people have the energy to be upset and to push back on it. Warzel: In keeping with this idea of the backlash, you mentioned it—I think everyone really feels that the Flock cameras, right? These, you know, their license-plate scanners. They’re taking photos; they’ve attracted a lot of attention. Some vandalism, a lot of news stories. In part because of reports that police officers are using them to follow or harass people in their lives, but also just because people are getting, like, dogged with tickets in their neighborhood, or just feeling like these things are showing up everywhere. And like, you know, where’s this information going? The vibes are so bad around the glasses that ICE recently barred the camera glasses from the force. And I mean, if you’ve lost ICE, where are we there? So we’re in this moment of the backlash. But why do you think that is? Because we’ve had license-plate scanners before; the glasses have actually been around for a while. Like, what do you feel like has changed in recent months, or in the last year, around this broader trend of surveillance, and people really having their, you know, spidey senses open to it? Sato: I do think it’s hard to disentangle it from the Trump administration. And this idea of, you know, a hostile presidency and the various ways that it’s watching what people do. And, you know, watching how people live their lives, and who’s here and who’s not, and your comings and goings. And, you know, tracking migrants and immigrants. And so I think already, people are primed to be fearful of being watched. The other part, if I could connect it to the social-media side, is like: We’re now, you know, several decades into the content machine. And it’s really ramped up in the last, you know, since COVID, when everyone was stuck at home. And I think people are kind of sick of being fodder for someone. In the case of Meta Glasses wearers, you know, people are sick of being like the background characters to the influencers’ main-character life, right? Like, We don’t want to be in the background of your videos. We don’t want you to record us and then post us online. And so I think part of it is like a backlash to influencers and to content creators as well, that you can kind of see percolating and bubbling up in other spaces. So I think there’s sort of a confluence of different things. And a lot of it is, you know, they’re mad at content creators who are then monetizing the content as they harass people, or, you know, as they try to pick up women and hit on them. Warzel: I think that’s such an excellent point about just the fatigue—people being tired of being fodder for these people. But what do you think all this is doing to us who are living in this world where we’ve genuinely, at this point, lost the expectation of privacy? You know—you hear stories of kids that are afraid to dance at school dances. They’re afraid of being filmed. People are like, I don’t really want to go on a date . I saw, I think it was a New York Post thing where there were just like two people kissing on a bench, and it turned into a story. What is it doing to us that we’re now living in this world with no expectation of privacy? Sato: It really makes us all into punishers. I hate the feeling of, you know, quantifying every moment of everyone’s life in order to find something scandalous or objectionable, or something you disagree with, or even just like don’t like. And I think, you know, it’s interesting that the glasses and the content from the glasses is coming now—at a time when people are really used to seeing strangers who are not public figures, who are not celebrities, who are not journalists or politicians talking on their screen. And the sort of rise of short-form video, where all you have to do is do a selfie video, and there’s a potential for it to get millions of views. That really creates an environment where a face on the screen is just that. You don’t sort of see them as just another private individual, because now they’ve chosen to make a video. And this idea that, you know, every moment of our lives should be up for consumption, should be up for criticism, should be available for people to comment on. We really sort of created those conditions over the last five years since TikTok. I don’t know; it’s dark. It’s not a healthy society where you, like, see two people kissing or whatever in the park and think, Who are they cheating on? It’s not good to see a woman in public and say, Ooh, she would make a good video . Right? Like, that’s a really dehumanizing way to think about your fellow humans. So yeah—we’ve been barreling toward this for a while. And I think, you know, the glasses just sort of supercharge it. And a lot of people also—I should say, some people—seem to find this content funny. Some people like it. And that is also kind of—well, they’ve learned that behavior over the last several years. Warzel: What it reminds me of is—as social media, text-based social media started to curdle, right? Like, I think about being on Twitter and just seeing people start to become the worst versions of themselves, and like picking people apart in very specific ways. And, you know. What I feel like you’re describing, which is real, and what video-based social media has done, as well as all these, you know, surveillance tools is—it’s basically taken that, and it’s ported it like into the reality of your actual physical life. Like, you in physical space, right? And there’s no way to separate that. This is you kissing on a park bench. Like, that’s just who you are. You can’t distance yourself from that. And that, to me, feels like that is like a rot. Like if we don’t eradicate that somehow, it gets dark real fast. Sato: Yeah. We should remember, too, that TikTok describes itself as an entertainment platform, not a social-media platform. I think about this with social platforms trying to move more and more into trying to get people to watch their content on a television, not on their phone. Like, YouTube is big on this. Instagram is saying it wants you to watch, like, Reels on TV. But you can see how people start to think that this is closer to a television show or like a reality-TV show, or a movie, rather than a post that a random person made one day. And that blurring of those lines, I think, contributes to it. Also the fact that like TikTok stars have gone on to become celebrities in their own way. And they just started as a teen girl in her room doing dances. So the way that people consume this is not like—there’s a random Twitter account who posted something embarrassing, or posted something that people are dunking on. Now it’s become: I see this person as entertainment, because the platform that I found them on is an entertainment platform. Warzel : To bring it slightly back to the glasses, I keep asking you a variation of a question of: Where does it all lead? And what we’re describing here, in some ways, is like a breaking of the social contract, right? A technologically enabled breaking of the social contract. And tech regulation is, in general, a rat’s nest, right? It’s very difficult. It’s always notoriously behind. But when we think about where we go with this—as a society that is kinda fed up with this but also has to deal with it—do you think the answer here ends up being regulatory? Or does it end up being cultural? Like, again, go back to Google Glass, when society’s like, Nope, not today. Sorry, we’re just not doing that. You look weird. Sato: Yeah. Warzel : Or third option—is this an example of these companies just steamrolling people? Like, where they’re dropping it into the world, forcing us to deal with it. Even if a lot of people are like, I don’t like what this is doing. I’m curious how you think about the next steps here. Sato: Yeah, I think a really straightforward sort of way to fence this in that doesn’t require regulators is, like, private businesses saying: You can’t wear these here . Which is something that is, you know, not that strange. We’re used to entering environments under rules that are not laws. Like, there’s no law that you can’t wear sneakers at this nice restaurant. It’s just a policy that they enforce. Warzel: Right. Sato: So if private businesses say, Well, you can’t record here anyway. You can’t do videography here anyway. So we can’t take the risk with you wearing these glasses here. I mean, that’s something that any private business can just, you know—that’s a rule that they can send down tomorrow. And in the case of my story, I think a lot of these incidents could have been avoided if there were clearer rules. But because it’s emerging tech, there’s a lot of gray area, and like things being sussed out still. You know, I’m not advocating for anyone to do this, but a really common response that I saw in the comments of my story was people just straightforwardly saying, If I see these glasses, I’m gonna take them off your face and like step on them . Which, a lot of it might be internet posturing. But also, that is a big way of people enforcing norms in society; like, I’m going to hurt you , or I’m going to, like, socially shun you . Warzel: Right. Shame. Sato: Because I don’t like this thing . So I think that’s definitely a big part of it. And some people actually did—I did see comments that said, like, I bought these glasses for a trip with my family, but because of all the bad actors recently, I’ve just felt really weird wearing them. So I don’t wear them anymore. So that is definitely an example of that sort of, like, reining it in through social pressure. Warzel: I thought maybe a way to end this would be, as long as these are out in the world, people do have to deal with them. They do have to come up with the norms, or what have you. And I was listening to a Verge podcast that you were on, where you fielded a very memorable question from a listener about how to use or not use these glasses consensually in the bedroom. And also fears that if he purchased these glasses, Meta might end up with a lot of footage of him using the bathroom, which he didn’t want. But he also really wanted the glasses. And I thought your advice was reasonably sound. So I wanted to ask you, just as we wrap up here, some of your thoughts—like, guideline-etiquette rules for using these glasses or encountering these glasses in the wild. And so I guess, first up, even if you disagree with the fact that someone has purchased these in general, what’s your etiquette advice for people when it comes to using them around other people, out in the world? Sato: Well, I think, if you’re with your friends, it depends on the setting, I guess. But I would say maybe let people know. Just say, you know: I’m wearing these glasses; I’m not recording; I’m not doing anything with them. You know what I mean? Warzel: Sounds like a super-cool thing to do at a party. Hey guys, I’m wearing these glasses. Sato: I know. Informed consent when you hang out with your friends. But that’s another part of this—like, these glasses really are a hindrance. Because who wants to say: Just so you know, I’m wearing these glasses that a lot of you really hate. But, like, I’m not doing the thing that you really hate. So don’t worry. But you know, I would probably say you should let people know. Because I think a lot of the bristling comes from the fact that people are realizing after the fact. Like: Wait a minute; are those Meta Glasses? And then it becomes a problem. Obviously, like don’t cover the light. That’s really creepy. That’s really weird and strange, strange thing to do. And I get that, you know, it’s useful for other things; like, some people really like listening to music that way. I get it. But you have to be sort of prepared for people to push back on it. Which I think is like—you know, that’s something that you don’t have to do if you have normal glasses. Warzel: This wonderfully brings us to the last question, which is: If you see them out in the wild, and you feel like somebody might be up in your space, possibly filming you or just making you a little uncomfortable, what is your advice—having talked to a lot of these people and reporting on these situations? What’s your advice for somebody who finds themselves in that situation? Sato: Yeah, I will say my understanding is that if you get close enough and say, Hey Meta, stop recording , it could work. There, the users can disable the voice-activation setting where it’s like, that doesn’t work. But it responds to any voice, not just the wearer’s voice. So if you think someone is recording—like, you see the light on the glasses on—you could try getting right up to them. And say, Hey Meta, stop recording , to see if that works. It might not always, but may be worth a shot if you really are feeling harassed. Warzel: Hey Meta, delete my account. Just unplug the servers. Sato : Hey Meta, forget I exist . Warzel: Jeez. Mia, thank you so much for coming on Galaxy Brain to talk about this. And thank you for your reporting, which I think has really shown the human impact of all this technology in the world. Thank you for all your work. Sato: Yeah; my pleasure. Warzel: If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, or on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work, and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. This episode of Galaxy Brain was produced by Hadley Robinson; the video was edited by Denny Thomas; and the audio was engineered by Miguel Carrascal. Our theme is by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Learn more about your ad choices. items.title: Commune de Bignona : une quarantaine d’arbres dangereux abattus
items.description: 42 arbres à risques sont abattus et ont servi à fabriquer 550 tables-bancs dédiés aux établissements scolaires de la commune. BIGNONA – Au total, 37 arbres sont abattus et 5 autres élagués, soit au total 42 arbres dans la commune de Bignona. Il s’agissait d’arbres centenaires qui menaçaient la quiétude des populations. Ces arbres sont transformés en tables-bancs réfectionnés gratuitement par les acteurs de la chaîne de valeur, notamment les exploitants forestiers, les menuisiers, les soudeurs qui ont accompagné le processus par leurs propres moyens au bénéfice de 11 écoles élémentaires et 3 collèges de la commune. Même les commerçants ont participé à travers l’achat de la peinture. « Dans ce contexte de rentrée scolaire, ce dont vient répondre à notre déficit en tables-bancs estimé à 690 tables-bancs », a magnifié Boubacar Konaté, Inspecteur de l’éducation et de la formation (IEF) de Bignona 2 vendredi à la réunion de restitution des travaux des opérations d’abattage et d’élagage d’arbres menaçant chute dans la commune de Bignona. Les communes de Djibidione et Oulampane, zones de retour des déplacés du conflit en Casamance, ont aussi bénéficié à raison de 20 tables-bancs chacune. Au total, 550 tables-bancs sont confectionnées et seront livrées dans les 10 prochains jours. Un déficit de tables-bancs noté dans la commune « Dès demain, les opérations de montage vont démarrer dans les 14 établissements qui ont bénéficié de ces tables-bancs », a indiqué Boubacar Konaté. Avec ce don, le déficit est réduit à 140 tables-bancs pour la commune. De leur côté, les soudeurs se sont engagés à aller monter les tables-bancs partout où elles seront destinées, y compris au niveau des lointaines communes de Djibidione et Oulampane. La mairie de Bignona, qui est à l'origine de l'initiative d’abattage des arbres, s'est engagée à reboiser les axes et lieux concernés par l’opération d’abattage et d’élagage des vieux cailcédrats. « Nous allons mettre des caïlcédrats par endroits mais aussi nous allons choisir d’autres espèces avec l’encadrement des eaux et forêts », a déclaré le maire de Bignona, Bacary Diatta. A lire aussi : Bignona : un élan communautaire pour restaurer 10 hectares de mangrove Mamadou Khouma, préfet du département de Bignona, a salué l’engagement citoyen et communautaire des exploitants forestiers, des menuisiers, des soudeurs qui ont aussi décidé de réparer gratuitement toutes les carcasses de tables-bancs. « Il y a un engagement communautaire. Même pour la distribution de ces tables-bancs, il y a une solidarité départementale parce que les arbres sont abattus dans la commune de Bignona, mais on va donner une part à Djibidione et Oulampane pour accompagner ces deux communes où il y a des villages de retour, de nouvelles créations », a dit magnifié le préfet. Kadidiatou SONKO (Correspondante)

Ouagadougou: un réseau clandestin de fabrication et de reconditionnement de boissons alcoolisées démasqué
items.description: La police municipale de Ouagadougou a démasqué un réseau clandestin de fabrication et de reconditionnement de boissons alcoolisées et interpellé des individus pour la suite de l’investigation, selon une information de la structure, ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026. Le mardi 22 septembre 2026, suite à une dénonciation, la Direction de la Sécurité Publique (DSP) a mené une intervention dans l’arrondissement n°06 de la Commune de Ouagadougou, visant un réseau présumé impliqué dans des activités clandestines de fabrication et de reconditionnement de boissons alcoolisées au sein d’une cour. Selon le texte de la Police municipale, les vérifications effectuées sur les lieux ont notamment permis de constater la présence de différentes boissons alcoolisées, dont du pastis, faisant l’objet d’un procédé présumé de fabrication et/ou de reconditionnement. Ce qui les a amenés à saisir «environ 500 bouteilles de boissons, ainsi que des fûts, des cartons contenant des boissons et divers matériels utilisés dans le processus » au cours de l’intervention. « Des personnes ont également été interpellées pour les besoins de la procédure», indique la source. Après avoir remercié les populations pour leur vigilance et leur collaboration, la Police municipale les encourage «à poursuivre la dénonciation de tout fait ou comportement susceptible de porter atteinte à la sécurité, à la salubrité et à la santé publiques» au N° Vert : 80 00 11 03 ou bien au contact WhatsApp: 70 00 83 41 pour des messages uniquement. Par Wakat Séra L’article Ouagadougou: un réseau clandestin de fabrication et de reconditionnement de boissons alcoolisées démasqué est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

L’ONU et Macky Sall : le Sénégal peut-il parler au-delà de ses divisions ?
items.description: Le soutien du président Bassirou Diomaye Faye à la candidature de l’ex-président Macky Sall au poste de secrétaire général des Nations unies pose une question qui dépasse les deux hommes : un État peut-il défendre une ambition internationale issue de son histoire politique alors que cette histoire demeure profondément débattue dans le pays ? Dans le cas du Sénégal, la question est sensible. Le président Bassirou Diomaye Faye est arrivé au pouvoir à la faveur d’une alternance nourrie de critiques profondes sur la gouvernance précédente. Ces critiques ne perdent ni leur légitimité ni leur importance parce que les autorités actuelles ont décidé de soutenir une candidature internationale. Les citoyens restent libres d’apprécier le bilan de l’ex-président Macky Sall, d’interroger les décisions prises sous sa présidence et de demander que les responsabilités éventuelles soient établies. Le soutien de l’État ne vaut pas conclusion sur ces questions. Il faut donc déterminer exactement ce que ce soutien change. Les autorités sénégalaises engagent désormais la diplomatie du pays en faveur de la candidature de Macky Sall. Elles ne parlent pas à la place de tous les Sénégalais, dont les jugements peuvent diverger. Elles donnent toutefois aux autres États une indication claire : le pays que Macky Sall a dirigé accepte aujourd’hui de défendre sa candidature devant les Nations unies. Dans une sélection où la confiance entre États compte autant que le parcours individuel, cette décision a une portée réelle. Elle ne préjuge pas du résultat. Cette distinction permet d’examiner deux questions qui se croisent sans se confondre. Quel jugement porter sur les années de pouvoir de Macky Sall ? Et quelles aptitudes présente-t-il pour diriger une organisation internationale ? Son parcours national fait nécessairement partie de la seconde appréciation. Il doit pouvoir être discuté dans toutes ses dimensions. Mais l’évaluation d’une candidature demande aussi d’étudier l’expérience diplomatique du candidat, sa conception de la fonction et sa capacité à travailler avec des États aux intérêts divergents. Sur ce terrain, la candidature de Macky Sall présente un intérêt à examiner. Douze années à la tête du Sénégal, puis l’exercice de la présidence de l’Union africaine, l’ont placé au contact de dossiers où les préoccupations africaines rencontrent les décisions prises à l’échelle mondiale : la dette, la sécurité alimentaire, les crises régionales, le financement du développement ou encore la transition énergétique. Son parcours l’a confronté aux contraintes d’États qui doivent négocier avec les grandes puissances tout en répondant aux attentes de leurs populations. Ces fonctions ne démontrent pas, à elles seules, qu’il serait le meilleur secrétaire général. Elles permettent de poser une question plus précise : quelle méthode Macky Sall a-t-il tirée de cette expérience, et comment entendrait-il la mettre au service de tous les membres de l’ONU ? Un secrétaire général doit pouvoir dialoguer avec les puissances sans être perçu comme leur porte-parole. Il doit entendre les pays moins influents sans réduire sa mission à la défense d’un groupe régional. Il doit chercher des possibilités d’accord lorsque les États ne partagent ni les mêmes intérêts ni la même lecture des crises. C’est à cette exigence que chaque candidature doit être confrontée. Dans une précédente contribution, je demandais si le monde avait besoin d’un secrétaire général venu d’Afrique. La question mérite toujours d’être posée, à condition de ne pas lui donner une réponse automatique. L’Afrique a une expérience particulière des inégalités de pouvoir, des effets de la dette, des conflits et des médiations. Cette expérience peut enrichir la réflexion sur l’avenir du multilatéralisme. Mais l’origine d’un candidat ne constitue ni un programme ni un titre à exercer la fonction. Sa valeur dépend de sa capacité à transformer une connaissance située du monde en une responsabilité véritablement universelle. Il serait également prématuré de confondre l’appui du Sénégal avec un consensus africain. Les États du continent peuvent apprécier différemment les candidatures et les priorités de l’organisation. S’ils souhaitent peser dans ce choix, ils devront débattre des qualités attendues du prochain secrétaire général et rechercher les accords qu’ils jugent possibles. La décision finale dépendra, elle, des équilibres propres aux Nations unies. Le soutien sénégalais donne à la candidature de Macky Sall une assise diplomatique plus claire ; il ne garantit aucune désignation. Le Sénégal peut-il alors parler au-delà de ses divisions ? Oui, si cela signifie prendre une position internationale sans exiger que les citoyens renoncent à leurs désaccords. Non, si l’on prétendait que cette position règle le débat sur le passé. Le geste du président Bassirou Diomaye Faye prend sa force dans cette limite même : il permet à l’État de défendre une candidature, tandis que l’appréciation de l’homme, de son parcours et de son projet pour l’ONU demeure ouverte. C’est dans cette liberté d’examen que le débat peut gagner en maturité. Par Khadiyatoulah Fall, professeur émérite

items.title: Coopération Togo-Russie : Lomé abrite la première session de la commission intergouvernementale à partir du 29 septembre prochain
items.description: Lomé, 25 sept. (ATOP) – La première session de la commission mixte intergouvernementale chargée du suivi de l’Accord de partenariat entre le Togo et la Fédération de Russie se tiendra du 29 septembre au 1 er octobre à Lomé. La rencontre permettra aux deux pays d’évaluer l’état de leur coopération et d’identifier de nouvelles pistes de partenariat. Prévue au Palais des congrès de Lomé, la session réunira les représentants des deux pays autour de l’examen des acquis de leur partenariat et de la définition de nouvelles perspectives de coopération. Elle intervient dans un contexte d’élargissement des relations bilatérales entre Lomé et Moscou. Les échanges porteront notamment sur le commerce, l’économie, les sciences, la culture et les technologies, avec une attention particulière aux échanges entre les opérateurs économiques des deux pays. Sur le plan universitaire, les discussions devraient également contribuer au renforcement du partenariat existant, notamment dans le domaine de la formation des étudiants togolais en Russie. La coopération universitaire et culturelle avait déjà été au centre des échanges, début septembre à Lomé, entre une délégation russe du Centre de diplomatie publique (CDP), conduite par Valentina Kolesnikova, et le ministre délégué chargé de l’Enseignement supérieur, le Professeur Gado Tchangbedji. Dans le cadre de la diversification des relations universitaires et culturelles, la création d’une « Maison Russe » à Lomé est envisagée. Cette structure devrait notamment contribuer à promouvoir l’apprentissage de la langue et la découverte de la culture russes au Togo. ATOP/HKM/AO
